Title: The Fed raised rates. What comes next?
Article_Text:
After four months of talking tough about inflation, Kevin Warsh finally followed through.
On Wednesday, the chair of the Federal Reserve announced with his colleagues that the central bank had raised interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point to a new range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent.
The move was widely expected, with financial markets ascribing over 90 percent odds to an increase before the gathering. The question now is what comes next.
Warsh, in an abridged news conference, sought to keep the Fed’s options open. He underscored his aversion to providing guidance about what the future path of policy might be and said plainly that he did not want to “prejudge any future decisions we make.”
But in parsing through Warsh’s comments Wednesday, and a new set of economic projections from officials that accompanied the rate decision, it was clear that the Fed was not done raising rates.
The most direct signal came from the updated “dot plot,” which aggregates on a quarterly basis what officials think will happen to borrowing costs over the coming years.
It showed that 16 of the 18 policymakers who submitted projections expected at least one more quarter-point move by the end of the year. That would push rates to a range of 4 percent to 4.25 percent. Most wanted rates to stay at or above that level throughout 2027. They also raised their estimates for rates for 2028 and beyond compared with three months ago.
Warsh, as in June, did not submit projections, in keeping with his opposition to the dot plot as a communications tool. But he appeared aligned with the message that the Fed’s work was not complete.
Warsh struck an upbeat tone about economic growth and the labor market, emphasizing that the Fed’s focus had to be on inflation at this juncture. He emphasized the unanimity around the rate decision, which he said showed “we’re serious about this.” And he made clear that he was unsatisfied with the recent trend in the data that showed lackluster progress toward the 2 percent inflation goal.
The comment that garnered the most attention, however, was his description of Wednesday’s move as the Fed having “removed a dose of accommodation so that financial and credit conditions would be more consistent with our ultimate objectives.”
That gave the impression that Warsh did not believe the Fed’s policy settings were weighing meaningfully on the economy and instead were bolstering it, conveying a more hawkish message than expected.
He was later asked how this related to his views of the “neutral” policy setting that neither spurs growth nor subdues it -- a concept that is often used by Fed officials when describing their rate outlooks. Warsh suggested that this “academic” framing had no bearing on Wednesday’s decision.
Without a sense of how Warsh saw the policy rate relative to an estimate of the neutral rate, economists and investors were left guessing how many more increases the chair believed were necessary to quell inflation.
In the absence of a specific steer, the consensus view is that the Fed will raise rates a couple of more times through the early part of 2027. Patrick Harker, who served as president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia for a decade-long tenure that ended in 2025, said he expected the Fed to reverse cuts that it delivered late last year to guard against a weakening labor market. That would suggest two additional moves, for a total 0.75 percentage-point increase in rates.
Raising rates just before the midterms would further anger President Trump, who criticized the Fed for taking action Wednesday. Speaking to reporters, he reiterated his belief that the United States should pay the “lowest interest rate anywhere in the world because we have the strongest credit.”
Trump, who picked Warsh for the top job, did not directly blame the new chair, in a break from his past practice of admonishing Jerome Powell, the former head of the central bank. Instead, he directed his anger at the six other members of the Board of Governors, two of whom were appointed by Trump.
The president, late Wednesday, said he told Warsh that he “might as well vote with the board because it’s just not going to matter.” He added, “The board is very hostile. They’re very political. They’re doing the wrong thing. They’re a bunch of politicians.”
The timing of future adjustments depends in large part on the incoming data. Signs that inflation was continuing to stall out, or worse, deteriorate further, would keep pressure on the Fed to deliver successive increases regardless of the electoral calendar.
The problem, said Seth Carpenter, a former Fed economist who is now at Morgan Stanley, is that “there is very clear tension within the committee in terms of how to think about a single data point.”
Warsh on Wednesday emphasized that he was most focused on trends in inflation rather than specific data points, which he described as “noisy.”
“Data point dependence is a dangerous preoccupation,” he said. “It’s not something that concerns me. Markets over time will come to understand how this Fed makes its decisions, what’s relevant and not.”
But other officials at the Fed, and financial markets more broadly, appeared to be ascribing a great deal of importance to incoming data, suggesting there were different thresholds for additional action for different people.
The risk is a breakdown in the unanimity seen Wednesday, a fissure that could grow more pronounced if there started to be a trade-off between taming inflation and maintaining a healthy labor market, said Derek Tang, an economist at the research group LHMeyer.
“Warsh is willing to hike right now and do this for inflation because there’s a low cost to doing so,” Tang said. “What’s not answered is: What if the cost of doing so is higher?”
Right now, that tension does not exist. The unemployment rate is low, consumers are still spending, and growth has stayed solid. But Daleep Singh, who formerly worked at the New York Fed and the Treasury Department, warned that achieving Warsh’s inflation pledge might require much more substantive tightening that could imperil that.
This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Title: Andrew Garfield leads a medieval revolt in 'The Uprising' — and its aftermath is the
Article_Text:
Something strange happened to Paul Greengrass’ new film, “The Uprising,” on its way to theaters. Early reports emphasized that the movie would be a realistic, semi-documentary-style reconstruction — very much in keeping with Greengrass’ usual approach — of the English Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, with Andrew Garfield playing a fictional peasant and one of the rebellion’s leaders, known only as “Ploughman.”
But about three weeks ago, the film’s U.S. distributors decided to add a baffling subtitle to its name: “The Rise of Robin Hood.” The internet erupted. Had Greengrass really made yet another Robin Hood movie? And if so, how exactly did that square with the fact that the folk legends about the mythical outlaw are set roughly 200 years before the events depicted in the film?
This is hardly the first time an original movie title has been altered to accommodate what distributors perceive as the ignorance of the average American viewer. Alan Bennett’s famous play “The Madness of George III,” for example, became “The Madness of King George” in Nicholas Hytner’s 1994 film adaptation because distributors feared American audiences might assume it was the third movie in a series.
In the case of “The Uprising,” however, the Robin Hood connection is not only historically implausible. The film’s British distributor also issued a statement saying promotional materials using Robin Hood’s image or name had neither been produced nor approved by it. So much for what Britain’s Guardian called a “marketing meltdown.” “The Uprising” seemed doomed before it ever reached the screen.
What is surprising about Greengrass’ new film is the way it applies his documentary-surveillance style to a historical story set in the 14th century.
Greengrass’ excellent early films focused on painstaking reconstructions of intense situations: the struggle between passengers and hijackers aboard one of the planes seized on Sept. 11, which ended with the aircraft crashing into a field in Pennsylvania in “United 93,” or the takeover of a container ship by Somali pirates in “Captain Phillips.”
Greengrass is not a pioneer in this regard. As early as 1964, British filmmaker Peter Watkins directed “Culloden,” presenting the famous 1746 battle, in which the British army defeated the Jacobite rebels, in the style of televised wartime news coverage.
Greengrass’ film does not include fictional interviews, as Watkins’ did, but it certainly portrays the violence with a camera that feels physically present inside the events themselves. The excellent cinematography is by Norwegian cinematographer Pål Ulvik Rokseth, who previously worked with Greengrass on “22 July,” his reconstruction of the 2011 massacre at a youth camp in Norway. Viewers sensitive to bloody imagery should take note.
At the center of the film is Ploughman, played by Garfield, who lost his family in the Black Death and barely manages to survive off his land. The crushing tax burden imposed in the aftermath of the Hundred Years’ War and intensified under the teenage King Richard II eventually triggers an uprising in one village that spreads through the surrounding counties.
The rebels decide to march on London and confront the young, seemingly inexperienced king, who is being manipulated by his scheming advisers, including the mayor, played by Jonny Lee Miller. Once they reach the capital, the revolt turns violent as the peasants slaughter Flemish merchants in an especially graphic massacre scene.
When they finally meet the king, he agrees to their demands. But what first appears to be a victory for the peasants quickly takes a horrifying turn — at least for viewers who did not bother reading the Wikipedia entry on the revolt beforehand.
This focus on the violent collision between government power and popular protest brings us back to one of Greengrass’ earlier films, “Bloody Sunday” from 2002, which meticulously depicted, from multiple perspectives, the January 1972 march against the British government’s policy of internment without trial. The protest ended in bloodshed in the Northern Irish city of Derry after British soldiers opened fire on demonstrators.
“The Uprising,” by contrast, follows a more conventional narrative, primarily because it focuses on a single character, Ploughman, rather than shifting among different figures and perspectives on the same event — an approach that also gave “United 93” much of its dramatic power.
In that sense, Ploughman’s heroic character, whose tragic and human dimensions remain relatively understated, resembles a kind of medieval Jason Bourne. Greengrass, after all, directed three installments in the Bourne series starring Matt Damon.
Ploughman may be fictional, but other characters in the film, as is often the case with Greengrass, are rooted in historical reality. These include Wat Tyler, played by Cosmo Jarvis, and the radical priest John Ball, played by Jamie Bell, both of whom were indeed among the leaders of the revolt.
Through Ploughman, Greengrass tries to adopt a bottom-up view of history through the eyes of an ordinary man. But casting Andrew Garfield makes that anonymity harder to sustain. Garfield carries with him a familiar screen persona as an idealistic hero of strong moral stature, from Spider-Man to Desmond Doss in “Hacksaw Ridge,” making it difficult from the outset to see Ploughman as simply another anonymous peasant.
Still, Garfield’s performance — like those of the rest of the cast — gives the film an immediate and compelling emotional presence.
It is difficult not to recognize contemporary echoes in the film, particularly when thinking about crowds around the world taking to the streets against authoritarian rule. Its realist style might have benefited from borrowing something of the smartphone aesthetic that has accompanied, and continues to accompany, such protests.
The overhead drone shots of crowds taking over the streets of London, for example, feel somewhat alien to Greengrass’ style. Yet the film’s strength also lies in its refusal to revel in the peasants’ moral righteousness.
Quite the opposite: it emphasizes their brutality and their excitement at bloodshed and the beheading of senior officials. A protest born of legitimate injustice, Greengrass suggests, is not immune to becoming cruel and indiscriminate violence.
“The Uprising” reaches its peak in the final act, when Greengrass creates a tense situation for anyone unfamiliar with how the historical events unfolded. Whether a historical event requires a spoiler warning is, of course, an interesting question in itself.
At this point, a character who until then had been relatively marginal also moves to the foreground: a young scribe, played by Sky Yang, who tragically finds himself taking on a far more significant role than the story initially seemed to have in store for him.
Praise is also due to young Woody Norman as King Richard II, who emerges as a shrewd, almost contemporary young man who is not under his mother’s thumb — a family dynamic that sounds disturbingly familiar.

Title: Xander Bogaerts falls short of cycle as red-hot Padres torch Rockies
Article_Text:
Field Level Media
                
18 Sep 2026, 03:55 GMT+10
            
(Photo credit: Isaiah J. Downing)
Xander Bogaerts homered and tripled in a seven-run second inning and finished a single shy of the cycle, and the surging San Diego Padres beat the Colorado Rockies 9-2 in Denver on Thursday.
Ty France and Dustin Harris also had three hits apiece and Jake Cronenworth and Samad Taylor each had two hits for San Diego (84-69), which finished 11-2 against Colorado this season.
The Padres have won 10 of 11 to increase their lead to four games over idle Arizona for the third and final NL wild-card berth.
San Diego is a game behind the Chicago Cubs for the top seed and a half-game back of Philadelphia for the second berth. The Phillies played at the New York Mets on Thursday night.
Michael King (12-9) tossed six solid innings, ending his day when he struck out Troy Johnston with the bases loaded and two outs. He allowed two runs on seven hits and two walks and fanned six.
Mickey Moniak and Brett Sullivan had two hits each for the Rockies (56-97), who have dropped 10 of 11 and are on pace for a fourth consecutive 100-loss season.
Jake McCarthy led off the bottom of the first with a triple and scored on Connor Norby's single to make it 1-0, but it disappeared when the Padres jumped on Colorado starter Tanner Gordon.
Bogaerts started the rally with a leadoff homer, his 12th of the season, and San Diego loaded the bases with a single and two walks.
Harris drove in a pair with a single to center, Manny Machado hit a sacrifice fly and France singled to left to put runners on the corners with two outs. Rockies right fielder Zac Veen had two fielding mistakes that resulted in back-to-back triples for Jackson Merrill and Bogaerts to make it 7-0.
Gordon (1-5) allowed seven runs on 10 hits in three innings.
The Padres added two more in the fifth when Taylor followed Cronenworth's leadoff triple with a double, and he scored on a Harris single.
Colorado scored in the sixth on a two-out single by Kyle Karros.
--Field Level Media

Article_Text:
Philadelphia police have linked seven missing women to a home where investigators recovered more than 1 million images and videos and also found five urns believed to contain human ashes, authorities said this week.
Initial analysis of the images showed two missing women — 27-year-old Gabrielle Amarando and 26-year-old Maribel Fresses — lying unconscious in the Chew Avenue home with apparent injuries, Philadelphia Police Department Deputy Commissioner Frank Vanore said in the press conference.
Metadata from the images show they were taken in 2017. "Both women remain missing and have not been seen," Vanore said, adding "to date, neither their bodies nor any DNA evidence have been recovered."
The home was occupied by Eugene Horsch, the son of deceased pornographer Raymond "R.C." Horsch.
The investigation began after Eugene Horsch was arrested in June.
Fox News has learned that R.C. Horsch wrote a book titled "Empathy: The Memoir of an Empathetic Serial Killer."
The book, which was published back in 2014, billed itself as the "autobiographical memoir of a caring, empathetic serial killer."
In the book, Horsch wrote about strangling a woman he called "Krista" — then described buying 100 pounds of sodium hydroxide and using lye in a basement bathtub to dissolve her body. But, Horsch was known to mix real details of his life with violent fiction, making it unclear what, if anything, actually happened.
The Philadelphia Police Department said investigators were "aware of the memoir, and it is being reviewed as part of the ongoing investigation."
Amazon removed it from its store and told Fox News on Friday, "Our content guidelines govern which books can be listed for sale, and we take proactive and reactive measures to prevent, detect, and remove content that violates those guidelines."
On June 19, a park ranger encountered Eugene Horsch, 44, and a female passenger sitting in a BMW outside of Philadelphia's Independence Mall, Vanore explained.
"During the course of that investigation, officers recovered two firearms, narcotics, and identification impersonating a federal law enforcement officer, and he was charged. Task force officers from the DEA were able to develop probable cause that same day and serve a warrant on Mr. Horsch's residence," Vanore said.
The female passenger presented false identification using the name Blair Tonzelli, a woman who has been missing since 2023, a spokesperson for the Philadelphia Police Department confirmed to Fox News Digital.
The true identity of the woman in the vehicle has not been released. Tonzelli's whereabouts remain unknown.
After obtaining a warrant, investigators conducted a search of the Chew Avenue home and found "a homemade laboratory of some kind in the basement area, five urns believed to contain human ashes, and a large amount of digital evidence — including computers, hard drives, flash drives, DVRs, cameras, and phones," Vanore said during the press conference.
Investigators have identified 58 total people in the videos and images they found in the home. Vanore said "four of those identified appear lifeless, with video depicting what may have happened to one of them."
Amarando and Fresses remain missing, and no DNA evidence or physical remains connected to them have been recovered.
Of the seven missing women, the Philadelphia Medical Examiner’s Office reviewed evidence showing four of them, police said in a statement issued after Wednesday’s press conference.
The medical examiner’s office advised that, "provided the recordings are authentic and unaltered, the women depicted appear to be deceased," the police department said. "However, because their bodies or remains have not been recovered, they cannot be conclusively declared deceased, and no cause or manner of death can be determined."
"Two additional women are reported missing but have not been observed in the evidence reviewed by investigators," the department added. "The identity and circumstances surrounding the seventh woman remain under investigation."
One video reportedly shows R.C. Horsch handcuffing a woman to a bed and zip-tying her neck until she became unconscious. Investigators believe this woman is Nicole Fusaro, according to FOX 29 Philadelphia. Police have not conclusively confirmed the identification.
Another missing woman reportedly connected to the home is R.C. Horsch's ex-wife, Amy McHale, who has been missing since 2016, FOX 29 reported.
"We have only processed a small fraction of the total media. Thousands of videos remain to be analyzed. We are working to corroborate what we see and gather physical evidence to prove our findings, supported throughout by the FBI as we determine our next steps," Vanore concluded Wednesday.
Fox News' Kimberly Ruiz contributed to this report.

Title: State Funding supports critical public works vehicle replacement in Shippensburg Township
Article_Text:
Shippensburg Township has been awarded $124,000 through the Commonwealth Financing Authority's Statewide Local Share Account (LSA) Program to purchase a new public works vehicle, strengthening the Township's ability to provide essential municipal services year-round.
"This investment ensures that Shippensburg Township can continue providing reliable, efficient services to our residents and businesses," said Marc Rideout, Chairman of the Township’s Board of Supervisors. "The new vehicle will strengthen our ability to respond to winter weather, maintain roadways, and perform critical public works functions while reducing the strain caused by maintaining aging equipment. We are grateful to Representative Catherine Wallen, Senator Greg Rothman, and the Commonwealth for recognizing the importance of this investment."
State Representative Catherine Wallen highlighted the value of supporting local governments as they address infrastructure and operational needs.
"Local municipalities depend on reliable equipment to keep roads safe, maintain essential services, and respond to the needs of their communities," said Representative Wallen. "This funding will help Shippensburg Township replace aging equipment with a modern vehicle that improves efficiency, reduces costs, and strengthens the Township's ability to serve residents every day."
The new vehicle will be deployed throughout the Township and will support approximately nine miles of roadways, municipal facilities, residential neighborhoods, and commercial areas. With increased hauling capacity, improved fuel efficiency, and enhanced snow removal capabilities, the vehicle will allow Township crews to operate more efficiently while reducing maintenance and operating costs.
State Senator Greg Rothman emphasized the long-term benefits of investing in core municipal
infrastructure. "Dependable public services help to keep our communities safe,” said Senator Rothman. "This
Statewide LSA investment will give Shippensburg Township the tools it needs to maintain critical infrastructure, support roadway safety, and deliver services more effectively for years to come. I was pleased to support this request and help secure funding for the Township."
The Statewide LSA Program provides funding for projects that enhance public infrastructure, community assets, and quality of life across Pennsylvania. The program awarded more than $384 million in funding to 1,378 projects across the Commonwealth in the current round.
For more information, contact Amanda Courson at parkandrec@shippensburgtownship.com.

Title: American Airlines Sees Strong Demand, but Fuel Spike Threatens Profit Outlook
Article_Text:
Key Points  
    -       Interested in American Airlines Group Inc.? Here are five stocks we like better.  
-       Demand remains strong: American Airlines expects third-quarter revenue growth of 16% to 19%, with broad-based strength across corporate, international, domestic, premium and coach travel.  
-       Fuel costs threaten profitability: Fourth-quarter fuel prices have risen about $1 per gallon in four weeks, potentially adding roughly $1 billion to quarterly fuel expense and prompting possible capacity reductions.  
-       Long-term growth initiatives continue: American is expanding premium seating, rebuilding its network and growing its AAdvantage-Citi co-brand partnership, which it expects could contribute $1.5 billion in pretax profit by 2030.  
American Airlines Group (NASDAQ:AAL) CEO Robert Isom said demand remains strong across the carrier's network, cabins and geographies, while volatile fuel costs remain the principal constraint on profitability.  
        Speaking at a Morgan Stanley conference, Isom said American expects third-quarter revenue growth of 16% to 19% year over year and continues to see broad-based strength in corporate, international, domestic, premium-cabin and coach demand. He said the carrier's capacity and unit-cost performance were also tracking in line with expectations.  
        → IonQ and NVIDIA Just Cracked a Major Quantum Computing Bottleneck  
            "I've never seen a revenue environment in terms of year-over-year improvement, especially for American," Isom said, while adding that the company still must contend with elevated fuel prices and refining margins.  
            Revenue Strategy Centers on Four Pillars  
        Isom said American's strategy is centered on rebuilding its network, improving the customer experience, growing premium revenue and strengthening its AAdvantage loyalty and co-brand card business.  
        → 3 Luxury Consumer Brands to Watch in a Beaten-Down Sector  
            American has rebuilt capacity at major hubs including Dallas-Fort Worth, Charlotte, Miami, Philadelphia, Phoenix and Chicago after what Isom described as undergrowth in its network following the pandemic. The company expects to receive five additional gates in Chicago by the end of the year, while future terminal additions at Dallas-Fort Worth could support further expansion.  
         The company is also investing in upgraded lounges, Flagship Suites, aircraft cabin reconfigurations, high-speed Starlink Wi-Fi and the return of seatback video. Isom said premium seating is expected to increase about 50% by the end of the decade as reconfigured aircraft and new deliveries enter the fleet.  
               → Micron's AI Memory Boom Could Send Shares 100% Higher  
       He said 30% of American's seats now generate 50% of its revenue, highlighting the importance of premium products. American also has recorded a 5-percentage-point improvement in customers buying up from Basic Economy fares, according to Isom.  
   -       Managed corporate revenue rose 26% in the second quarter, marking a fifth consecutive quarter of double-digit growth.  
-       American has regained its prior corporate position following sales and distribution changes, though Isom said it has not yet achieved its "full fair share" of corporate business.  
-       Corporate yield is nearly double that of other channels, Isom said.  
Fuel Volatility Clouds Otherwise Strong Outlook  
       While executives expressed confidence in operating trends, both Isom and Chief Financial Officer Devon May said fuel costs have risen sharply. May said fuel for the fourth quarter had increased by about $1 per gallon over the past four weeks compared with levels reflected in the company's prior forward guidance.  
          May said each one-cent change in fuel prices is worth approximately $10 million per quarter to the airline, implying about a $1 billion run-up in fourth-quarter fuel expense from the recent increase.  
       "For everything that is controllable, we feel great about it," May said, citing revenue, capacity and unit-cost performance. He said American may adjust late-fourth-quarter capacity, including December flying, in response to higher fuel prices.  
       Isom said the company has recovered a substantial portion of higher fuel costs through pricing, though it has accepted somewhat lower load factors in exchange for stronger unit revenue. If fuel prices remain elevated, he said the industry may need to make further capacity adjustments.  
       Loyalty Program and Citi Partnership Offer Growth Opportunity  
       Isom highlighted record AAdvantage enrollments and the company's new relationship with Citigroup as major longer-term revenue drivers. American expects approximately $8 billion in co-brand cash remuneration this year and said that figure is projected to exceed $10 billion by 2030.  
          The company also anticipates the Citi relationship could add $1.5 billion in pretax profitability by 2030. Isom said American is expanding card offerings, including initiatives aimed at small and medium-sized businesses, while free Wi-Fi is helping drive loyalty-program enrollments.  
       American's balance sheet has also improved, Isom said. The company reduced total debt from a peak of $54 billion a few years ago to roughly $36 billion, with a target of $35 billion. May said the airline has its lowest debt level in more than a decade and substantial liquidity.  
       Management Sees Margin Potential Beyond Fuel Pressures  
       Isom said American remains focused on expanding margins and profitability rather than prioritizing a single operating metric. He reiterated that the company's prior targets included mid- to high-single-digit pretax margins and potentially mid-teen-plus EBITDA margins.  
       According to Isom, American would have been positioned to make significant progress toward those targets this year absent fuel volatility. He said the company's revenue opportunity does not require excessive capital investment because its fleet and capital-expenditure plans are largely in place.  
          For the fourth quarter, about 25% of bookings had been made at the time of the conference. Isom said trends were consistent with a strong finish to the year, with demand holding up in both premium and coach cabins. He added that American expects to grow less in 2027 than it had anticipated several months earlier, while continuing to rebuild a competitive network and manage profitability.  
       About American Airlines Group (NASDAQ:AAL)  
       American Airlines Group Inc is a holding company whose principal subsidiary, American Airlines, provides scheduled passenger air transportation and cargo services. The airline serves destinations throughout the United States and connects customers to international markets across the Americas, Europe, Asia and other regions through its own network and partnerships.  
       American Airlines offers multiple travel classes and related services, including reservations, onboard products, travel rewards through the AAdvantage loyalty program, and freight transportation.

Title: RFK Jr. gives keynote at anti-vaccine conference – NBC New York
Article_Text:
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. gave the keynote address Thursday at a conference of an anti-vaccine activist group he once chaired, telling the hundreds in attendance that they had a friend in President Donald Trump's White House.
It was Kennedy's first time appearing at the Children's Health Defense conference since he became secretary. Kennedy took leave from the group when he launched his bid to become president in 2023, but his speech Thursday served as a sort of homecoming, offering him a platform from which to hail the administration's steps to scale back vaccine guidance and reassure the activists in attendance that he was working to turn their priorities into policy.
“Let me be clear: You have a strong and steadfast friend in the White House. We've accomplished in 19 months things that would have seemed unthinkable two years ago,” he said.
Watch NBC 4 free wherever you are
The speech, peppered with questions about long established vaccine safety, also highlighted how once fringe views on vaccines have been given a prominent pulpit under the Trump administration.
Kennedy boasted about the administration's moves to downsize the childhood vaccination schedule and reshape a key vaccine advisory board — steps that have since been halted by a judge.
Kennedy lauded Trump for pushing ahead with attempts to overhaul vaccine guidance, including an executive order last month calling for spacing out the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, against medical groups' recommendations.
That executive order and now Kennedy's keynote speech at the Children's Health Defense conference mark a pivot by the White House and the Department of Health and Human Services, who earlier this year had appeared to be moving beyond vaccine efforts and toward a less contentious agenda on healthy food ahead of November’s midterm elections. HHS promoted the speech on its social media channels.
Kennedy, a longtime anti-vaccine activist, chaired Children’s Health Defense for years. He served as the group’s chief legal counsel and expanded it. After becoming health secretary last year, Kennedy moved at a blistering pace to overhaul public health guidance and revamp long-held precedents in vaccine policymaking.
Critics, among them many of the country's top medical associations, have said the moves risk stoking vaccine hesitancy and sowing confusion among Americans who endured a crisis of trust in their public health agencies following the COVID-19 pandemic. That public confidence continues to erode.
“We have not taken vaccines away from anybody. We have preserved access. But we have started asking the questions that you and millions of American parents have been asking for years,” Kennedy told the group.
Mary Holland, the CEO of Children’s Health Defense, referred to Kennedy as “Bobby” and said the group has “gratitude beyond words” to the HHS secretary for “recognizing there are real consequential issues around childhood vaccinations.”
Kennedy's appearance Thursday comes as the country faces its worst year for measles since 1991 and has seen seven reported measles-associated deaths in the last two years — more than the combined total of reported deaths over the previous three decades.
Pennsylvania officials have reported four measles-associated deaths this year. None of the four were vaccinated, according to the state health department. When state officials last month announced the first two of those deaths, it ignited a public feud between Gov. Josh Shapiro and Kennedy.
Shapiro blasted Kennedy's appearance on the social media site X Thursday, saying Kennedy “chose to spend his time today addressing the premier vaccine-denial conference in America.”
Shapiro said the HHS secretary should have encouraged people to get vaccinated for measles, "yet he couldn’t bring himself to do it. Instead, he pushed a narrative that continues to stoke fear and mistrust.”
A representative from the White House did not respond to an Associated Press request for comment on Kennedy’s appearance at the event.
Following Kennedy onstage Thursday was Andrew Wakefield, an author of a since-discredited study that linked the MMR vaccine to autism, which has fueled the anti-vaccine movement even though it was retracted.
Widespread scientific consensus and decades of studies have firmly concluded there is no link between vaccines and autism.
Shaughnessy Naughton, founder of 314 Action, a group that recruits scientists to run for public office, said Kennedy's decision to give a speech at the conference shows “the lack of seriousness he brings to HHS.”
"With a deadly measles outbreak killing people in Pennsylvania, the best thing Kennedy can do for Americans is step aside.”

Title: The 10 Best Crime Miniseries of All Time, Ranked
Article_Text:
Miniseries have become more and more common lately, thanks in part to the proliferation of streaming platforms, and they can be a great way of telling a contained story with a designated endpoint, as opposed to continuing for season after season. And in a TV landscape where content is streamed and often enjoyed in one sitting, a miniseries can make for the ultimate binge-watch.
The format has proven to be a great way to tell crime stories, in particular, from horrifying crimes in suburbia to massive drug cartels, and indeed, some of the most compelling miniseries of recent years have been just that. Many of the best crime miniseries have been based on books, either nonfiction dives into large-scale crimes or fictional stories that blend characters' personal lives with the crimes they've become caught up in.
10 'The Cry' (2018)
In The Cry, as new mom Joanna (Jenna Coleman) is struggling to adjust to life with an infant, the child goes missing on a cross-country trip from Scotland to Australia. Her boyfriend and the baby’s father, Alistair (Ewan Leslie), fight for custody of his daughter from a previous marriage. On top of concern for her son, Joanna is forced to deal with public scrutiny of the situation. The Cry was based on the novel of the same name by Helen FitzGerald.
The Cry was a riveting series, with baby Noah’s fate and who was responsible remaining a mystery until the end through the show’s many twists and turns, all told through a nonlinear structure which constantly forced the audience to reconsider what information they had and what they were seeing play out. It was as much a psychological thriller as it was a crime drama, with multiple characters as possible suspects—Joanna was exhausted and overwhelmed, Alistair was cold and manipulative, and his ex-wife was hurt and vindictive.
9 'Under the Banner of Heaven' (2022)
In Under the Banner of Heaven, devout Mormon Detective Jeb Pyre’s (Andrew Garfield) investigation of the brutal murder of a woman and her baby led him to uncover the dark, violent past of the Mormon religion and its effects on modern-day extremist Mormons. The series was a fictionalized account of real events and was based on the book of the same name by Jon Krakauer. Dustin Lance Black served as showrunner.
Under the Banner of Heaven was somewhat controversial for its portrayal of the Mormon religion, but it still presented a compelling story. The killing of mother and baby was horrific, but the series was also about faith—Pyre was questioning his faith just as two men committed a brutal murder in the name of theirs. The cast all impressed, including Rory Culkin in a small but memorable role as the brother of the victim’s husband.
8 'Dopesick' (2021)
Dopesick is a fictionalized account of America’s opioid crisis from the perspectives of everyone involved, from Purdue Pharma’s dishonesty about the addictive nature of OxyContin down to their reps selling the drugs and even those who battled with addiction as a result, as well as regulators determined to hold the company accountable. It was based on the book Dopesick: Dealers, Doctors, and the Drug Company that Addicted America by Beth Macy.
Crime series usually take on subjects like homicides, but Dopesick was a compelling drama about the damage done by an entire pharmaceutical company. The star-studded cast all delivered impressive performances, especially Michael Keaton as the fictional Dr. Samuel Finnix, whose community was ravaged by addiction due to him prescribing the drug without knowing the truth about how addictive it was. Michael Stuhlbarg was unnerving and callous as Purdue president Richard Sackler.
7 'Unbelievable' (2019)
After a teenage girl, Marie (Kaitlyn Dever), reported being raped, she was pressured into recanting her story and, upon doing so, was charged with filing a false report in Unbelievable. Three years later, two female detectives investigated a series of assaults exactly like Marie’s and proved she was telling the truth, and could have been prevented if she had been believed. The series was a Netflix original and was based on actual events.
Unbelievable was critically acclaimed, and the harrowing, emotional story leaves an impression. Dever delivered one of her best performances as Marie. The story centered on Marie as a victim, from the initial assault to the ways the legal system and even those around her re-traumatized her, and addressed how people can be affected by trauma, how memory can be faulty, and how that can be weaponized.
6 'Candy' (2022)
Candy told the story of 1980s Texas homemaker and mother, Candy Montgomery (Jessica Biel), who had an affair with her neighbor’s husband, then violently murdered her with an axe, but claimed she acted in self-defense after she was attacked first when confronted about the affair after it ended. When Candy’s case was brought to trial, a jury believed her story, and she was acquitted. The series was based on a true story.
Biel was unsettling as Candy, alternately a warm, caring person and cold and calculating, in one of the best performances of her career. Melanie Lynskey also impressed as Candy’s neighbor and victim, Betty. Although it was a crime story, the series also dealt with the pressures women face as wives and mothers, particularly when perfection is expected, and addressed the mental state of Candy, particularly leading up to Betty’s death.
5 'Griselda' (2024)
Colombian drug queenpin Griselda Blanco (Sofía Vergara) created one of the most profitable cartels in history, and the Netflix series Griselda was a fictionalized retelling of her story. The series charted Griselda’s success through the ‘70s and ‘80s, from the very beginnings of her business dealings as she fled Medellín for Miami with her three children through her work as she built her business and ultimately rose to success. The series was told partly through flashbacks, establishing why Griselda left her life in Medellín behind.
Griselda was a hit for Netflix and earned critical acclaim. It presented a fascinating story, and it addressed the theme of women proving themselves through both Griselda and police officer June Hawkins (Juliana Aidén Martinez). Vergara, who was best-known for her comedic role on the sitcom Modern Family, was almost unrecognizable and showed a completely different side as the titular character, known for her ruthlessness, and impressed with the best performance of her career.
4 'A Friend of the Family' (2022)
Friend of the Family tells the shocking story of a family whose young daughter, Jan, was abducted multiple times by a family friend during the 1970s—first when she was 12, then again two years later at 14. The series detailed the ways the family was manipulated into trusting him. The series was based on a true story, and the actual Jan Broberg served as co-producer, along with her mother, Mary Ann.
A Friend of the Family was a terrifying look at the lengths a person will go to when they’re targeting someone, and it served as a cautionary tale of not just how it could happen but that it could happen to anyone. Despite solid performances from the entire cast, Jake Lacy stood out as kidnapper Bob “B” Berchtold, playing him with a charm that shows how he was able to get close to the family while also managing to show what an alarming sociopath he was.
3 'Adolescence' (2025)
In Adolescence, 13-year-old Jamie Miller (Owen Cooper) is arrested for the murder of a girl from his school. His father, Eddie (Stephen Graham), struggles to process the accusation while Detective Inspector Luke Bascombe (Ashley Walters) investigates the case and psychologist Briony Ariston (Erin Doherty) attempts to understand Jamie’s state of mind. Created by Graham and Jack Thorne, the four-part Netflix limited series unfolds largely through the perspectives of those closest to the crime.
Each episode of Adolescence is filmed in one continuous take, creating an almost unbearable sense of immediacy. Cooper delivers a remarkable breakout performance, while Graham brings enormous emotional weight to a father forced to confront questions he never imagined asking. The series ultimately works as a disturbing examination of how violence can take root where you least expect it.
2 'Sharp Objects' (2018)
In Sharp Objects, journalist Camille (Amy Adams) returns to her hometown to cover the murders of two preteen girls. Her return also meant reuniting with her estranged family and dealing with her own demons, especially the death of her sister at a young age and her relationship with her mother. The series was based on Gillian Flynn’s debut novel of the same name, and she also served as a writer for the series.
Sharp Objects was largely faithful to the book, and it was a hit for HBO—though its dark subject-matter dealing with the secrets of small-town America meant it wouldn’t get a second season. Camille was a great yet troubled character, and Adams did a fantastic job at bringing her to life in one of the best performances of her career. But just as impressive was Patricia Clarkson as Camille’s cold mother, Adora.
1 'Mare of Easttown' (2021)
In Mare of Easttown, a detective, Mare, in a small Pennsylvania town outside of Philadelphia, is tasked with investigating a murder after a body of a teen mother is found in a creek after a party. At the same time, she struggles with her personal life, as she mourns the loss of her son. She's also coming to terms with her ex-husband’s new engagement and pursuing a new relationship herself.
Mare of Easttown was critically acclaimed and a hit with audiences. While it did present a compelling crime, the series was also more than a police procedural, as it dealt with the themes of loss and regret. Kate Winslet delivered a stellar performance as detective Mare, a compelling character who experienced a lot of growth over the course of the series.

Title: Five women feared dead in connection to Philadelphia home where disturbing images were recovered
Article_Text:
(CNN) — What began as a search into an illegally parked BMW that led police to discover bizarre fake IDs, drugs and weapons has spiraled into a sprawling investigation into the whereabouts of five potentially missing, and feared dead, women.
Philadelphia officers first found 44-year-old Eugene Horsch in June parked illegally in a space reserved for law enforcement, with a woman in the vehicle’s back seat.
Inside his car, according to a criminal complaint, investigators found guns, drugs, weapons and a fake Drug Enforcement Administration ID bearing Horsch’s photo, though authorities say he never worked for the federal agency.
The woman with him had her own puzzling ID, police said: It showed her photo, but carried the name of a missing woman.
Searches of Horsch’s home in the city’s Olney neighborhood turned up more drugs, more weapons and a staggering trove of digital evidence, including videos – some of which police say are likely linked to Horsch’s late father, reportedly an erotic filmmaker whose work depicted violent themes.
Among what was uncovered were photos and videos of at least five women who appear unconscious or possibly dead — evidence police said in a news conference Wednesday they are still working to corroborate as the search for answers continues.
Critically, police say they have yet to find physical evidence, DNA or any bodies.
Horsch was arrested following the June traffic stop on charges related to the weapons found, and CNN has reached out to his legal representation for comment. He remains in custody.
A disturbing cache of videos
During their June search, police found over a million digital images and thousands of videos during searches of the home, strewn across computers, hard drives, flash drives, cameras and phones.
Others are videos of what appear to be unconscious, and possibly lifeless, women.
Police indicate Eugene Horsch may not have made the videos, but rather, his father: Raymond “RC” Horsch. He’s seen in some of the disturbing images, police said.
Horsch’s father was a “known drug manufacturer and erotic filmmaker who had published several works of fiction with violent masochistic themes,” the Philadelphia Inquirer previously reported. Law enforcement sources said police were considering the possibility that the writings were part of a novel or screenplay, according to the newspaper.
The elder Horsch, who was previously a resident of the home, died last year, further complicating the investigation.
New video analyzed by Philadelphia Police homicide detectives appear to show a woman being strangled by a zip tie in the home until she “appeared to be lifeless” and two more images of unconscious women with injuries, Deputy Police Commissioner Frank Vanore said Wednesday. That’s in addition to recordings recovered from the house showing two other women “apparently deceased,” police said in August.
“Let’s remember, he was making movies,” Vanore said. “Some of his movies are there on this digital evidence. So, that’s the part, where you know, some of this is play acting, and some of it we believe could be real.”
“We need to corroborate what we see, we need to find evidence to prove what we think, and the FBI is here to help us,” he said.
The elder Horsch was previously married to a woman who went missing in 2016, according to CNN affiliate WPVI.
The missing women
Inside the basement of the Olney home, police found what they described as a “homemade laboratory of some kind.”
Various chemicals in bottles, drums and other plastic containers littered the space, as well as a 55-gallon drum connected to water lines. Five urns believed to contain human remains were also found. Three of the urns are believed to be RC, his sister and a friend, while the other two are unidentified.
Of the five women feared dead, two have previously been named by the Philadelphia Police Department: 26-year-old Maribel Fresses and 27-year-old Gabrielle Amarando. Police have identified two other women but are not naming them at the request of the families, and one other woman hasn’t been identified, Vanore said. Two other missing women are also tied to the investigation: Blair Tonzelli, the woman whose ID was found when Eugene Horsch was arrested, and Amy McHale, whose family says she was married to the elder Horsch.
The FBI is working with the Philadelphia Police to process all of the digital evidence, with Special Agent in Charge Wayne Jacobs saying about 30% of the review has been completed.
“The volume of material, the forensic work that’s still underway, the care required in reviewing this, all of the material,” he said, “means that this process cannot be rushed.”
In total, 58 different people have been identified in the images police have seen, Vanore said. Ten later overdosed and were found at a different residence in Philadelphia, according to investigators. Authorities have interviewed 16 people, which Vanore said were “not very cooperative,” and police are scheduling interviews with 25 others.
“They don’t really want to talk about what occurred in that house,” he said of those that authorities had reached.
Three people seen in the images told police: “You’re going to see images of us, but we’re not coming in to talk to you, and we’re not coming back,” according to Vanore.
After the June search of his vehicle, Eugene Horsch was arrested and charged with a federal count of felony possession of a firearm and municipal drug and weapons charges. Court records show he has not entered a plea.
Vanore said the weapons charges were transferred to the US Attorney’s office and Horsch is in federal custody.
“At this point, the federal authorities are dealing with Mr. Horsch,” he said.
Eugene Horsch’s defense attorney, Jerry Brown, previously told CNN he plans to enter pleas of not guilty. CNN has reached out to Brown for comment on the new developments unveiled Wednesday.

Title: Dallas Cowboys 2026 Week 2 rooting guide for fans
Article_Text:
While the Cowboys didn’t handle their own business last Sunday night, they weren’t the only projected NFC contender with a bad season opener. In addition to hoping Dallas corrects course in Week 2, what else can we root for in this week’s schedule?
2026 Week 2 rooting guide for Cowboys fans
Do you think the Eagles and Giants will win this week?
Last week, the preseason favorite Los Angeles Rams were dominated at home by the 49ers and lost Myles Garrett for at least a month. The Packers were the only NFC North team to lose a game, getting blown out by the Vikings and… Carson Wentz?!
Will Week 2 go more according to the oddsmaker’s script, or will we be reevaluating our predictions for the NFC? For the Cowboys’ sake, let’s hope last week was the outlier.
In addition to Dallas righting the ship against the Commanders, what else should Cowboys fans be rooting for in Week 2?
NFC East teams
- Titans d. Eagles
- Rams d. Giants
Until we’re much further down the road, it’s hard to imagine ever rooting for one of our division rivals to win. That’s especially true here: both Philly and New York are 1-0, and their opponents are relatively irrelevant to Dallas. The Rams losing last week only makes it easier to root for them, even if they’re still a top threat for playoff seeding.
Unfortunately, Tennessee might be one of the worst teams in the league this year. So if they hang a loss on Philadelphia, even as the home team, it will be a huge upset.
NFC vs. NFC
- Falcons d. Panthers
- Vikings d. Bears
- Cardinals d. Seahawks
Some of this may be splitting hairs, but we expect Carolina, Chicago, and Seattle to be more competitive overall this season than their Week 2 opponents. These picks are about those projected contenders taking losses, which will hopefully help Dallas later with playoff seeding. You never know how a September result could help decide who gets a bye week, home game, or some other postseason bonus.
NFC vs. AFC
- Bills d. Lions
- Jets d. Packers
- Ravens d. Saints
- Browns d. Bucs
- Dolphins d. 49ers
It’s a heavy interconference slate this week, and we can freely root for the AFC in every matchup. About the only time we’d root for an NFC team to win one of these is if it helped us with a future draft pick, like whenever the Steelers or Texans face an NFC opponent. But outside of those, or perhaps some rare scenarios that present themselves later this season, NFC losses are always preferred.
AFC vs. AFC
- Patriots d. Steelers
- Bengals d. Texans
As we just mentioned, monitoring the Steelers and Texans’ games is relevant for Dallas because of the 2027 draft. We own the Steelers’ fourth-round pick from the Broderick Jones trade, and the Texans’ seventh-rounder after sending them Nate Thomas.
Scenarios may present later where we’d prefer that Pittsburgh or Houston win, like when the Steelers play the Eagles in Week 11. The Texans will play every NFC East team this year, and we’d certainly prefer losses for our division foes to a higher seventh-round pick.
But for now, against other AFC teams, our rooting choice is clear.

Title: Conversations with Maya: Shantanu Gaur
Article_Text:
Conversations with Maya: Shantanu Gaur
Maya Ajmera, President & CEO of Society for Science and Executive Publisher of Science News, sat down with Shantanu Gaur, Founder and CEO of Allurion Technologies, who created an FDA approved medical device for the treatment of obesity. Gaur is an alumnus of the 2003 and 2004 International Science and Engineering Fair (ISEF), a program of Society for Science. A graduate of Harvard College with an M.D. from Harvard Medical School, Gaur has more than 40 patents. Gaur also serves on the Society’s National Leadership Council.
You competed at ISEF in 2003 and 2004. What impact did that have on you and your career?
Twenty years later, two things still stick out to me. One, ISEF was the first time I had an opportunity to see what exceptional science and engineering really looks like. I grew up in a small town in southwestern Pennsylvania, and suddenly I was standing alongside students from all over the world doing genuinely cutting-edge work. It was eye-opening. I could see a level of talent I hadn’t encountered before, and it motivated me. It also gave me a sense of community. I had aspirations to become a scientist, and for the first time I felt like I wasn’t alone in that. I was surrounded by people who shared the same drive.
For my junior year ISEF project, I studied a rare genetic mutation in the Afro-Caribbean population of Trinidad and Tobago that raises the risk of prostate cancer. We investigated whether screening for that mutation could help to ensure that the limited resources in Trinidad and Tobago could go to those patients at highest risk. During my senior year, I worked with chicken embryos on a protein involved in retinal development. It was my first time doing wet-lab work with a live specimen. In my senior year project, I learned about the power of negative results to advance a field and so much about the joys and challenges of wet lab science.
You founded Allurion while you were still in medical school. What made you choose that path, and what did the people around you think?
Allurion started as a weekend project — something my classmate Sammy and I found interesting outside of class. As we got encouragement from faculty, I eventually had to decide whether to finish my residency or leave to build the company. I went to my dad, who’s a math professor, for advice. And he laid it out in stark, quantitative terms: As a physician, you have one pair of hands. You’ll see patients for decades and touch the lives of maybe 100,000 or 200,000 people, and that’s a meaningful, fulfilling career. But if you build a company around a real problem, you have the potential to touch the lives of millions. There is a risk, however, that if your business never gets off the ground, you may touch no one’s life. He asked me a simple question: Do you want to maximize your life for impact or not?
That question is what pushed me toward Allurion and has shaped everything else in my life since. My advice is to take the risk and work on big problems because the potential payoff, in lives changed, can be enormous.
Obesity is one of the most complex and stigmatized conditions in medicine. What convinced you it was the problem worth solving?
Two billion people worldwide are overweight, and a billion have obesity. More people die every year from obesity-related disease than died from COVID-19 at the height of the pandemic. It’s the health issue of our generation, and like other chronic diseases, it’s not going to have one miracle-pill solution. As a second-year medical student, one of the patients I met was a young woman who’d had bariatric surgery. She spent weeks in intensive care afterward and ultimately recovered, but seeing how physically and emotionally invasive that experience was, my classmate and I kept thinking: There has to be a better way.
How does the Allurion balloon work?
The whole concept behind Allurion is this: Could we develop a non-surgical way of getting a device inside the stomach so that it can start helping people feel full? We know that bariatric surgery works because it reduces the volume of the stomach. Why not put something inside the stomach instead and avoid the surgery?
We developed a capsule with a balloon inside it that is attached to a thin tube, about the width of a piece of cooked spaghetti. A patient swallows the capsule in a doctor’s office. Once it’s in the stomach, we attach a bag of water to the tube and fill the internal balloon over about five minutes, with no anesthesia or sedation. Once the balloon is filled — about half a liter, weighing around a pound and a quarter — we withdraw the tube and the patient goes home with what amounts to an implanted meal sitting in their stomach. The human stomach is roughly the same size in every adult regardless of height or weight, so one size fits nearly everyone. The balloon stays in place for four months and is there to give patients time to build new habits, without invasive surgery or taking medications.
Were there moments you almost gave up?
Constantly. There’s a line from Angela Duckworth’s book Grit: The Power of Passion and Perseverance that captures it for me: “Enthusiasm is common, endurance is rare.” Every startup begins with excitement about the science and the vision, and then you actually have to build it. That’s when you realize that if building a company were easy, everyone would be doing it.
When we were raising our first round of financing, we went to a hundred investors and got a hundred nos. We were medical students with no business or engineering background, trying to fund a device we’d only demonstrated by filming a prototype pushing against the walls of an animal’s stomach. After our savings ran dry, we scraped together $25,000 and $50,000 at a time from family, friends and professors to fund our first real animal and human studies.
Even today, some investors still doubt there’s room for a technology like ours, especially with GLP-1 drugs on the market. The lesson is that there will always be more people who doubt you than believe in you. The job of an entrepreneur is just to keep enduring, because changing minds takes years.
What role does AI play at Allurion, and where do you see it going in medical devices more broadly?
We don’t use AI in the balloon itself, but it’s central to our digital platform. Managing any chronic disease — obesity, diabetes, hypertension — ultimately comes down to changing daily habits, and there simply aren’t enough dietitians and coaches in the world to support the two billion people who want to lose weight. Our app includes a conversational AI coach, Iris, that looks at a patient’s data and nudges them accordingly — reminding them to weigh in or serving up content on sleep if that’s where they’re struggling.
Beyond the patient experience, AI is changing how we run the company: we use it to analyze product complaints, track lot history and monitor regulatory changes across the more than 80 countries where we’re approved. I don’t think AI will change what a medical device physically is, but it’s already changing how devices are developed, personalized and supported over time.
What’s next for Allurion?
We have an exciting pipeline at Allurion. We are working on a version of the balloon that stays in the stomach for a full year instead of four months and one that could function as a platform — slowly releasing a GLP-1 medication, vitamins or something that supports the gut microbiome rather than just occupying space. With 2 billion people around the world in need, even after all these years, we have only just begun.
What books did you love as a child and what are you reading now?
I loved historical fiction as a child, with the Civil War trilogy Gods and Generals, The Killer Angels and The Last Full Measure at the top of the list. Now, I am working my way through The Obstacle is the Way, a must-read for any scientist or entrepreneur!
What worries keep you up at night?
I worry that in a world of abundance, fueled by the technological advances made possible by AI, that knowledge and power becomes more — not less — concentrated. I want my children and their children to live in a world where knowledge is abundant and accessible and anyone has an opportunity to advance a world-changing idea.
What gives you hope for the future?
Entrepreneurs give me hope for the future. Every problem has a solution, and I take comfort in the fact that humans will inevitably find the solutions to any problems that imperil our future.

Title: Tax sale for delinquent Schuylkill properties held despite lawsuit
Article_Text:
Schuylkill County moved forward with a property tax sale of roughly 300 parcels Thursday, pushing past a resident’s lawsuit challenging the auction’s legality.
The upset sale, as it’s called, is a public auction where a county sells properties with severely delinquent real estate taxes for a starting bid equal to the back taxes and fees owed. The buyer is responsible for any existing mortgages or liens.
The county originally advertised and scheduled the sale for Thursday, Sept. 10, but changed it to Sept. 17, since Pennsylvania law states that no tax sale be held before the second Monday of September, county officials said. The Schuylkill County Tax Claim website was updated to correct the date.
The error should have resulted in the sale being pushed back beyond Sept. 17, though, said Kevin Sponenberg of St. Clair, who sued the county over the matter.
Since the originally listed date of Sept. 10 was illegal, so was the rescheduled date, he said.
Sponenberg said that holding the auction Thursday violated the rights of the more than 800 property owners originally included in the sale. That number was reduced by the time the auction got underway, as numerous property owners paid their taxes before the auction commenced, including Sponenberg himself.
Schuylkill County Judge A.J. Serina ruled Monday on Sponenberg’s petition, placing a stay on the sale of his property pending an Oct. 26 hearing. However, the ruling allows the remainder of the sale to proceed as scheduled.
Sponenberg said this week that he disagreed with Serina’s decision, saying that the entire auction should have been moved to a later date, as he requested in his lawsuit.
By allowing the auction to take place, the county was exposing itself to “millions of dollars in post-sale structural liability,” he said.
Joining Sponenberg as a petitioner in the suit was his girlfriend, Jodie Forney, who lives with him.
Serina was not available for comment.
At Wednesday’s meeting of the Schuylkill County Commissioners, David Rice, the county’s assistant solicitor, read correspondence from Samuel A. Falcone, attorney for Elite Revenue Solutions, the company that the county contracts with to run its tax claim office.
The letter said that Pennsylvania’s Real Estate Tax Sale Law dictates that upset sales can be adjourned or continued without requiring additional public notice of the sale. A motion to continue was filed on Sept. 4, and the Court of Common Pleas granted the continuance on Sept. 11, setting the new date for Sept. 17, he said.
Rice said the postponement actually benefits delinquent taxpayers by giving them extra time to pay, which a number of them did.
During the meeting Jeff Dunkel of Palo Alto challenged the legal validity of the continuance, citing Commonwealth Court precedents involving Luzerne and Lackawanna counties.
Rice and county officials maintained that the continuance was 100% legal and that the upset sale would proceed as rescheduled.
Falcone could not be reached for comment.
Sponenberg said that when his hearing is held, he plans to challenge the legality of the entire sale.

Title: Penn Medicine Launches Mobile Unit to Bring Sight-Saving Care to Vulnerable Residents
Article_Text:
Newswise — PHILADELPHIA—Residents in underserved areas of Philadelphia and beyond will now have opportunities in their own neighborhoods to get their eyes screened for glaucoma, cataracts, and more via Penn Medicine’s brand-new ophthalmology mobile unit.
Made possible by generous gifts from Rick Campbell and family, Save Vision Foundation, and Envision Health Technologies, the all-electric Scheie Eye Institute In MOTION (Mobile Ocular Testing In Our Neighborhoods) will provide free screening for the four leading causes of blindness: glaucoma, macular degeneration, diabetic retinopathy, and cataracts.
“To get out there and prevent diseases that could rob people of their sight, we know we have to get creative,” said the project’s lead physician, Lama Al-Aswad, MD, MPH, a professor of Ophthalmology and Engineering and the Irene Heinz Given and John La Porte Given Research Professor of Ophthalmology II. “Putting a clinic on wheels allows us to meet people where they are, where they haven’t gotten the attention and care they need and are experiencing advanced and often preventable eye disease. Through this, we can address issues before they become these serious problems.”
Al-Aswad was part of an outreach effort at her previous post in New York City that screened more than 8,500 individuals. More than half of them had never seen an eye doctor before, regardless of whether they had insurance.
“The data made it clear that access was the real barrier to care,” Al-Aswad said. “With the same underlying problem here as I’d seen before, I knew part of the solution could be bringing Philadelphia a robust mobile eye unit.”
Taking eye screenings to the road
Planning for the Scheie Eye Institute In MOTION has been underway for more than a year.
When in action, the 11.5-foot tall and 26-foot long van—which is powered by electricity instead of gasoline—will serve as many as 25 people a day. Within the van are six stations operated by three-to-four “crew” members using the type of equipment patients would encounter in any eye clinic, including devices that test for intraocular pressure and peripheral vision, as well as machines that do imaging of the optic nerve and retina. An ophthalmologist will be on-call and available through telemedicine each time the unit journeys out.
If patients are found to have conditions that need further care, they’ll be connected with Penn Medicine providers for follow-up appointments. The exams in the Scheie Eye Institute In MOTION clinic will be free for the uninsured, and a pathway has been created to help those without insurance to get the care they need.
“We want to make this something as comfortable, natural, and easy for patients as possible,” said Bennie Jeng, MD, chair of Ophthalmology and director of the Scheie Eye Institute. “You’ll be stepping onto a van, but we see this as being almost indistinguishable from a visit to a brick-and-mortar office. It just happens that this is one that has rolled up to your neighborhood. It’s unique, but also typical of the kind of service we’re committed to providing to our community.”
More on wheels and in the community
Last summer, Penn Medicine launched another mobile unit that offers mobile breast cancer screenings, building on the health system’s commitment to making cancer screenings as accessible as possible.
Likewise, the Scheie Eye Institute In MOTION unit fits into community work done within Ophthalmology at Penn Medicine. The Shared Vision initiative seeks to bring care out of the clinic and into neighborhoods in the Philadelphia area, particularly focusing on providing screening and care to the underserved and to the unhoused population. The Shared Vision team plans to help the mobile unit with care coordination and patient education.
“It’s a privilege to serve communities across the region, and sometimes that means thinking unconventionally to reach everyone,” said Kevin Mahoney, chief executive officer of the University of Pennsylvania Health System. “Across Penn Medicine, we’re committed to finding creative, practical ways to expand access and reduce barriers to care, and the Scheie Eye Institute In MOTION is the latest example of that work in action, bringing the resources of our health system beyond the hospital walls and directly into neighborhoods.”
Enhancing eye care understanding
Alongside its screening work, Scheie Eye Institute In MOTION will provide eye health education to help residents better understand eye disease and the importance of seeking care. Al-Aswad’s prior research identified low eye health literacy as a major barrier to care. Her research found that patients often did not understand their diagnoses and did not follow up on care after screening.
The mobile unit team plans to create a health literacy survey to measure patients' baseline understanding of eye health and their conditions, then test how their eye health education impacts follow-up rates and the overall burden of disease in the communities served.
“Having a unique initiative like the mobile unit provides us with an invaluable opportunity to not only educate, but to further research,” said Jonathan A. Epstein, MD, dean of the Perelman School of Medicine. “The better we understand the communities we’re serving, the greater the impact we believe we can make. The potential for this mobile unit across so many areas is extremely exciting.”
###
Penn Medicine is one of the world’s leading academic medical centers, dedicated to the related missions of medical education, biomedical research, excellence in patient care, and community service.
The organization consists of the University of Pennsylvania Health System and Penn’s Raymond and Ruth Perelman School of Medicine, founded in 1765 as the nation’s first medical school.
The Perelman School of Medicine is consistently among the nation's top recipients of funding from the National Institutes of Health, with $580 million awarded in the 2023 fiscal year. Home to a proud history of “firsts,” Penn Medicine teams have pioneered discoveries that have shaped modern medicine, including CAR T cell therapy for cancer and the Nobel Prize-winning mRNA technology used in COVID-19 vaccines.
The University of Pennsylvania Health System cares for patients in facilities and their homes stretching from the Susquehanna River in Pennsylvania to the New Jersey shore. These facilities include the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania, Penn Presbyterian Medical Center, Chester County Hospital, Doylestown Health, Lancaster General Health, Princeton Health, and Pennsylvania Hospital—the nation’s first hospital, chartered in 1751. Additional facilities and enterprises include Penn Medicine at Home, GSPP Rehabilitation, Lancaster Behavioral Health Hospital, and Princeton House Behavioral Health, among others.
Penn Medicine is an $11.9 billion enterprise powered by nearly 50,000 talented faculty and staff.

Title: Kennedy tells anti-vaccine activists they have a friend in Trump's White House
Article_Text:
Kennedy tells anti-vaccine activists they have a friend in Trump’s White House
Posted September 17, 2026 4:38 pm.
Last Updated September 17, 2026 6:25 pm.
WASHINGTON (AP) — Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. gave the keynote address Thursday at a conference of an anti-vaccine activist group he once chaired, telling the hundreds in attendance that they had a friend in President Donald Trump’s White House.
It was Kennedy’s first time appearing at the Children’s Health Defense conference since he became secretary. Kennedy took leave from the group when he launched his bid to become president in 2023, but his speech Thursday served as a sort of homecoming, offering him a platform from which to hail the administration’s steps to scale back vaccine guidance and reassure the activists in attendance that he was working to turn their priorities into policy.
“Let me be clear: You have a strong and steadfast friend in the White House. We’ve accomplished in 19 months things that would have seemed unthinkable two years ago,” he said.
The speech, peppered with questions about long established vaccine safety, also highlighted how once fringe views on vaccines have been given a prominent pulpit under the Trump administration.
Kennedy boasted about the administration’s moves to downsize the childhood vaccination schedule and reshape a key vaccine advisory board — steps that have since been halted by a judge.
Kennedy lauded Trump for pushing ahead with attempts to overhaul vaccine guidance, including an executive order last month calling for spacing out the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, against medical groups’ recommendations.
That executive order and now Kennedy’s keynote speech at the Children’s Health Defense conference mark a pivot by the White House and the Department of Health and Human Services, who earlier this year had appeared to be moving beyond vaccine efforts and toward a less contentious agenda on healthy food ahead of November’s midterm elections. HHS promoted the speech on its social media channels.
Kennedy, a longtime anti-vaccine activist, chaired Children’s Health Defense for years. He served as the group’s chief legal counsel and expanded it. After becoming health secretary last year, Kennedy moved at a blistering pace to overhaul public health guidance and revamp long-held precedents in vaccine policymaking.
Critics, among them many of the country’s top medical associations, have said the moves risk stoking vaccine hesitancy and sowing confusion among Americans who endured a crisis of trust in their public health agencies following the COVID-19 pandemic. That public confidence continues to erode.
“We have not taken vaccines away from anybody. We have preserved access. But we have started asking the questions that you and millions of American parents have been asking for years,” Kennedy told the group.
Mary Holland, the CEO of Children’s Health Defense, referred to Kennedy as “Bobby” and said the group has “gratitude beyond words” to the HHS secretary for “recognizing there are real consequential issues around childhood vaccinations.”
Kennedy’s appearance Thursday comes as the country faces its worst year for measles since 1991 and has seen seven reported measles-associated deaths in the last two years — more than the combined total of reported deaths over the previous three decades.
Pennsylvania officials have reported four measles-associated deaths this year. None of the four were vaccinated, according to the state health department. When state officials last month announced the first two of those deaths, it ignited a public feud between Gov. Josh Shapiro and Kennedy.
Shapiro blasted Kennedy’s appearance on the social media site X Thursday, saying Kennedy “chose to spend his time today addressing the premier vaccine-denial conference in America.”
Shapiro said the HHS secretary should have encouraged people to get vaccinated for measles, “yet he couldn’t bring himself to do it. Instead, he pushed a narrative that continues to stoke fear and mistrust.”
A representative from the White House did not respond to an Associated Press request for comment on Kennedy’s appearance at the event.
Following Kennedy onstage Thursday was Andrew Wakefield, an author of a since-discredited study that linked the MMR vaccine to autism, which has fueled the anti-vaccine movement even though it was retracted.
Widespread scientific consensus and decades of studies have firmly concluded there is no link between vaccines and autism.
Shaughnessy Naughton, founder of 314 Action, a group that recruits scientists to run for public office, said Kennedy’s decision to give a speech at the conference shows “the lack of seriousness he brings to HHS.”
“With a deadly measles outbreak killing people in Pennsylvania, the best thing Kennedy can do for Americans is step aside.”
___
Stobbe contributed from New York.
Fatima Hussein And Mike Stobbe, The Associated Press
