Title: Advocates organize 108-mile Women's Water Walk against Constitution Pipeline
Article_Text:
Advocates organize 108-mile Women’s Water Walk against Constitution Pipeline
SOUTHERN TIER (WBNG) -- Advocacy groups and community members announced plans on Thursday for a 108-mile demonstration along the route of the opposed Constitution Pipeline.
Organized by the Waterfall Unity Alliance, the Women’s Water Walk aims to spotlight environmental concerns surrounding regional waterways, agricultural land and nearby communities.
The proposed natural gas pipeline, sponsored by the Oklahoma-based Williams Companies, would stretch from northeastern Pennsylvania across upstate New York into Schoharie County.
While New York regulators denied permits for the project in 2016, citing water quality risks, developers and federal agencies are currently pursuing efforts to renew approvals.
“We are working to bring it so that human societies are not in conflict with the laws of nature and the natural world. We know that many people feel a deep sense of uneasiness about the imbalance that we’re living in right now,” said Karenna Gore, executive director of the Center for Earth Ethics at Union Theological Seminary.
The walk begins Saturday, Sept. 19, at 11 a.m. at Arctic Lake in Oquaga Creek State Park with a public ceremony. The opening event will feature a beachside fire ceremony and traditional musical performances by the Onondaga Women’s Singers, musician Bethany Yarrow and community artists.
“This Saturday, Indigenous grandmothers, community members, farmers, faith leaders, artists and more will begin the Women’s Water Walk,” said New York Frack Action Director Renee Vohelsang. “We’ll visit rivers, lakes, and other waterways, sing and pray, host educational events every evening and raise awareness throughout these communities that the Constitution Pipeline that we collectively stopped 10 years ago is unfortunately back again.”
Participants will reach the proposed pipeline corridor on Sunday while walking through Pine Hill State Forest near Sidney.
Walkers will then head into the village for a public reception scheduled from 3 p.m. to 6:30 p.m. at La Patrona on Main Street.
The reception will include performances by folk artist Dar Williams alongside community speakers, offering an informational forum on pipeline developments accompanied by discounted food.
The coordinated journey marks a renewed campaign among regional residents and environmental advocates following widespread protests against the pipeline a decade ago.
“This is a fight that we already fought in 2015. The sad thing is that these zombies keep coming back. They come back from the dead. It was already stopped. We showed that it was going to destroy all these waterways. None of that has changed. The only thing that’s changing now is Trump’s insistence that this happens,” said environmental advocate, actor and director Mark Ruffalo.
Organizers encourage everyone, including men, to participate in the Women’s Water Walk.
Information about the route, daily schedule, participation and ways to support the walk is available at womenswaterwalk.org.

Title: Try some international fare at Frankfurt's Kleinmarkthalle
Article_Text:
A visit to Frankfurt’s Kleinmarkthalle reminded me of one of my favorite pastimes when visiting home in southeastern Pennsylvania, close to Amish country: shopping at indoor farmers markets.
At the markets back home, it’s easy to get lost wandering among the stands of fresh vegetables, homemade baked goods, candies, meats, cheeses and countless handicraft items.
The Kleinmarkthalle offers the same bustle and variety as the Pennsylvania Dutch version, albeit with a distinctly international flair.
In English, the name translates to “little market hall.” But with nearly 160 vendors and about 1,500 square meters on mostly two floors, the place is anything but tiny.
The original market hall welcomed its first customers in 1879. The building was destroyed in the March 1944 heavy bombing raids on the city during World War II. The current hall opened in 1954 about 200 meters southwest of the original site.
On a recent Friday afternoon, the market was bustling with locals stocking up on pantry staples. Meandering tourists and an after-work crowd getting an early start on the weekend began filling up one of several wine bars in the hall. The variety of colors, sounds and smells was a jolt to the senses.
The diverse sellers and their range of products represent much of Europe — including Germany, Italy, Spain, Belgium and Greece — as well as the United Kingdom, the Middle East, Asia and South America.
The Pinocchio stand was an Italian foodie’s dream. I counted 14 different varieties of olives and an even wider assortment of smoked sausages, including horse and Napoli seasoned with fennel. I tried my first arancini, a traditional Sicilian deep-fried, breaded rice ball. I opted for the spinach and mozzarella version over the minced meat. It was buono, though it would have been better heated up.
Another sausage stall belongs to Ilse Schreiber, a fixture at the market since its opening in 1954, who has come to be known as the “Frankfurt Sausage Queen,” according to a story about her earlier this year in the Frankfurter Rundschau newspaper. She serves four kinds of sausage: yellow, meat, beef and Krakauer, cold with mustard.
Fresh vegetable stalls abound with uncommon produce, such as wax gourd, wild broccoli, purple tomatoes and a Thai cooking staple — holy basil. A bundle of seven herbs to make Frankfurt’s famous green sauce can also be purchased.
Other items that stood out included free-range chicken eggs with a light-blue hue, selling 10 for six euros. At the Tel Aviv Street Food stall, I found some unusual hummus varieties, including red beet, dark and peanut butter chocolate, espresso, paprika and tomato, along with the traditional version.
I was disappointed to find the Kinya Japanese food stand had closed early. I was eager to try some fresh sushi and miso soup. But I found Japanese street food at Inari-san, one of the newest vendors at the market. Its menu features drinks made with either cold matcha and oat milk or hojicha (roasted green tea). I tried one of the spring specials, the pink matcha cloud with hibiscus, elderberry, lychee and strawberry flavors and creamy matcha. The strong matcha flavor was noteworthy.
If you’re planning a trip to Frankfurt, the Kleinmarkthalle is worth a stop. My advice is to come hungry, as there are several bistros with seating and daily specials. The risotto with shrimp and zucchini, and tiramisu looked especially appealing on the day I visited. If you’re not hungry, there are several coffee shops and wine bars, including one on an outdoor terrace. I also recommend taking some cash, as not all vendors accept credit cards. And don’t forget some shopping bags and a cooler with ice for fresh cuts of meat or seafood from the basement fishmonger.
On the QT
Address: Hasengasse 5-7, 60311 Frankfurt am Main, Hesse, Germany
Hours: 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. Monday to Friday; 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. Saturday; closed Sunday and holidays.
Information: Online: kleinmarkthalle.de

Title: Trump administration repeals order coordinating Chesapeake Bay cleanup and restoration
Article_Text:
Trump administration repeals order coordinating Chesapeake Bay cleanup and restoration
The Trump administration has repealed an executive order that sought to coordinate the efforts of federal, state and local governments to protect and restore the Chesapeake Bay.
President Trump issued an executive order Wednesday to repeal a previous executive order that was established under the Obama administration back on May 12, 2009.
The original measure, known as Executive Order 13508, was designed to improve protection and restoration efforts for the Chesapeake Bay, the largest estuary in the United States.
According to a statement announcing the repeal, Executive Order 13508 "instituted a broad mandate for states and municipalities to contribute to improving the environmental health of the Chesapeake Bay, without providing clarity on how to implement that order's requirements."
In some instances, "this lack of clarity has led to harmful economic impacts on affected Americans," the statement added.
One example cited by the Trump administration is that the original order resulted in many localities having to implement stormwater management fees, commonly referred to as "rain taxes."
These fees sometimes reached hundreds of dollars in annual financial burdens imposed on residents and small businesses, even though nothing in the order required or explicitly justified such measures, the administration said, "with little to no measurable benefits to Chesapeake Bay or to those residents."
Administration says other programs have improved Chesapeake
Since Executive Order 13508 was signed, numerous other federal, state and local government initiatives and programs have resulted in significant improvements in the Chesapeake Bay, the administration noted.
Examples cited of this progress involved multiple jurisdictions of the Chesapeake Bay watershed, which includes New York, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Virginia, the District of Columbia, Delaware and West Virginia. These areas have collectively met 100% of their goal for sediment reduction, 90% of their goal for phosphorus reduction, and 57% of their goal for nitrogen reduction, according to Wednesday's statement.
These results are improving Chesapeake Bay health and have resulted "in thousands of acres of restored reefs and remain consistent with commitments made in the 2025 revised Chesapeake Bay Watershed Agreement," the administration said.
It was also noted that in 2026, scientists from the College of William & Mary, the Virginia Institute of Marine Science, FlowWest and the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science reported that the Chesapeake Bay's annual dead zone was projected to be among the smallest since 1985, or about 31% below the long-term average.
"Given this significant progress, and the need to provide clarity on how to continue improving the environmental health of the Chesapeake Bay, it is appropriate to revoke Executive Order 13508, which relevant jurisdictions have erroneously relied on to impose rain taxes, and to implement new actions and best practices that promote the economic health and wellbeing of the communities the Chesapeake Bay serves," the statement said.
Chesapeake Bay Foundation disappointed in new order
In response to the latest executive order, the Chesapeake Bay Foundation said the move "is jeopardizing decades of Bay restoration progress."
"For more than 40 years, the federal government has worked in partnership with the states across the watershed to reduce pollution to the Chesapeake Bay. That partnership was strengthened in 2009 when EO 13508 established a new framework for federal leadership, coordination, and accountability. Water does not respect state or political boundaries. What happens upstream affects people downstream," the foundation added.
The statement noted that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) recently recorded significant progress toward reducing pollution and restoring the Chesapeake Bay, however the new executive order "dismantles a key part of the federal-state framework that helped drive that progress."
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore also issued a statement condemning the move, as did Annapolis Mayor Jared Littmann.
"Trump's decision to slash federal support for the Chesapeake Bay is yet another attack against Maryland — this time on our farmers, fishers, and millions of people who rely on the watershed to filter their drinking water. The Bay is our jewel moving Maryland's economy forward, and we will protect it at all costs," Moore said on social media.
"Today we learned that environmental policies put in place 15 years ago to protect the Chesapeake Bay were revoked by the Trump Administration. The environmental health of the Chesapeake Bay, and local tributaries that feed the Bay, is not open for debate; it is not a policy preference that can be dialed back by Executive Order," said Littmann. "For Annapolis, protecting our waterways is a core duty to our residents, the local economy, and the future that we hand to the next generation."

Title: News of the Weird: Week of September 17, 2026
Article_Text:
I Do Not Like It, Not One Little Bit
It started with some posts and AI-made memes. Now authorities are warning of some strange social schemes. Newsweek reported on Sept. 10 that the Cat in the Hat, the character of Dr. Seuss fame, is at the center of a viral social media trend that has made its way around the globe. Images and videos -- sometimes AI-generated, sometimes of a real person in costume lurking outside of homes and schools at night -- of the Cat in the Hat are accompanied by menacing text warning of where the "Cat" is headed next and listing specific people or schools as its next targets. Students in Kansas, Georgia, Alabama and Kentucky have been apprehended and face criminal charges for participating in the hoax, and school districts in Pennsylvania, North Dakota and Minnesota have put their communities on alert. In Canada, the online hoax turned into a real nightmare when a teenage girl in British Columbia was chased by someone wearing a Cat in the Hat costume. She arrived home safely, but authorities are still looking for the perpetrator. "People should understand that behavior intended as a prank can have serious consequences when it causes another person to reasonably fear for their safety," said Corporal Devon Gerrits of West Kelowna RCMP. [Newsweek, 9/10/26]
Dumpster Diving Gone Awry
An alleged dumpster diver had to be rescued from a garbage truck on Sept. 2, the LA Times reported. A driver for Recology, a commercial waste collection company, picked up and emptied a dumpster, and then ran the trash compactor before hearing yelling from inside the truck and calling 911. When firefighters arrived, they couldn't just reach in and pull the man out -- he might have had crush injuries -- or have the driver dump all the trash out, which could have released hazardous material, such as glass, batteries and even vermin. What followed was a two-hour rescue effort. Paramedics were able to get an IV in the man's arm while firefighters carefully removed the trash with pike poles. The man was conscious when firefighters reached him, and he was taken to a local hospital. The extent of his injuries was undisclosed; one firefighter suffered a laceration injury during the rescue but is in stable condition. [LA Times, 9/3/26]
Stay on top of the news of the day
Subscribe to our free, daily e-newsletter to get Milwaukee's latest local news, restaurants, music, arts and entertainment and events delivered right to your inbox every weekday, plus a bonus Week in Review email on Saturdays.
The Golden Age of Air Travel
An unnamed Italian man made it all the way from Miami to Turin, Italy, with a dried crocodile head in his luggage, The Guardian reported on Sept. 8. The Turin unit of Italy's financial police squad said in a statement that the man wrapped the head in brown packing paper in an evidently feeble attempt to keep it from the astute eyes of customs officers. The man was swiftly taken into custody upon discovery of the croc, and is accused of smuggling a specimen belonging to a protected species. If convicted, the man could have to pay up to $270,000 USD or face a prison term of up to one year. [The Guardian, 9/8/26]
People With Issues
"So this is an interesting case, she thinks the neighbor is having relations with her husband so she pushes her way into the victim's house and then throws poop on the victim, a bucket of poop," is an actual thing a judge said during a recent bond hearing for Yirsi Machado Rivera, 50, of Miami. NBC 6 reported that on Sept. 8, Machado Rivera was arrested on charges of burglary and battery after attacking her neighbor with a bucket of human feces the night before. Machado Rivera told police that she did, in fact, have such a bucket that she was using while her toilet was out of commission; however, she denies dumping the doody, instead claiming that the neighbor attacked her with a bat. Judge Mindy Glazer ordered Machado Rivera to be held without bond and appointed a public defender. Oh, and leave the poor neighbor alone. [NBC 6, 9/9/26]
Rubber Duckie, You're the One
Police in Chatham County, Georgia, are looking for an unusual suspect. Among his questionable behavior? "Becoming infatuated" with a rubber duck that he played with for 10 minutes while soaking in a hot tub -- uninvited -- at someone else's home. According to WOTC, video footage from Sept. 1 shows an unidentified male trespassing on private property and going for a dip in the pool before availing himself of the hot tub sometime between 2 a.m. and 5 a.m. He also helped himself to over $1,000 worth of beach towels before riding away on his bicycle. "It's obviously not the biggest crime we've dealt with this month, but it has a lot of ick-factor," the local police department said in a social media post. "So, we'd like to find this guy so he doesn't do this to someone else." [WTOC, 9/9/26]
Not-So-Speedy Delivery
CBS News reported on Sept. 3 that the City of Denton Animal Services in Texas was contacted by employees at a local FedEx office after they discovered an unusual attempted shipment -- 191 tortoises and turtles. The shelter took custody of the animals and contacted the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, which began an investigation. The turtles and tortoises were then moved to the Dallas Zoo for secure shelter. "This unusual rescue is just one example of how our animal services team supports the community," the animal shelter said. "We're grateful for the strong partnerships with our animal welfare colleagues, who help us coordinate responses in unique situations like this." [CBS News, 9/3/26]
|  | 
Price Check on Corn Snakes
Shoppers browsing at the Heron Foods grocery store in Maryport, England, recently got a little more than they bargained for. On Sept. 2, BBC reported that a baby corn snake had been found in the bread aisle. "Crumbs," as the snake was called, was first taken to a local veterinary practice but ended up being put in the care of an animal education organization. Ben Nicholson of Pet Encounter said the organization has rescued more than 20 snakes so far this year. Whether Crumbs had been abandoned in the grocery store or had escaped from somewhere is unclear, but Nicholson said he believes high costs and a lack of education are playing parts in pets being abandoned. [BBC, 9/2/26]
Oh, Deer!
St. Johns County Sheriff's Office received a call about an unusual home break-in -- one that involved a large buck making its way into the bathroom. According to a Sept. 4 report from WSVN, after moving furniture and offering a few words of encouragement, the deputies were able to guide the buck out of the house ... only for it to fall into the pool outside the home's doorway. With further guidance, the buck got out of the pool and took off running. However, it came back one more time for a quick plunge before making its way back into neighboring trees. The sheriff's office social media post said, "The buck fled before deputies could issue a warning for trespassing." [WSVN, 9/4/26]

Title: Graber Duo Aims For Grade 1 Success At Hoosier
Article_Text:
Swan Good Bi will say hello to the Grand Circuit for the first time in his budding career when the undefeated Indiana-bred trotter meets nine rivals in the $475,100 USD Peter Haughton Memorial, a Grade 1 stakes for two-year-old colts and geldings, on Friday, Sept. 18 at Harrah’s Hoosier Park.
Trained by Henry Graber Jr., Swan Good Bi is five-for-five this season, with all of his races at Hoosier Park, and will head to the Haughton as the 8-5 morning line favourite. Four of his five victories have been against exclusively state-bred competition, including three triumphs in preliminary legs of the Indiana Sire Stakes for freshman male trotters.
Graber also will send out a Rbssouthwindcentra in the night’s other Grade 1 event, the $483,350 USD Jim Doherty Memorial for two-year-old female trotters. Rbssouthwindcentra, who joined Graber’s stable in late August after making her first three starts for co-owner/trainer Ronald Burks, is one-for-one for her new connections and the 3-1 third choice on the morning line.
The official winner of each the Haughton and Doherty, if Breeders Crown eligible as of June 1, will advance directly to their respective Breeders Crown final at Eldorado Scioto Downs in October, with no entry fee, and entitled to draw for post one through five.
Swan Good Bi, a son of Swan For All-Bange Bi, was a $42,254 yearling purchase at last fall’s Midwest Standardbred Horse Sale. He is owned by Indiana Stables of Rochester, Indiana, Frank Baldachino of Harvey Cedars, New Jersey, Michael Rosenthal of Las Vegas, Nevada and James Zito of Washington, Pennsylvania.
In his five starts this season, the gelding has shown the ability to win from both the front or from behind for Graber and driver Jordan Ross. He has won once gate-to-wire and twice when getting the lead on the way to the half. In his second race, Swan Good Bi came from seventh place at three-quarters, eight lengths back, to win by three-quarters of a length in 1:55.2 thanks to a :26.4 kick home. He posted another :26.4 final quarter in his next start as he rallied from fifth to win in a career-best 1:55. He also has a :26.3 last quarter to his credit in his most recent race on Aug. 22.
“Jordan has done it however he’s wanted to do it so far,” said Graber. “[Swan Good Bi] has raced any way, and he just tries his hardest. There were a couple of starts where he had to go :26.4 to get to the wire first, and that’s what he did.”
Swan Good Bi was scratched from a race on Sept. 2 at Hoosier Park, but Graber said, “We got the issue taken care of and I think he’s ready to roll.” The trainer added that the earner of $116,200 this season has been a professional on the track from the beginning.
“We never put [ear] plugs in him until he qualified,” said Graber. “That’s the first time he ever wore anything. In the barn, he never runs out of energy, but on the track, he’s the complete opposite. Anybody could drive him. He just does his work and he loves it.
“I feel we’re as good as anybody else in Indiana. He’s been pretty good to us.”
Swan Good Bi will leave from post four in the Haughton Memorial as he faces a number of out-of-state visitors.
Presidente, the 5-2 second choice, has won in 1:52 in the Kentucky Championship Series for trainer Nancy Takter and driver Scott Zeron and will start from post five. Dream Shaq (driver Dexter Dunn, post three, 7-2 odds), Big Time Trot S (Yannick Gingras, post eight, 12-1), Yankee Boss (Tim Tetrick, post nine, 15-1) and Red Andray (Mike Wilder, second-tier post 10, 20-1) all have won on the Pennsylvania stakes circuit while Southern Hanover (John DeLong, post six, 9-1) has triumphed on the Grand Circuit.
In the Jim Doherty Memorial, Rbssouthwindcentra will leave from post two with David Miller in the sulky as she looks for her fourth win in five starts, but her first in stakes company. She posted two wins and a second in conditioned races at Hoosier Park for her previous connections before being purchased by Hillside Stables of Dundee, Ohio, Hickory Hollow Stables of Spencerville, Indiana along with Baldachino and Indiana Stables.
The daughter of Tactical Landing-Cocktails N Dreams heads to the Doherty off a 7-3/4-length 1:55.1 victory in a conditioned race (two-year-old fillies, non-winners of $30,000) on Sept. 7 at Eldorado Scioto Downs with Ronnie Gillespie in the sulky.
“She beat them like a good horse is supposed to beat a group in a class like that,” said Graber. “She was pretty impressive. I was very happy with her.”
Birr Castle is the 2-1 morning line favourite in the Doherty after winning the Pennsylvania Sire Stakes championship on Sept. 7 at Pocono Downs at Mohegan Pennsylvania. She has four wins and a second in five starts and will leave from post one with Zeron driving for trainer Marcus Melander. Peaceful Way (Grade 1) winner Athenas Girl, another Melander trainee, is 5-2 and will go from post four with Dunn in the sulky.
“There are some pretty nice fillies in there, so she’s definitely going to have to take a step forward, but I think she can,” Graber said about Rbssouthwindcentra. “I’ve got confidence in her. She drew good, and she trained really good [on Tuesday]. We’ll see what happens.”
Rbssouthwindcentra is eligible to the Breeders Crown. Swan Good Bi is not Breeders Crown eligible.
“But we’re going for a lot of money, so if I get a cheque, I’ll be tickled,” said Graber.
Racing begins at 5:30 p.m. at Hoosier Park. The Peter Haughton Memorial is race 11 and will be followed by the Jim Doherty Memorial. For free Hoosier Park past performances, click here.

Title: Traveling WV: New River Otter Laps
Article_Text:
Traveling WV: New River Otter Laps
FAYETTE STATION, W.Va. (WCHS) — If there's ever been anyone who lives life to the fullest it's Nick "Nugget" Parsons.
A 21-year veteran whitewater guide, Parsons has made countless trips down the New, Gauley, Meadow and Blackwater rivers in West Virginia and the Youghiogheny River in Pennsylvania. Not to mention the Colorado River through the Grand Canyon.
It's an impressive resume and bragging would be understandable, but Parsons remains one of the most genuine people you will ever meet.
And make no mistake, he's a loyal West Virginian to the bone.
"My senior year in high school, the only thing I knew is that I didn't want to go to college," Parsons said. "I was getting into trouble a little bit, nothing horrible. Fortunately I had a teacher who said, 'You ought to go train to be a raft guide, it's free and if you're into it, great, if not, you got to have an experience,' and I just got hooked on it."
Hooked would be an understatement. Parsons sleeps, eats and breathes being on any river.
Always one for a challenge, Parsons and a few fellow rafting guides decided to try something new a few years ago, actually swimming the New River with no boat, no paddle, just a life jacket, helmet and their knowledge of the river.
"At first we were like, 'Do you want to swim it?' Then, just being goofy, we said, 'I feel like a mermaid. Let's call it a mermaid lap." Parsons said.
That mermaid lap moniker was quickly replaced after a bizarre encounter with a wild river otter. Parsons and his good friend Matt Sutterland were in the middle of a mermaid lap.
"This otter pops up and just stares at my buddy, it was like a minute-long stare, so ever since that otter stared at him we're just like, 'Dude, this is an otter lap,'" he said.
The name stuck.
At first you might feel like Parsons and company are nothing but adrenaline junkies, risking their lives for a new thrill or bragging rights. Parsons explains that couldn't be farther from the truth.
"Somebody that's not used to whitewater, they think we're doing it for some Evel Knievel-like rush," he said. "Knowing where the hazards are and knowing the differences between water levels, we wait until it gets to five feet or 10,000 CFS (cubic feet per second) at that magic number or higher. It's just waves. I've done it at least 40 times now, it's more of a Zen thing, a connection with the water."
However, Parsons warns these otter laps aren't for everyone.
"We're not swimming it without knowing the river really well," he said. "It's crucial."
For anyone with limited or zero river experience rafting or kayaking, Parsons has five words.
"That's a bad move man."
If you'd like to see more of Parsons' otter laps and his other whitewater adventures, you can follow and subscribe to his YouTube channel.

Title: How Sept. 17 Became Constitution and Citizenship Day
Article_Text:
Sept. 17 is Constitution Day and Citizenship Day in the United States, and it commemorates the signing of the U.S. Constitution, which took place on that date in 1787.
The signing marked the start of a stand for the American way of life that took a harrowing journey through the American Revolution.
But it officially began when 42 delegates to the Constitutional Convention met for the last time in Philadelphia, and 39 signed onto what became one of the founding documents of this country.
Here’s what to know about Constitution Day and Citizenship Day—often simply called Constitution Day—and why it’s worth celebrating.
The Road to Ratification
While most of us know the results of America’s rebellion from England, it’s easy to forget that the founding of the nation was done with intention and procedure.
Delegates from each colony came together with instructions to revise the original framework of government, called the Articles of Confederation.
Instead, they did what many early Americans did and threw out the rulebook, creating a new governmental system.
The debate took months, but eventually a division of power was decided upon, and the resulting Constitution took shape, splitting power between three branches of federal government and reserving other powers to the states.
Only three delegates declined to sign, with one of their primary objections being the absence of a Bill of Rights, which was ratified in 1791.
However, as the new system of government required, the signing by the delegates did not immediately make it the law of the land; ratification by the states was required.
The new form of government needed at least nine of the 13 states to sign off. Delaware was the first to take that step, and New Hampshire was the ninth, on June 21, 1788.
The federal government began operation under the newly ratified Constitution in 1789.
Constitution Week
While Sept. 17 is the official Constitution Day, it is just one part of Constitution Week, which will be observed from Sept. 17 to Sept. 23 of this year.
Observance of Constitution Week began in 1956 and features a presidential proclamation and a spotlight from many in government.
This year, President Donald Trump issued a proclamation commemorating the 239th anniversary of the signing of the Constitution and the founding of the Republic.
“Over two centuries later, we remain more committed than ever to protecting and cherishing the fundamental values of America and the vision of our forefathers for a just, prosperous, and free Nation,” Trump said.
The presidential proclamation reminded Americans that the Founding Fathers took their own lives into their hands when they assembled at Independence Hall to sign the document and “form a more perfect Union.”
Trump called on school teachers, as well as state and local leaders, to “educate America’s pupils on the rights and responsibilities of citizenship under our constitutional order.”
Federal Requirements
Constitution Day is more than just a holiday to remember a significant event in American history.
In fact, every federal educational institution that receives federal funds must provide materials about the Constitution on Sept. 17.
This was reiterated this year by the United States Department of Education, which issued a reminder on Sept. 16 to educational institutions about their responsibility.
While the law doesn’t state what instruction must be offered, or how the information needs to be presented, some suggested activities include providing students with the opportunity to recite the Pledge of Allegiance, hosting a mock Constitutional Convention, and conducting a public reading of the Constitution.
Interestingly enough, however, Constitution Day is not a federal employee holiday.
Frequently, Constitution Day is marked by naturalization ceremonies at federal courts.
The U.S. Courts describe the observance of those ceremonies as one way to participate in the day.
While U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services is typically responsible for the naturalization ceremonies, federal judges often hold events when they fall on Citizenship Day.
History of Citizenship Day
While the Constitution was signed in the late 1700s, the “citizenship” part of the holiday was added much later.
The modern Citizenship Day was established in 1940 and was initially on the third Sunday in May. It was called “I Am an American Day.”
During a time when the nation was still dealing with the aftermath of WWI and the immediate impacts of WWII, the day was meant to recognize those who attained their American citizenship.
An act by Congress moved the observance to Sept. 17 in 1952, and also renamed it “Citizenship Day,” coinciding with the anniversary of the signing of the Constitution.
Congress officially named the day Constitution Day and Citizenship Day with the stated purpose of commemorating the Constitution and recognizing those who, “by coming of age or by naturalization, have become citizens.”
In his proclamation for the year 2026, the president asserted that “Guided by the most righteous political document ever conceived, America remains the greatest force for good in the history of the world.”

Title: Isaac Yiadom promotion puts Commanders cornerbacks on immediate notice
Article_Text:
The Washington Commanders' decision to sign cornerback Isaac Yiadom from the practice squad to their active roster sent an unmistakable message. Those in power were not satisfied with the Week 1 performance, and the stakes have risen.
Yiadom is a well-traveled cornerback. He's never been a world-beater, but he's experienced and can play well in the defensive rotation or on special teams. If the former Boston College standout has been called up this quickly, he's obviously made a good impression.
And the corners who underperformed against the Philadelphia Eagles are now nervously looking over their shoulders.
Isaac Yiadom gives the Commanders another physical cornerback if others fail against the Cowboys
Amik Robertson and Rasul Douglas performed well, especially in the former's case. Mike Sainristil did not, and the frustration was big enough that head coach Dan Quinn criticized him in public.
With the Dallas Cowboys' potent wide receiver George Pickens and CeeDee Lamb up next, the Commanders have given themselves another option. And even though Yiadom would be thrown into the proverbial fire if he saw the field, he has more size and length than anyone else in the cornerback room besides Douglas.
This might be crucial if Sainristil or Robertson get exposed.
Washington isn't in a position to sit back and let things play out. They have too much riding on this season, and starting 0-2 would be disastrous. Yiadom may not be able to solve every issue, but it's another body who knows how to slot in at a moment's notice.
It's not the perfect answer, but it will have to do for now. Especially with 2025 second-round selection Trey Amos currently on injured reserve with an ankle sprain.
Both Quinn and defensive coordinator Daronte Jones believe Sainristil can turn things around if he adds some extra urgency to his game. But general manager Adam Peters was right to acquire a contingency plan quickly if Lamb and Pickens get the upper hand at AT&T Stadium.
Expecting miracles from Yiadom is unrealistic. He played just 16 percent of defensive snaps in 14 games for the New Orleans Saints last season. The 2018 third-round pick gave up an 86.7 percent completion rate and a 133.1 passer rating when targeted. But he is long and physical, which might be enough if his number is called.
And if this lights a fire under Sainristil or any other cornerback in a prominent role, that's an added bonus.
The situation remains precarious for the Commanders. They know the danger Pickens and Lamb possess, and quarterback Dak Prescott has torched Washington throughout his career. The defensive front seven has to apply pressure, which they did effectively versus Philadelphia, but the coverage has to do its job against arguably the league's best wide receiver duo.
Anything less, and the Commanders will have a big problem. And then, it wouldn't be surprising to see Yiadom introduced at some stage.
Time will tell on all fronts.

Title: After ending winless ruts, NYCFC, Red Bulls meet for high-stakes derby
Article_Text:
Field Level Media
                
18 Sep 2026, 02:35 GMT+10
            
(Photo credit: Mark Smith)
Bragging rights in the Hudson River Derby might be secondary given the precarious nature of the playoff positioning for New York City FC and the New York Red Bulls when the teams convene Friday night at Yankee Stadium.
Both teams have nine games remaining and are separated by two points after stopping lengthy winless skids last week.
NYCFC (8-9-8, 32 points) begin the week in eighth and own the goal differential tiebreaker over ninth-place Cincinnati since they have outscored opponents 39-33, while Cincinnati has been outscored 59-52. NYCFC trail seventh-place Philadelphia by one point and sixth-place Orlando by two points, and those teams also have nine games remaining.
New York City heads into Friday 1-3-4 over the past eight matches. The Pigeons earned their first win since July 25 on Saturday with a 2-0 victory at Real Salt Lake, when Nicolas Fernandez and Luighi scored on either side of the halftime break.
'I think we found quite a decent balance when we play against the Red Bulls, but we're also very aware of what's at stake,' NYCFC coach Pascal Jansen said. 'It's a derby, it's emotional, means a lot to our fans from both sides. So it's going to be an intense game no matter what and for us, it's mainly about making sure we keep things under control, stick to the plan that we will make and make sure we get a good result.'
The Red Bulls (8-11-6, 30 points) sit in 10th and are two points behind NYCFC and Cincinnati while carrying a minus-15 goal differential. New York is attempting to win consecutive matches for just the third time this season and the first time since May 9-13.
Like their rivals, the Red Bulls ended a lengthy winless rut (0-4-2) Saturday with a 1-0 victory at Columbus. Ronald Donkor broke the stalemate in the 89th minute with his second goal of the year.
'We have not had enough to show for ourselves on certain days,' Red Bulls coach Michael Bradley said. 'We feel really good that now in this week-long road trip we take four points, two shutouts, and so, we are going to use this as a way to really build momentum.'
--Field Level Media

Title: USMNT camp highlighted by presence of 16-year-old F Cavan Sullivan
Article_Text:
Field Level Media
                
18 Sep 2026, 01:25 GMT+10
            
(Photo credit: Vincent Carchietta)
After taking MLS by storm over the past two months, 16-year-old Cavan Sullivan will get his first chance to play with the United States men's national team when it reconvenes this weekend at Atlanta.
The USMNT will take the field for the first time since the World Cup when it faces Peru on Sept. 26 at Orlando, Chile on Sept. 29 at St. Louis, Mexico on Oct. 3 at Glendale, Ariz., and Canada Oct. 6 in St. Paul, Minn.
Sullivan, who has put a charge into the Philadelphia Union of late, will headline a group of young players being introduced to national team duty. The other half of the team will be made up of USMNT veterans, although forwards Christian Pulisic and Folarin Balogun will not be on the squad.
Head coach Mauricio Pochettino stressed that the roster in no way represents the group that has priority heading toward the next World Cup in 2030.
'The 28 players that are going to be involved in these four games, for different circumstances, are the best players we want see and we want to work with. That's it,' Pochettino said at a press conference in New York on Thursday.
Pochettino will have 28 players in camp, with 13 of those seeking their first USMNT appearance.
Sullivan, a Philadelphia native, has shown his promise with six goals and 11 assists in 23 matches (16 starts) this season. He has goal contributions in seven consecutive games to lead Philadelphia's 10-game unbeaten run since the end of the World Cup break.
Among other players invited to USMNT camp for the first time are defender Neil Pierre, Sullivan's Union teammate, midfielder Zavier Gozo of English side Crystal Palace and forward Julian Hall of the New York Red Bulls, all of whom are 19 or younger.
Those players will get their first taste of USMNT culture alongside World Cup participants in Sebastian Berhalter, Alex Freeman, Gio Reyna, Auston Trusty and Malik Tillman.
'This is the beginning of a fresh start for everyone, and we are excited in these first matches to bring a group of experienced players along with some young talents who have great potential,' Pochettino said.
The United States got off to a promising start at the World Cup with a dominating victory over Paraguay before going through the red-card controversy created when Balogun was ejected from a knockout-round victory over Bosnia and Herzegovina only to be reinstated for the round-of-16 game against Belgium.
The USMNT was eliminated in a lackluster 4-1 loss to Belgium.
'It's a completely different approach than it was in the past,' Pochettino said of the start to another World Cup cycle. 'The World Cup is in four years. We need to work with different objectives and goals.'
--Field Level Media

Title: BMW Told Owners This Part Was Maintenance-Free. A Lawsuit Says Otherwise
Article_Text:
UPDATE: 2026/09/19 11:29 EST BY CHRISTOPHER SMITH
Another Lawsuit For Transfer Cases
We've updated the post with information on another class action lawsuit against BMW for more powertrain issues, this time related to alleged transfer case problems.
According to a class action lawsuit that was filed last month, BMW owners in Pennsylvania allege that they were deliberately misled about their cars' maintenance needs. According to the suit that names BMW North America as a defendant, certain X5, X6, and X7 SUVs have a defective front differential design that can fail prematurely, despite a purported "lifetime" maintenance interval for its diff fluid.
The named plaintiff in the class-action case is Alex Heckler, the owner of a 2020 BMW X5 M50i that he purchased second-hand in 2021 with about 10,000 miles. It suffered front differential failure in 2024, something the lawsuit alleges is due to the automaker not providing a maintenance interval despite evidence one was needed.
The Plaintiffs Have An Issue With BMW's Recommended Service Schedule
The class-action lawsuit is a collective filing taken by owners, represented in part by Heckler, of the G05 X5 from the 2019 to 2026 model years, the G06 X6 sold from 2020 to present, and the G07 X7 from 2019 to present. The suit claims that BMW was aware of potential failure points in the front differential, both due to its design and by not requiring fluid changes, that could lead to failure. Per the complaint, Heckler's front differential failed at 47,000 miles in November 2024, as confirmed by a technician at his local BMW dealership.
The mechanic noted that there was a fair amount of metallic material in the fluid, suggesting some of the hardware had worn down to the point of failure. According to the lawsuit, the front differential was still full after being removed, proof that the breakdown wasn't the result of a leak but instead failure of the differential fluid to provide adequate lubrication and heat protection over years of use.
Per the suit, the dealership technician who worked on Heckler's X5 said that front differential failure was a common occurrence in the vehicles that the claim represents. Although Heckler's X5 was still within BMW's standard 50,000-mile powertrain warranty limit, it had just recently timed out since it had been more than four years since the SUV's first in-service date. As a result, the plaintiff paid $6,199.01 in parts and labor for his front differential to be replaced in its entirety.
What Does The BMW Lawsuit Claim?
According to the filing, which took place at the United States District Court for the eastern district of Pennsylvania, BMW was aware that its lifetime differential fluid needed to be changed occasionally in order to work. The lawsuit contends it has proof, pointing to the drain and fill holes found on the front differential of the X5, X6, and X7. According to the plaintiff's logic, BMW wouldn't include service ports on the front differential if it truly believed the fluid to have a forever lifespan.
That said, we doubt that alone is proof that BMW knowingly advertised a faulty product with a "lifetime" guarantee. There are other reasons to drain and refill a front differential aside from scheduled maintenance. For example, in the event of an accident or other misfortune that damages the diff, it would need to be replaced with a new OEM unit. It wouldn't make any sense for BMW or its suppliers to ship a part that had been pre-filled, so the repair shop would have to add the fluid on their own.
As of 2025, BMW now recommends draining and refilling front and rear differentials and the transfer case for its all-wheel-drive M cars, a subset that would include Heckler's X5 M50i, every five years or 50,000 miles. The lawsuit contends that had that maintenance schedule been in place before, the BMW owner wouldn't have had a problem. Factually, however, that seems inaccurate. The SUV hadn't yet reached 50,000 miles, and if it had only been "slightly over" four years old at the time of failure – as the lawsuit claims given the expired warranty – it wouldn't have gotten to the five-year threshold either.
We asked BMW if it could either acknowledge or refute the lawsuit's claims, and the automaker said that it would not be able to comment on pending or ongoing litigation matters.
This Might Not Be The Only Case
All that said, Heckler's problems with his X5 were not isolated occurrences. One participant in the G05/G06 forum on BimmerPost aggregated 65 total reported front differential failures across the site's X5/X6/X7 communities as of January 2026, most of them applying to 2020 or 2021 models. Per the accumulated data – which has not been verified and was self-reported by forum members – the average mileage of the failure was around 47,000 miles, coinciding with Heckler's BMW's front differential replacement.
If front differential failure is as widespread as the lawsuit claims, BMW could potentially solve the problem by recalling affected vehicles and opening an avenue for its owners to claim refunds on prior repairs. Nonetheless, the class action is demanding more than $5 million in restitution for the plaintiffs' vehicle failures and mechanic costs.
Another Lawsuit For Transfer Cases
It seems fluid in front differentials isn't the only powertrain issue BMW owners are having with their vehicles. A class action lawsuit was filed in December 2025 against BMW, with several plaintiffs alleging a defect in the transfer case for just about every BMW model equipped with one from 2019 through 2025. That includes BMW's best-selling vehicle, the X3. The lawsuit alleges BMW was aware of a defect in the transfer case that could eventually lead to failure.
Per the lawsuit, transfer cases in affected vehicles "have a uniform defect that causes the clutch system to improperly transmit torque between the front and rear wheels." This causes a shuddering sensation in the driveline, which could eventually lead to failure. The suit cites a BMW technical service bulletin calling for fluid changes as proof BMW is aware of the problem, and claims BMW requires owners to pay out-of-pocket for fluid changes that ultimately do not fix the problem.
CarBuzz Insight – Why This Matters
Consumer protections on faulty products are fairly robust in the United States, so if the class action goes to trial as its filing requests, there's a decent chance that BMW will have to fork over the cash. There are some issues with the lawsuit that could damage the plaintiffs' claim – like the inaccurate conclusion drawn from the front differential's fill and drain ports – but that may not be enough to keep a jury of peers to find the carmaker at fault.
At the very least, it should give consumers pause when they see lifetime guarantees on anything, especially vehicle maintenance items.
                        Source: ClassAction.org

Title: Looking for Public Transit Votes
Article_Text:
The problems with public transit in the San Francisco Bay Area have been building for years. The election this November could determine whether they get better or much, much worse.
Prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, Bay Area Rapid Transit, the agency that runs trains between San Francisco, Oakland, and other nearby cities, was the pride of the region. The agency made more of its revenue from rider fares than nearly any other transit system in the country. When ridership dropped, first because of the pandemic shutdowns and later because of the lasting shift to remote work, revenue dropped too. It was a similar story for the patchwork of smaller public-transit agencies within San Francisco and in the surrounding counties that make up the regional transportation network. Federal pandemic-relief funds and one-off state support have held things together, precariously, until now. But without new funding, agencies say they’ll need to cut service and hike fares, resulting in fewer choices for people moving around the region.
This is a political challenge. Backers of the upcoming Connect Bay Area Transit measure, which would raise the sales tax by 1 percent in San Francisco and 0.5 percent in the four surrounding counties, are hoping voters will agree to pay more essentially to preserve something they already have. That’s a tough ask at a time when the cost of living is the most politically salient issue around the country. To be sure, the campaign for the November ballot measure is highlighting the improvements that agencies could make with the estimated $1 billion annual revenue hike, including safety upgrades and better integration of regional services. But their basic pitch is to “save” public transit.
If the transit measure had been referred to the ballot by a local or county government, it would have required approval by two-thirds of voters. But because the measure is a citizen initiative, it needs only a bare majority of votes in order to pass. Backers of the measure designed it that way on purpose, with state enabling legislation sponsored by Bay Area Democrats having passed last year.
“The polling on this issue has been consistent for several years now and it is polling in the mid-50s,” says Adina Levin, director of the advocacy group Seamless Bay Area. But the public’s appetite to pay for transportation improvements is a moving target, even though the idea tends to be popular with voters. Most public transit referendums, raising sales taxes to pay for transit improvements, are successful once they make it to the ballot. But it depends a lot on what specifically the electorate is being sold, and on who is doing the selling.
Nashville voters in 2018 resoundingly rejected a transit tax that was meant to pay for an ambitious rail plan developed by a mayor who, by the time of the vote, had resigned amid a sex scandal. Half a decade later they approved a more modest plan to improve bus service along with upgrades to streets and sidewalks. So far this year voters around the country have approved 33 ballot measures supporting public transit and rejected four, according to the American Public Transportation Association. One measure that went down to defeat was a statewide gas tax increase in Oregon tied to an ill-fated transportation funding plan. The plan was focused largely on roads, but its defeat has been bad for transit riders too. Portland’s transit system, TriMet, instituted widespread service cuts in August and eliminated two bus lines altogether. Philadelphia’s transit system is still waiting for additional funding from the state, but the politics of the state legislature, with a Senate dominated by rural Republicans, have made it a tough sell. Other measures are on the ballot this fall, including a half-cent sales tax to support transportation improvements and other programs in Tempe, Ariz., and expansion of a transit-dedicated sales tax in Seattle.
A proposal to build intercity passenger rail service on Colorado’s Front Range, the booming population center in the eastern part of the state, will go before voters too. That proposal has been in the works for years, as the communities along Interstate 25 have grown and traffic in the area has worsened. The measure would create a 0.333 percent sales tax to fund rail service within the Front Range Passenger Rail District. Colorado Gov. Jared Polis had initially pushed to have the tax on the ballot in 2024. But planners wanted to continue refining the concept, especially in light of disappointment over a voter-backed plan to build out rail transit in the Denver area a few decades ago that failed to deliver on its goals. Two years ago, Denver area residents also approved a measure allowing the regional transit authority to spend more of the revenue it collects.
The funding environment for transit is in some ways more difficult now than it was a few years ago. Passenger rail received new support during the Biden administration, and ridership is up on Amtrak. Some new services, like the restored Gulf Coast train between Mobile, Ala., and New Orleans, have exceeded expectations for ridership. But Congress has yet to renew the surface transportation spending package, and some active proposals would reduce federal funding for transit and passenger rail.
The Colorado intercity rail service will start slow, eventually running 10 daily trips between Denver and Fort Collins to the north and eight daily trips between Denver and Pueblo to the south, according to a service plan. The trains would run on existing tracks. Partly because of the uncertainty surrounding federal funding, the service plan doesn’t rely on federal grants at all — unusual for new rail service.
“We want to be able to deliver regardless of where the political winds are blowing,” says John Putnam, a former U.S. Department of Transportation official who chaired the Front Range Passenger Rail District. (Putnam clarified he was speaking only in his personal capacity, not on behalf of the campaign for the tax measure.)
Asking voters to approve higher taxes is always a risk, and perhaps especially so when affordability is a driving political concern. But it’s not as if the future looks any easier.
“Things generally get more complicated and more expensive the longer you wait,” Putnam says. “Our hope and anticipation is that this is the right time.”

Title: Josh Shapiro's not an AI "doomer," but the Pa. governor wants federal regulations for the industry
Article_Text:
Josh Shapiro’s not an AI ‘doomer,’ but the Pa. governor wants federal regulations for the industry
“I am not a doomer,” the governor said at a tech summit, but he pressed for stronger safety regulations.
Gov. Josh Shapiro on Thursday called on the federal government to enact new guardrails on artificial intelligence, days after a number of tech industry figures raised concerns about the danger posed by AI’s rapid development.
As he spoke in Pittsburgh, the Democratic governor was critical of both House Speaker Mike Johnson (R., La.) and President Donald Trump for refusing to erect such safety measures “whether out of willful ignorance or personal greed.”
And, he said, he does not believe that concern about this technology “is a hoax, as our president has called it.”
But as he urged more regulation of the industry, he also warned against adopting an overly pessimistic view of the technology.
“I am not a doomer. I don’t think it is inevitable that AI is going to take over the world, or that someone will misuse it to kill us all or to do harm,” Shapiro said.
Shapiro’s appearance at the AI Horizons PGH Summit, sponsored by Microsoft and the Bank of New York, helps position the governor as a leader on the issue among Democrats.
Last week, former President Barack Obama urged Democrats running for the White House to define the risks of AI, according to the Washington Post.
That advice — and Shapiro’s speech — followed warnings from AI executives last week that the technology is developing too quickly, and that it poses threats to human life.
“I won’t lie to you — there are real dangers,” said Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, adding that the development of AI has accelerated much faster than he had expected.
Shapiro — who has consistently led his November opponent, Stacy Garrity, in polls — is widely expected to pursue a presidential run in 2028 after this fall’s reelection contest.
A growing concern among voters, AI is expected to continue being a significant issue for candidates, and Shapiro has shifted his stance in recent months to reflect questions about the technology.
In August, he issued an executive order that restricts data center development in the state, a noticeable shift from when he enthusiastically supported a $20 billion commitment from Amazon last year to build at least two data centers in Bucks and Luzerne Counties.
Shapiro now says future developments require local approval for projects to receive state permits, which in effect may block many developments from moving forward.
“The real folks I listen to are the people of Pennsylvania,” Shapiro told Politico before Thursday’s speech.
Six in 10 likely Pennsylvania voters oppose construction of data centers to house artificial intelligence, according to last month’s poll from The Inquirer, the New York Times, and Siena University.
In contrast to the growing voices calling for AI guardrails, President Donald Trump on Monday wrote on social media that the only guardrail the industry needed it already had: “a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.”
Shapiro, in his speech, said he is calling on the federal government to establish “strict rules of the road” regarding AI, and then to enforce those rules.
“I’ve called on the federal government to step up and regulate the AI industry, just like they do for nearly every other industry,” he said.
Industry leaders should not exclusively guide the regulatory process, Shapiro said. The government should also work with leading researchers.
What is vital, Shapiro said, is establishing rules that require independent third-party oversight of “frontier” — most advanced — models, increasing transparency into the development of these models, and prioritizing safety.
Protections might mean placing some limits on technology sharing and slowing down frontier AI development until we can be sure that these systems are safe, Shapiro said.
Acknowledging that building a regulatory network from the ground up is hard work, Shapiro took a jab at Congress, and Johnson in particular, when he said “too many in Congress are content to do absolutely nothing.”
Shapiro noted that the speaker adjourned the House until after the election just days after companies issued “apocalyptic” warnings about the real dangers of AI.
“He has abdicated his responsibility to lead at a time when we cannot afford weakness and retreat,” Shapiro said of Johnson.
The United States should work with other nations on an international consensus on how to use AI, but that is hard to do when Trump has “isolated” us from the world, Shapiro said.
When Trump meets with Chinese President Xi Jinping next week, Shapiro said, he hopes Trump will “leave bluster and the showmanship at the door” and engage productively with him.
As for the home front, Shapiro said, “I’ll be leading the conversation here in Pennsylvania for safe and responsible use of AI.”

Title: Pa is asking for CDC more emergency aid, but only if measles deaths are reported
Article_Text:
Pa. is asking CDC for more emergency aid, but only if measles deaths are reported
State health officials requested more help from the CDC on the condition that the agency publicly recognize four deaths here linked to the disease.
Pennsylvania is seeking more emergency aid from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to respond to the state’s largest measles outbreak in more than 30 years, but only if the federal agency acknowledges the four measles-associated deaths Pennsylvania has reported.
The CDC has so far declined to publicly report Pennsylvania’s measles-associated deaths, reportedly at the direction of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
The CDC’s measles dashboard says the agency is still reviewing death data and developing a new standard definition of a measles-associated death.
Public health experts say it is highly unusual for the CDC to challenge routine disease surveillance by states, and delaying death reporting could affect efforts to control Pennsylvania’s outbreak, which has sickened more than 700 people and is now this year’s largest in the country.
“The CDC’s choice not to publicly recognize the deaths undermines our response,” Pennsylvania Health Secretary Debra Bogen wrote in a Wednesday letter to CDC Director Erica Schwartz, a nominee of President Donald Trump who was confirmed to the post last month. The state shared the letter with The Inquirer.
Bogen wrote that the CDC’s Epi-Aid program, which provides short-term technical assistance and subject matter expertise during health crises, will benefit Pennsylvania’s outbreak response only if she can assure her staff that the CDC’s assistance “will not will not undermine their efforts and will partner with them toward a common goal, including publication of timely, accurate information about the outbreak.”
The CDC said it had not received Pennsylvania’s Epi-Aid request “through its normal channels” and accused state leaders of politicizing outbreak response. Federal outbreak assistance and national mortality reporting are separate issues, the agency said.
“CDC will not submit to political blackmail that conditions critical public health assistance,” the agency said in a statement Thursday. “The people of Pennsylvania should never be used as leverage in a political dispute over how deaths are classified.”
The back-and-forth comes after the CDC has said the state is not cooperating with the agency and, for days, highlighted the fact that health officials here had not requested an Epi-Aid team from the agency, as other states with measles outbreaks have done.
An ongoing political clash
Pennsylvania defines a “measles-associated death” as one that occurs within 30 days of symptom onset in a person with clinical evidence of infection and a positive laboratory test, and who did not die of another unrelated cause, like a car crash.
The state announced its first two measles-associated deaths in late August, but provided no information on them beyond that both were in unvaccinated Lancaster County residents. The county coroner later said he did not believe measles caused one of the deaths, involving an infant with a lacerated spleen who tested positive for measles, though physicians have noted measles can weaken the organ and make it more likely to rupture.
The coroner, an elected Republican, said a second death, in another infant with a fatal genetic condition, was caused by measles.
Two other measles-associated deaths were reported this week in Mifflin and Jefferson Counties. Mifflin County’s coroner confirmed the death of an unvaccinated 18-year-old who died from a serious neurological complication of measles; Jefferson County’s coroner said measles led to the death of an unvaccinated 40-year-old woman with severe respiratory conditions.
Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, has criticized Kennedy, a longtime anti-vaccine activist, for spreading misinformation and contributing to lower vaccination rates that he says have allowed the virus to spread through 38 counties in Pennsylvania.
Kennedy had accused the state of “fabricating” two deaths, although he later acknowledged one was caused by measles.
Both have said the other is politicizing the deaths, the first reported in Pennsylvania and the highest death toll linked to the virus nationally in more than three decades.
On Wednesday, the state reported that 731 people have been sickened in Pennsylvania so far this year — with 117 cases reported in the last week alone. Just over 140 people had been hospitalized, with 18% of them under 18.
An Epi-Aid team typically works with a state for one to three weeks to provide technical assistance investigating an “urgent public health problem,” according to the CDC’s website.
“The focus of an Epi-Aid investigation is to assist partners in making rapid, practical decisions for actions to control and prevent the public health problem,” the website reads.
In the letter sent to Schwartz on Wednesday, Bogen said that the state is already working closely with the CDC and recently made two requests for “technical assistance” from agency staff.
She said the state appreciated “the CDC professional staff’s timely and thoughtful responses.”
Since the state is still seeing measles cases and deaths, Bogen said, officials are now requesting an Epi-Aid team from the CDC.
But Bogen will rescind the Epi-Aid request “if CDC is unable to transparently and accurately communicate information about those measles-associated deaths,” the letter said.
“While our professional teams have collaborated well on the measles outbreak response, including the identification and reporting of four measles-associated deaths, CDC’s public communication about the deaths has not been reflective of our close collaboration,” she wrote.
Protocol on counting measles deaths
The CDC’s measles web page, updated weekly with new case information, has featured an asterisk in the column for 2026 deaths.
The CDC initially posted an explanation saying it had omitted Pennsylvania’s deaths because “available information does not establish whether measles caused or contributed to the deaths or whether the individuals died from other causes while infected with measles.”
The agency later updated its asterisk language to note that the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) “does not currently have any death records from 2026 that indicate measles is the underlying cause.”
The web page also says that the agency is working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to develop a standardized case definition for measles deaths, in an effort to promote “consistent classification and reporting of measles deaths across jurisdictions.”
Pennsylvania health officials said their definition of a measles-associated death is modeled after existing CSTE definitions for deaths from other respiratory illnesses, like flu.
In the interim, the CDC will wait to report measles-related deaths until the NCHS “identifies measles as the underlying cause based on death record information submitted by the states,” the agency said in a statement to The Inquirer.
Relying on the NCHS for measles deaths is a departure from the CDC’s standard protocol for tracking infectious diseases, said Demetre Daskalakis, a former director of the National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases, which oversees state immunization efforts and disease surveillance within the CDC.
In the past, the CDC has relied on the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System, its system for monitoring dozens of diseases, such as meningitis, pertussis, botulism, and measles. States submit new case reports as they obtain them.
States will typically alert the CDC in advance of entering data into the database when it is urgent — for instance, signs of an infectious-disease outbreak or a death associated with an outbreak.
This is the approach Pennsylvania’s health department said it took to report its first measles-associated deaths earlier this month.
By contrast, the NCHS database tracks all deaths in the United States, and is the source of the routine Vital Statistics reports. States upload death certificates, and the CDC’s system skims data about primary and secondary cause of death, and any additional details noted. The process can take weeks because states enter each death individually.
With both databases, information entered by states is reviewed for completeness (for instance, to ensure no required fields have been left blank) and then recorded.
“Generally, they are cleaning data to make sure it’s coming in as quality data. They’re not litigating the decisions on a death certificate,” Daskalakis said. “This relitigation is highly atypical.”
Deaths in which measles is listed on the death certificate will eventually be logged by the NCHS, but relying on this database will mean a longer delay between when a death occurs and when it is reported nationally.
The CDC did not answer multiple requests for comment explaining its updated protocol.
Slowing down measles death reporting could minimize the outbreak, and give Kennedy time to design new definitions that will manipulate how measles deaths are counted, Daskalakis said.
Daskalakis was among the top CDC officials who resigned last summer after its director at the time, Susan Monarez, clashed with RFK over vaccine recommendations and was fired.
He said he worries that “the goal of the secretary is to say that measles doesn’t kill anyone. And that’s not true, but when you own the keys to the kingdom …”

Title: Violence toward journalists is a symptom of a terminally ill U.S. democracy
Article_Text:
Violence toward journalists is a symptom of a terminally ill U.S. democracy
From Trump’s unhinged outbursts to calling the cops on a student journalist, a free press dies in tandem with the American Experiment.
Some days it’s hard to know what’s worse for America: the wars Donald Trump is losing — most notably in Iran, as U.S. motorists pay painful reparations at the gas pump — or the ones he’s winning, like his onslaught against a free press.
This February will mark 10 years since the president first declared that journalists are “the enemy of the people,” and he has spent much of the last decade making good on his threat — in constant lawsuits, in wielding federal licensing power like a nightstick, in criminal investigations, and in verbal assaults on journalists that have escalated to lunging.
Americans are sadly used to such appalling behavior at the White House, but what’s much more alarming is the countless ways hostility, contempt, and Trump-flavored threats to a free press have filtered down to town halls, college campuses, the football field, or other mileposts of Main Street USA.
One glaring example: Tensions between student journalists asking the right questions about labor disputes and other problems at Southern Illinois University at Edwardsville (SIUE) and the school administration escalated to the point where officials demanded to sit in and monitor interviews by reporters for the Alestle. When the paper’s editor complained in an email, a top university official called the cops and triggered a university police investigation. SIUE’s Nicole Franklin had reported that a journalist questioning school policy “has become an unsafe environment for me.”
Another: A bad on-the-field encounter between ESPN sideline reporter Holly Rowe and Texas football coach Steve Sarkisian was made much, much worse when a) some knucklehead on social media used AI to alter the footage to end with the Longhorns’ coach slapping Rowe, and b) their highly touted quarterback Arch Manning told a news conference he found the video “hilarious,” prompting laughter.
The fact that Manning later apologized for the incident, and that the Edwardsville cop who had to go out and interview Alestle editor Dylan Hembrough was embarrassed by the probe, only means that respect for the First Amendment and the humans struggling to uphold it 235 years later is hanging by a thread.
The stinking fish at the head of all this — Trump — hasn’t physically attacked a White House reporter … yet. But he sure came close last weekend, lunging at ABC News’ Rachel Scott as she tried to ask the president about his harebrained scheme to send every American a $5,000 check, wagging his finger and screaming, “Not you!”
But out in the American streets, actual violence — as well as unconstitutional arrests and other restraints — is happening on a routine basis. During Trump’s first year back in office, 2025, the Freedom of the Press Foundation found a massive upsurge in assaults on journalists. It said the 170 incidents were roughly equal to the prior three years combined. The attackers ranged from federal immigration agents to riot cops under the control of big-city Democratic mayors.
But things were deteriorating well before Trump became the 47th president on Jan. 20, 2025. The year before, a survey of working U.S. journalists by the International Women’s Media Foundation revealed that 36% have experienced either physical threats or actual violence.
I’m publishing this piece on Constitution Day, and a nation that has long touted the guarantees of its then-landmark 1791 First Amendment as proof of American exceptionalism ought to be ashamed that our current press freedom ranking from Reporters Without Borders has plunged to 64th out of 180 nations, the lowest ever.
But I’m also writing this column now because a) I’m terrified that the climate in which everyone laughs at AI videos of a journalist getting slapped is the prelude to somebody getting killed in the real world, and b) I, and it’s safe to say most of my colleagues, feel an increasing climate of contempt toward just the day-to-day stuff of answering a reporter’s questions or providing basic information about how our government is spending our tax dollars or policing our streets.
I’ve been a full-time journalist for 45 years now — a half century if you throw in high school and college — and the changes I’ve witnessed over the course of a lifetime have been remarkable, epitomized by the evolution from phone books that listed almost everyone’s number to call-screening and spam filters that make it virtually impossible to connect with people and tell their stories.
When they threw me onto the night shift at the Washington (Pa.) Observer-Reporter in September 1981, the job consisted of calling hospital emergency room nurses who’d happily volunteer the names and conditions of that night’s car-crash victims, and then police desk sergeants who’d chit-chat and tell you about any major crimes.
It’s good, actually, that HIPAA was enacted and medical information can’t be volunteered to the public, but it’s bad that police departments — whose track record for honesty runs neck-and-neck with the current administration in the White House — now dole out as little information as possible through stage-managed press releases.
I thought a lot about those hazy days as a rookie reporter out in Western Pennsylvania this summer, as I tried to report on local police cooperation with federal immigration agents on this side of the state. Police chiefs and township officials batted 1.000 when it came to not returning phone calls or emails. In person, they insisted the federal government told them not to divulge how much of their taxpayer-funded time is spent on busting immigrants instead of protecting neighborhoods.
Whatever your personal opinion toward journalists, the arrogant and autocratic stance of today’s public officials is spreading to what they think of you, the everyday citizen, and your right to know. This was summed up this week by the police chief of Pitcairn, Pa., who, after listening to public complaints that his 287(g) cooperation pact with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement was reached without a council hearing or vote, said, “I’ve been listening to this crap all night.”
A couple of important points: Like so many of my colleagues, I’ve felt the growing threats firsthand, from various efforts on social media to map where I live or describe my house, to the time someone drew a bullet hole on a sheet of paper and mailed it to my home.
But, as a white man, I know things are many, many times worse for my friends and colleagues who are Black or brown or women or in the LGBTQ+ community.
It’s no accident that the worst invective gets slung toward a female sideline reporter like Rowe, or that Trump goes out of his way to abuse Black female journalists like ABC’s Scott. It’s impossible to draw the boundaries between media hatred and the racism and misogyny that fuel American fascism. That is also clear in the Trump regime’s unconscionable targeting of on-the-ground journalists from immigrant communities like Nicaraguan exile Luis Galeano, detained this week by ICE in Florida.
It’s all connected.
Second, my love for journalism and the role we must play in a healthy democracy is exactly why I also believe the media deserves tough scrutiny for the many times we get it wrong. (And I have my receipts from CNN, the New York Times, the Washington Post, etc., etc.) The back-and-forth of media criticism is also the mark of a healthy society in every way that anti-media violence and government officials’ contempt for your right to know are not.
We can acknowledge that we live in a world where our privacy is under constant assault and needs to be protected — yet also believe, at the same time, that there’s no excuse for government officials or police to hide information that needs to be in the public domain, such as whom they’re arresting and why.
» READ MORE: In LA, police nightsticks are clubbing press freedom to death | Will Bunch
That requires a vibe shift from all of us — whether it’s not laughing at a video of a female journalist getting slapped, or not dialing 911 when a journalist asks a well-intended question. It means privileged white reporters need to object and walk out of the room the next time Trump verbally assaults a Black female reporter.
But that also means we need to be as vocal in praising the times journalists get it right — ProPublica’s scoop about Vladimir Putin’s pal paying for the president’s son’s wedding springs to mind — as we are in carping at the many peccadillos of elite media.
What’s scary is that all of this is happening at a time when vulture capitalists are cutting news organizations to the bone, especially in rural and small-town news deserts. The fewer working journalists that are left, the easier it will be to crush what remains.
That’s why I was so taken by what a Lexington, Ky., City Council member, Emma Curtis, just said about destructive layoffs at her local paper by the corporate pooh-bahs at McClatchy.
“All of us who sit up here have been held accountable at one point or another by the Herald Leader,” she said. “Not everything that they have ever written about me is stuff that I’ve liked, but our community is better for it. We are smarter, more informed citizens because of it.”
I wish more of our leaders — and heck, more regular folks — would talk about this more often. Any attack on a journalist — whether it’s physical or verbal, or some ridiculous AI video posted on X, and whether it comes from the president of the United States or a college quarterback — is ultimately an attack on our sick, barely breathing democracy.
