Title: Things to do: Concerts, festivals, and more
Article_Text:
🎸 🩰 A weekend of tunes, grooves, and moves | Things to do
Music festivals and concerts. Plus, the opening of Philadelphia Ballet Center and the start of Hispanic Heritage Month.
This weekend is for lovers of performance art.
British pop tunes, pulsating electro-funk, retro-soul, and other genres will take center stage across several concerts and music festivals — everywhere from Revolutionary War grounds to the Delaware waterfront.
There’s also the opening of Philadelphia Ballet’s new home, the celebration of Latin culture and heritage, and more to explore this weekend.
Read below to see what’s happening this weekend:
— Earl Hopkins (@earlhopkins_, Email me at thingstodo@inquirer.com)
If someone forwarded you this email, sign up for free here.
Grand opening of the Philadelphia Ballet Center
Philadelphia’s new eye-catching, four-story home for ballet on North Broad Street officially opens its doors Friday.
After 19 years of trying to consolidate its operations in one building, the Center for Dance on North Broad Street’s arrival is a significant feat.
Architecture critic Inga Saffron argues that the ballet’s building has missed an opportunity to show, as well as tell, what’s going on inside.
Take a peek yourself during the center’s open house. Guests can enjoy studio tours, dancer meet-and-greets, arts and crafts, and beginner-friendly dance lessons.
Read Inga’s review of Philadelphia Ballet’s new home here.
The best things to do this week
🎨 Sho your creativity: Food vendors, street dancers, musical ensembles, and of course, the work of artists from across the city, will be on display at LOVE Park during the ODUNDE Art Sho on Friday.
🎺 Jazz up your weekend: More than 20 locations will be celebrating Montco Jazz Fest with live performances, free swing dancing, and an outdoor movie night. Swing by for special tributes to jazz greats across 30-plus events.
🧵 Straight from the runway: Watch stylish Philadelphians strut their finest garments during Philly Fashion Week. There will be runway shows, shopping events, a design competition, and the Avant-Garde Ball and Philadelphia Fashion Awards at Vault XXVII.
🎉 Happy birthday to the Kimmel: In celebration of the Kimmel Center’s 25th anniversary, the venue is hosting the FREE Philadelphia Fall Arts Fest on Saturday. The event will shine a light on performance groups such as Opera Philadelphia, the Philly Pops, and others.
📅 My calendar picks this week: Rittenhouse Square Fine Arts Show, Upper Darby International Festival, Hero Thrill Show. Here’s our full list for the week.
Hispanic Heritage Month kicks off this week
Philadelphia will honor the culture and contributions of the Latin American community through Hispanic Heritage Month.
Upcoming events include international dance celebrations, music performances, and food festivals from now through Oct. 15.
On Saturday, salsa your way to the Esperanza Arts Center to see international dancers Ashley Rivera and Elian Gomez. They will join the local salsa orchestra, Siempre Salsa All-Stars, who will be backed by singer Carlos Sanchez and percussionist Willie Torres.
There will also be the Sazón Latin Food Festival at Two Locals Brewing on Saturday. The event will boast Caribbean, Central and South American cuisine, plus other pay-as-you-go offerings throughout the day.
Additional events will take place at various Free Library of Philadelphia branches throughout the month-long celebration.
Late summer fun this week and beyond
🍲 Restaurant week in Manayunk: Have a festive evening at Manayunk Restaurant Weekend. Prix fixe lunch and dinner specials, ranging from $15-$45 per person, and other offerings will take place at local faves like Lucky’s Last Chance, Mia Ragazza, Bayou Bar & Grill, and others through Sunday.
🎃 Experience Halloween underwater: Who says it’s too early for Halloween? Fintastic Pumpkin Glow is bringing the seasonal treat to Adventure Aquarium. Glowing pumpkins in the shape of stingrays, sharks, and sea turtles will be on display through Nov. 1.
🎷 Celebrating Coltrane: The celebration of John Coltrane’s 100th birthday continues at the Philadelphia Museum of Art. On Sunday, activities include hands-on art making, gallery activities, and a live performance by The Hines Creative Arts Legacy Youth Ensemble.
🖼️ New exhibition at the Barnes: The Barnes Foundation’s newest exhibition, “Noguchi to Asawa: Designing Postwar America,” highlights Asian American artists affected by incarceration and forced relocation during World War II. The exhibition opens on Sunday and runs through Jan. 10, 2027.
Staffer picks
Here’s pop music critic Dan DeLuca’s list of the best concerts this weekend.
🎤 Friday: After an earlier show at Liacouras Center, Boyz II Men is back. Only this time, as headliners with the Philly Pops at TD Pavilion at the Highmark Mann on Friday.
🎸 Friday and Saturday: The War on Drugs returns to action for a headlining performance at the Queen in Wilmington on Friday. On Saturday, the group heads to the Jersey Shore for Asbury Park’s Sea.Hear.Now Festival at 8 p.m.
🔊 Friday to Sunday: XPoNential Music Festival is back on the Delaware River waterfront in Wiggins Park in Camden. The weekend kicks off with Los Angeles brother act Dawes headlining, followed by performances from Alaska-born singer John Gourley’s Portugal. The Man, retro-soul band St. Paul & the Broken Bones, and others.
♾️ Friday to Sunday: David Pianka’s electronic music-plus fest, Making Time ∞, is in its sixth year at Fort Mifflin, the Revolutionary War-era fort near Philadelphia International Airport. Over 120 acts will perform this weekend, including DJ-producers like Bicep, Daphni, Skee Mask, and Jewelsea.
🎤 Saturday: British megastar Ed Sheeran is slated to take center stage at Lincoln Financial Field on Saturday for his “Loop Tour,” which he plays solo, building layered tracks by triggering prerecorded instrumentals with foot pedals.
Check out Dan’s full concert list here.
❓Pop quiz
What was the original name of Philadelphia Ballet?
A) The Philadelphia Ballet Company
B) Commonwealth Ballet Dancers
C) Pennsylvania Ballet
D) PA Dance Co.
Here’s the answer to last week’s question: How many groups were a part of the first Philadelphia Fringe Festival in 1997? Answer: 60
Ask Earl anything
Many of you have questions about each week’s listings, and others about Philly’s arts, culture, and entertainment scene.
I have you covered. Have a question? Email me for a chance to have it answered in an upcoming newsletter.
That’s all, folks. Make time in your schedule for some of these picks this weekend.
– Earl Hopkins

Title: Tom Cruise Suri Update Revealed After She Legally Dropped His Name
Article_Text:
By providing your information, you agree to our Terms of Use and our Privacy Policy. We use vendors that may also process your information to help provide our services. This site is protected by reCAPTCHA Enterprise and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply.
Just two months after Page Six reported that Tom Cruise’s daughter Suri legally dropped “Cruise” from her name in 2024, the Top Gun actor graced the cover of GQ and sat down for a rare, in-depth interview. However, according to gossip columnist Rob Shuter, Cruise made it clear to the magazine that questions about his estrangement from Suri, 20, were strictly off-limits.
“Everyone understood the rules,” an insider told Shuter’s Naughty But Nice. “Movies, stunts, ambition — ask away. Suri? Don’t even try. There was going to be no discussion about their estrangement or why she dropped Cruise from her name.”
The source added that Cruise gives the media “access” to his life and career, but only on his terms. “He’ll unbutton the shirt, talk about being intense and sell you the Tom Cruise fantasy,” they continued. “But the nipples stay covered, Suri stays off-limits, and Tom stays completely in control.”
According to voter registration records via Page Six, Suri registered to vote in Pennsylvania in October 2024 under the name “Suri Noelle.” Her new surname reportedly honors her mother, Katie Holmes, whose full name is Kate Noelle Holmes.
Cruise’s reaction to Suri’s legal name change was “almost nonexistent,” per a a source close to the Hollywood icon. “He’s not angry, he’s not making phone calls, and he’s certainly isn’t trying to change her mind,” they told Naughty But Nice in July 2026. “As far as Tom is concerned, this chapter of his life ended years ago.”
Suri had already publicly distanced herself from the Mission: Impossible star before the legal change. At her high school graduation in 2024, she was listed as “Suri Noelle” in the program, which sources told Page Six was a way for her to “praise” her famous mother and establish “her own identity” before heading off to college.
Holmes and Cruise welcomed Suri on April 18, 2006, a few months before their wedding. Their marriage ended in 2012, and Cruise hasn’t seen Suri since. The former couple’s custody agreement allowed the four-time Oscar nominee to see Suri 10 days a month, but he never did.
“Every person is allowed to see their child if they wanted to,” a source told Us Weekly in 2018. “He chooses not to because she is not a Scientologist.”
By 2023, a separate insider revealed that Cruise was not part of Suri’s life and hadn’t seen her in several years.

Title: Nicole Fusaro's family files complaint against police, say they've been mistreated in Olney investigation
Article_Text:
Cousin of a Raymond Horsch victim criticizes police for sharing graphic details at news conference before telling family
The cousin of Nicole Fusaro said he was disturbed by the level of detail police shared at the news conference with the public — but not in private with his family.
Jonathan Halloran-Koren said he watched with horror as Philadelphia police brass described the graphic details of his cousin Nicole Fusaro’s killing during a Wednesday news conference.
Deputy Police Commissioner Frank Vanore said investigators recovered videos that show Raymond “R.C.” Horsch giving her drugs and money, then handcuffing her to a bed. Horsch, naked and holding a camera, with another mounted in the corner of the room, then used pliers to put a zip tie around the woman’s neck until she fell unconscious, Vanore said.
None of this, Halloran-Koren said, had been shared when he and his mother had met with homicide detectives about her case just four hours earlier. All they were told, he said, was that Horsch had filmed himself strangling her.
“I didn’t need to know that. The public didn’t need to know that,” Halloran-Koren said of the details shared in the news conference. “I’ve seen some really graphic and horrible things in my life, but to turn around and hear how my cousin died in a press conference, all I could feel was deep sadness, sorrow, and rage.”
On Thursday, Halloran-Koren, a security consultant, sent a letter to Mayor Cherelle L. Parker and members of City Council, calling the action of city police officials “appalling.”
Sgt. Eric Gripp, a spokesperson for the police department, said detectives traveled to northern New Jersey to speak with the family members ahead of the news conference Wednesday, though he declined to discuss the details of a private conversation.
The department did not name Fusaro during the news conference, in deference to other relatives.
“Our deepest sympathy remains with every family whose loved one may be connected to this extraordinarily complex and deeply troubling investigation,” Gripp said, and police will “pursue every lead, work to locate the missing women, and provide verified information to their families as responsibly and compassionately as possible.”
Joe Grace, a spokesperson for the mayor’s office, referred questions to the police department.
Fusaro’s case is part of a sprawling local and federal investigation into the drug, sex, and porn operation Horsch ran out of his home on West Chew Avenue in Olney. Police now say Horsch, who died last year at 82 from lung disease, is linked to seven dead or missing women.
While sifting through more than a million photos and videos recovered on Horsch’s hard drives, police said, investigators have recovered footage that appeared to show five women lifeless, including Fusaro, Maribel Fresses, and Gabrielle Amarando. There are also two unnamed women: a 25-year-old whose identity relatives asked to remain private, and a woman in her mid-20s investigators are still working to identify.
Two other women — Blair Tonzelli, reported missing in 2023, and Amy McHale, Horsch’s ex-wife, who disappeared in 2016 — were also reportedly last seen at the Olney home, which Horsch shared with his son, Eugene. The younger Horsch is in prison on federal charges stemming from his June 19 arrest after a car stop near Independence Hall. In the car, a federal park ranger found a fake ID with Tonzelli’s name, which launched the investigation.
Fusaro, 27, was last seen in Kensington on July 19, 2018. Her mother, Diane, spent years searching the streets for her only child before she died in January 2020. Fusaro’s father, Thomas, died in 2009.
Halloran-Koren had fallen out of touch with his family after years living overseas, but reconnected with them in 2020 and learned his cousin was missing, he said. He started working with friends of his aunt and cousin to try to find her.
In 2024, he said, he filed a report with the National Missing and Unidentified Persons System, and Fusaro’s information was later entered into the national database.
In August, after police identified Fusaro as the woman Horsch appeared to have killed, detectives met with one of Fusaro’s paternal relatives to notify them of the discovery. The relative, who declined to speak with an Inquirer reporter, asked police not to publicly release her name.
Several weeks later, that relative told Halloran-Koren what police had told him: that they believed his cousin was dead. Halloran-Koren, a cousin on Fusaro’s mother’s side, then identified her publicly because he said he wanted her story to be known.
“Nicole deserved to have people fighting for her when she was missing. She deserves people fighting for her now,” he said. “I will make sure that happens.”
Halloran-Koren later contacted city police and requested additional information. Detectives scheduled a meeting with him and his mother on Sept. 16 to formally notify them of her likely death.
He learned more, he said, from watching his television several hours later.
In his letter to Parker and Council members on Thursday, Halloran-Koren said he understood the police department had “an obligation to provide information to the public and answer legitimate questions from the press.”
“But there is an enormous difference between legitimate public disclosure and providing a victim’s family with less information about their loved one’s death than is subsequently provided to the public only hours later,” he said.
He said he hopes to review the department’s handling of the case, and whether police violated any laws or internal policies in their communication with his family.
“Our family deserved better,” he wrote. “Nicole deserved better.”

Title: PFAS exposure on Pa. military bases linked with high blood pressure and elevated cholesterol, study says
Article_Text:
PFAS exposure near Pa. military bases linked to high blood pressure, cholesterol. Researchers find cancer cluster.
A separate analysis showed cancer clusters in those communities, but more research is needed to determine if there is a correlation between cancer rates and the water.
A major study of PFAS-contaminated drinking water among people living near military bases in Bucks and Montgomery Counties shows associations with elevated cholesterol, increased blood pressure, and lower childhood development, according to preliminary findings.
PFAS, or per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, are a family of compounds known as forever chemicals because they resist breaking down in the environment and in the human body.
A separate analysis showed cancer clusters in those communities, but more research is needed to determine whether there is a correlation between cancer rates and the water, the study’s investigators say.
Lead researchers from RTI International and Temple University presented the findings Wednesday at Hatboro-Horsham High School during an event hosted by the Buxmont Coalition for Safer Water.
The ongoing study, part of an effort by the federal Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, examined PFAS exposure in Pennsylvania and seven other states: California, Colorado, Massachusetts, Michigan, New Hampshire, New Jersey, and New York. It included 5,826 adults and 710 children ages 4 to 17.
» READ MORE: People who lived near Bucks, Montco military bases had higher level of toxic compounds in blood than U.S. average
Wednesday’s presentation focused on Pennsylvania, where researchers collected blood from residents in 11 townships in Bucks and Montgomery Counties who lived near military bases where firefighting foam contaminated local drinking water supplies for decades. About 180 people attended the meeting.
“We have waited a long time for these study results to be released,” said Joanne Stanton, of the Buxmont Coalition for Safer Water, a grassroots organization formed after the PFAS contamination was first identified. “For the past 12 years, our community has carried an unimaginable heavy burden.”
According to baseline testing, local participants had elevated concentrations of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in their blood. Levels of PFAS and associated compounds — PFOS, PFOA, PFHxS, and PFNA — exceeded national averages. Pennsylvania ranked second highest nationally among all study sites for PFOS and PFHxS.
“These higher levels [of PFAS] are consistent with decades of exposure to firefighting foam used at the military bases,” said Linda Brown, the Pennsylvania study’s director from RTI International, an independent research institute.
Impacts on blood pressure, immunity, cholesterol, IQ
Brown said 1,251 adults and 89 children from Pennsylvania gave blood for the study.
“Adults with higher PFAS levels in their blood tended to have higher blood pressure,” she said.
High blood pressure is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease, she said.
Brown also said elevated PFAS levels were associated with higher cholesterol, including LDL, the so-called bad cholesterol. All four PFAS compounds were associated with higher cholesterol in both adults and children.
She said, however, that preliminary results did not find a clear pattern linking PFOS levels with heart disease, diabetes, thyroid disease, or obesity.
Overall, children with higher PFAS levels had lower levels of certain antibodies that help the body fight infection, she said. The findings suggest PFAS may affect the immune responses, including the response to vaccines. But the findings do not tell researchers whether any individual child’s vaccines were less effective.
Higher levels of exposure to PFAS during pregnancy and early childhood also showed patterns of lower abilities of language, reasoning, and cognition. But she cautioned that the patterns cannot tell parents how PFAS may have affected their own child.
Cancer clusters
The study had too few cases of individual cancer types to complete a statistical analysis from the blood samples given. Cancer is not part of the original study.
To fill the gap, Temple researcher Resa Jones said, the group used a grant from Pennsylvania to separately look at overall cancer cases in 12 counties.
Jones said researchers pulled data from the state’s cancer registry to find the rate per 100,000 people. Mapping showed geographical clusters of elevated kidney, thyroid, breast, endometrial, and ovarian cancer incidence in Bucks and Montgomery Counties.
“We definitely have spatial clustering of the cancers,” Jones said of the two counties.
In municipalities with the highest totals of breast cancer, half had PFAS levels above minimum reporting levels for drinking water, Jones said.
But Jones stressed that more research is needed and that the results are preliminary.
Kidney function
In addition, Robin Taylor Wilson, another investigator from Temple, said longer exposure to PFAS was also associated with lower kidney filtration rates and chronic kidney disease.
The study highlighted heightened renal vulnerability among specific subpopulations, reporting that older residents, individuals with a history of blood transfusions or thyroid disorders, and cancer survivors faced significantly higher risks of chronic kidney disease.
Hope Grosse, of the Buxmont Coalition for Safer Water, said the release of preliminary results of the study gives future researchers a solid foundation for further study into PFAS.
“While these study results cannot undo the damage or bring back what we have lost, we hope that they are the beginning of the answers that we deserve,” Grosse said.

Title: Chances of a shutout, where Jalen Hurts ranks, and what else they're saying about the Eagles in Week 2
Article_Text:
Chances of a shutout, where Jalen Hurts ranks, and what else they’re saying about the Eagles in Week 2
The Eagles will face a Titans offensive line that struggled against the Jets. What’s in store for a superior Birds defensive line?
Week 1 of the NFL schedule is in the books, and the first look at each team has generated lots of discussion heading into Week 2.
Despite the Eagles’ 24-22 win last Sunday against the Commanders, many felt the highly anticipated new offense under first-year coordinator Sean Mannion fell flat. With Landon Dickerson on injured reserve for at least four games because of a bone bruise in his knee, the national focus heading into Sunday’s game against the Titans in Nashville (1 p.m., Fox) is still fixed on the offensive line.
Here’s what NFL analysts are saying:
Titanic struggles
ESPN’s matchup predictor gives the Birds a 69.7% chance of winning at Nissan Stadium. ESPN analyst Ben Solak gave one of the boldest predictions of the week, theorizing a possible scoreless game for the Titans.
“I cannot remember a team that looked less functional on offense in Week 1 than the Titans in Sunday’s loss to the Jets,” Solak said.
» READ MORE: Eagles vs. Titans in Week 2: Here are the numbers that matter
“After watching the way the Titans’ offensive line struggled against the Jets (they made Kingsley Enagbare look like Maxx Crosby), I cannot bear the idea of the Titans’ upcoming game against Philadelphia,” Solak wrote. “The Eagles’ front was as dominant as ever against a poor Commanders line in Week 1. It collected 19 pressures, a single-game best in the Vic Fangio era, despite the fact that starting edge rusher Jonathan Greenard wasn’t even healthy enough to play.”
Replacing Dickerson
Stepping in for Dickerson is a big role to fill, and his replacement is being kept under wraps. But the leading candidates appear to be second-year linemen Drew Kendall and Willie Lampkin. The Athletic’s Zach Berman said a one-for-one swap with Kendall is his favored choice, despite talk of a position swap that could have Kendall at center and Cam Jurgens moving to guard.
“The Eagles will miss the best version of Dickerson,” Berman wrote. “That’s not the version that was on the field against the Washington Commanders in Week 1. It would be too ambitious to expect Kendall (or Lampkin) to play like 2024 Dickerson. It’s not ambitious to expect Kendall (or Lampkin) to be better than Week 1 Dickerson.”
» READ MORE: Eagles odds against the Titans, plus player props for Jalen Hurts and more
Comparing QBs
NFL.com analysts bumped Jalen Hurts up six spots to 12th in their quarterback rankings, calling his performance “a classic Jalen Hurts Week 1 game, connecting on a handful of downfield shots while willing Philadelphia’s offense down the field with well-timed scrambles against Washington. The Eagles still need to be more consistent offensively on a per-play basis, but for one week, Hurts was able to carry them out of the muck to victory.”
The Eagles’ next opposing QB is ranked No. 30. Titans quarterback Cam Ward had a disappointing Week 1, completing 19 of 32 passes for 140 yards.
The overall national consensus isn’t debating an upset for the Titans. Rather, analysts are weighing how lopsided the matchup will be.

Title: Philly City Council returns with dueling plans for the city's trash
Article_Text:
Philly City Council returns with dueling plans for the city’s trash | Council roundup
Also this week in Council: One member floated a new structure for the law department and another wants to ban new storage facilities from his district.
Philadelphia City Council members are considering dueling proposals over how the city eliminates its garbage, with one lawmaker leading an effort to immediately block the city from shipping its garbage to a trash incinerator and another taking a longer-term approach.
Councilmember Mark Squilla on Thursday introduced legislation authorizing Mayor Cherelle L. Parker’s administration to, within three years, develop a plan to dramatically reduce the city’s reliance on both trash incineration and landfills over the next 20 years.
Squilla’s proposal, which he drafted with input from Parker’s administration, is something of an alternative for lawmakers to consider as Councilmember Jamie Gauthier has for months pushed for a more aggressive approach to stop the city from incinerating trash this year.
Both lawmakers hosted news conferences this week alongside their allies to rally support for their cause, part of a long list of events Council members hosted as the legislative body returned Thursday for its first meeting of the fall session.
» READ MORE: After a messy budget fight, Philly City Council turns to its unfinished business: Trash, taxes, and a new arena
The first meeting after the summer break typically has a jovial, first-day-of-school feel. But the mood briefly shifted Thursday when City Hall was evacuated and Council abruptly adjourned after a suspicious package was found on the floor where Council was meeting.
» READ MORE: Philly City Hall was evacuated for a bomb squad investigation, but no explosive device was found
Police cleared the package, and Council resumed its business Thursday afternoon.
Here’s what else happened this week:
What was this week’s highlight?
Incinerator issue heats up: Gauthier has for months sought to pass legislation that would ban the city from continuing its long-term practice of sending about a third of its garbage to a trash incinerator in Chester, about 15 miles south of the city. She argues that incineration is bad for the environment and harms Chester residents’ health.
Parker’s administration opposed the legislation, called the Stop Trashing Our Air Act, and Gauthier in the spring failed to gain enough support for it in Council.
Now, Gauthier is trying to block the Parker administration from renewing its contract with Reworld, the incineration facility. The administration needs Council approval to enter into a new four-year contract with the firm.
Gauthier has several members on her side, including three fellow progressive lawmakers, as well as Councilmember Isaiah Thomas, who is the Democratic majority whip.
Squilla’s proposal in some ways offers members an off-ramp. His bill calls for a “circular waste” system that includes new techniques for waste disposal, such as composting and “anaerobic digestion,” a process that breaks down organic waste.
Managing Director Carlton Williams said Wednesday during a news conference with Squilla that the city is looking to build out an anaerobic digestion system within four years.
Squilla said that while the administration is already working toward a more modern waste disposal system, passing a law would “codify what we had as plans and resolutions before.”
Gauthier said that she supports Squilla’s goal of moving toward a more sustainable system, but that his legislation “is a plan to create a longer-range plan.”
“It in no way changes the decision in front of Council,” she said. “We can move away from this practice right now.”
What else happened this week?
Severing the law department: The city law department serves as legal counsel for both the mayor’s administration and Council, a dynamic that can sometimes cause friction when the city’s elected officials disagree.
Council on Thursday approved a resolution by Thomas to hold a hearing “to consider the separation of the [law] department’s functions between the administration and City Council.”
The department is led by City Solicitor Monique Galloway, whom Parker appointed to the role in July.
Thomas has clashed with Parker’s administration, and he said he became interested in looking at the department’s structure due to concerns that Council was not receiving independent legal advice on some issues.
He pointed to the Philadelphia School District’s controversial facilities plan, which involves the closure of 17 school buildings and was adopted by the school board in April over the objections of many Council members.
And he said recent legal proceedings around the city’s business income and receipts tax were “part of the motivation” to hold a hearing on the law department.
In 2025, after a Massachusetts company sued the city seeking to overturn a popular tax break program that primarily helped small businesses, the law department said it had determined the lawsuit was likely to succeed. The Parker administration eventually settled the case and persuaded Council to eliminate the tax break. Some Council members at the time complained that the city did not defend the tax break more vigorously.
» READ MORE: Mayor Cherelle L. Parker’s administration defends move to eliminate tax break that helps small businesses
The department already silos off some of the work it does on behalf of Council from the rest of the administration, such as when it drafts bills proposed by lawmakers. Council also may hire outside legal counsel, but must pay for those services out of its own budget.
A law department spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Storage wars: Councilmember Mike Driscoll introduced legislation on Thursday that would ban new self-storage facilities from his district in lower Northeast Philadelphia.
The storage industry boomed during the COVID-19 pandemic, as consumer spending shifted from services to goods, many families struggled to afford larger homes, and low interest rates juiced development.
Northeast Philadelphia saw a particularly large boom in self-storage buildings because of its rich supply of properties zoned for industrial development. Driscoll said that advocates in the Tacony neighborhood felt their community had become oversaturated.
“They want more affordable housing and [self-storage units] are taking valuable sites for that,” Driscoll said.
Self-storage facilities are gold mines for developers. They suffer little wear and tear, they have few utility costs, and labor costs are low after construction.
According to online industry search portal StorageCafe, Philadelphia has 89 self-storage sites containing more than seven million square feet of space. About a third of that has been built since 2019.
Other municipalities have moved to limit the spread of self-storage facilities in recent years. New York City banned them from industrial areas to preserve jobs, and Denver blocked them from properties close to light rail lines. Providence, R.I., in 2023 banned new facilities from the city altogether.
Driscoll said that he may further limit his legislation to the Tacony neighborhood.
“I don’t want to hurt another part of my district that maybe wants these things,” he said.
Embracing affordability: Multiple members of City Council said this week that tackling affordability is their primary objective this fall, including Councilmember Nicolas O’Rourke, whose office published a lengthy report outlining dozens of proposals aimed at reducing costs.
Some may be more realistic short-term goals than others.
The report, which was drafted by a Cost of Living Task Force made up of community advocates and industry leaders, recommended the city explore everything from opening municipal grocery stores to creating a local Medicaid supplement program.
It also recommends restructuring existing housing programs to more aggressively target the poorest residents, and establishing a Transit Access Fund that would fund free or reduced-fare transit passes for low-income households.
O’Rourke, a member of the progressive Working Families Party, plans to hold a committee hearing on the task force report this fall.
Council President Kenyatta Johnson will also introduce an affordability measure this fall. He plans to bring forward legislation that would establish a permanent Food and Nutrition Security Coordination Office, he said in a statement.
Quote of the week
No bones about it: That was Councilmember Jeffery Young Jr., who called for hearings on the planned closure of the Academy of Natural Sciences.

Title: Parents drove teen charged in Penn State student's killing to Colorado after suspects' photos shared on TV
Article_Text:
Parents accused of driving teen charged in Penn State student’s killing to Colorado ordered to stand trial
The judge's ruling came after prosecutors presented evidence on how they allegedly helped their son evade capture following the June killing of William "Billy" Schmidt.
The parents of one of two teenagers charged with killing a Pennsylvania State University student in June drove him from Philadelphia to Colorado Springs, Colo., within hours of local television stations airing surveillance footage of the suspects police were seeking in the case, prosecutors said Thursday.
Kaiseem Smith, 16, and Azzubair Outen-Fleming, 16, are charged with murder, conspiracy, and related offenses in the shooting death of William “Billy” Schmidt, 22, who was killed June 6 after a robbery on a South Philadelphia sidewalk turned deadly.
Philadelphia police and the U.S. Marshals Service searched for Smith and Outen-Fleming for weeks before taking them into custody. Marshals found Outen-Fleming on July 1 in Colorado Springs. Smith surrendered to Philadelphia police the following day.
At a preliminary hearing Thursday, prosecutors detailed how Outen-Fleming’s stepfather, Donte Abdulmalik, 35, and mother, Milika Abdulmalik, 45, allegedly drove him more than 1,700 miles to Colorado Springs — a roughly 45-hour trip spanning several states — and how police detectives traced the journey through cell phone records and license plate reader data.
Donte Abdulmalik was arrested June 30 and Milika Abdulmalik on July 3. Both are charged with hindering apprehension, obstruction of justice, and related offenses.
After hearing the evidence Thursday, Common Pleas Court Judge Gregory Yorgey-Girdy ordered the parents to stand trial.
Detective Thorsten Lucke testified that the couple’s cell phone records showed they began the drive around 10:30 p.m. June 10, after surveillance videos and images of the suspects aired during local 10 p.m. newscasts.
That night, a phone registered to Milika Abdulmalik called and texted a Colorado Springs number, Lucke said, before beginning to travel west in tandem with a phone registered to Donte Abdulmalik.
The phones arrived in Colorado Springs on the evening of June 12, Lucke testified, and began heading east again June 14 before returning to Philadelphia.
Detective Frank Mullen, who also testified Thursday, said police arrested Donte Abdulmalik near a black Mercedes-Benz that investigators believe was used to drive Outen-Fleming to Colorado Springs. License plate readers captured the vehicle near the home where Outen-Fleming was later found, Lucke said.
Defense attorneys for the parents argued, however, that the evidence was thin and failed to connect their clients to the alleged crimes.
Donte Abdulmalik’s attorney, Carmen C. Nasuti III, made plain what he thought of the case during a cross-examination of Lucke: “So, essentially, what you showed us was two phones took a trip to Colorado Springs?” Nasuti asked.
“Yes, that’s correct,” Lucke replied.
Smith, Outen-Fleming, and Fleming also appeared in court Thursday but waived their preliminary hearings.
Schmidt, a Penn State senior, was walking home from a neighborhood bar where he had watched the NBA Finals when the two teenagers approached him near 20th and Wolf Streets around 1:30 a.m., according to prosecutors and surveillance footage described in court records.
Prosecutors have said Outen-Fleming grabbed Schmidt’s cell phone, punched him, and rifled through his pockets before the pair knocked him to the ground. As the teens walked away, Outen-Fleming threw the phone down the block.
A neighbor’s surveillance camera recorded Schmidt running after them, police have said. Smith then turned and fired a single shot into Schmidt’s chest, prosecutors said.
Authorities also connected Donte Abdulmalik to the case through a woman who was inside a South Philadelphia home searched by police while they were looking for Outen-Fleming’s brother, Kadafi Fleming, according to an affidavit of probable cause for Donte Abdulmalik’s arrest.
Fleming, 19, is accused of stealing the SUV the teens took to and from the area before and after the killing.
The woman, identified in the affidavit only by her initials, told detectives she recognized Outen-Fleming from news coverage of the case and identified the second suspect — whom she said was the shooter — as his cousin. She also told investigators that Outen-Fleming’s stepfather had driven him to Colorado, according to the affidavit, and showed officers a speeding ticket that had arrived in the mail: a citation for a June 14 infraction in Simla, Colo., issued to a Mercedes-Benz registered to a deceased family member.
Hours later, detectives interviewed the woman again while Donte Abdulmalik waited outside on the porch, according to the affidavit. She stood by her identification of the two teenagers but retreated from the rest of her account, telling them she did not know who had driven Outen-Fleming to Colorado.
Prosecutors did not call the woman as a witness Thursday or introduce evidence from those interviews.
In his closing argument, Nasuti said records showing a phone in Colorado did not necessarily place his client there. Donte Abdulmalik, he argued, could have handed the phone to his stepson.
“No one who can place my client in the car,” he said. “No one who can place that phone number in his hand. They need to do that, even at this level.”
Yorgey-Girdy, the judge, said he found the evidence persuasive, however. He also denied requests from Nasuti and Scott Gessner, Milika Abdulmalik’s attorney, to reduce the couple’s bail after Assistant District Attorney Lauren Crump argued they posed a “severe flight risk.”
“This whole case,” Crump said, “is about flight.”
The parents are each being held on $250,000 bail, court records show.
Smith and Outen-Fleming are scheduled to return to court in October, along with Donte Abdulmalik, Milika Abdulmalik, and Fleming.

Title: Head of Conviction Integrity Unit in DA's office steps down after judge points to possible crimes, sources say
Article_Text:
Head of conviction integrity unit in DA’s office steps down after judge points to possible crimes, sources say
ADA Matthew Stiegler stepped down from his supervisory role, but would remain a prosecutor with the office, the sources said.
The head of the conviction integrity unit in the Philadelphia District Attorney’s Office has stepped down from his supervisory role, sources said, days after a federal judge said his actions in a contentious post-conviction case could amount to crimes.
Assistant District Attorney Matthew Stiegler resigned from his position as supervisor of the unit on Thursday, said the sources, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss a sensitive personnel decision.
Stiegler would remain a prosecutor with the office, the sources said, though it was not immediately clear what his role would be.
Stiegler did not respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for the district attorney’s office also did not respond.
The personnel shake-up comes as Stiegler faces scrutiny over his role in a controversial case that has since drawn extraordinary attention and criticism from a federal judge — and raised questions about one of District Attorney Larry Krasner’s key policy initiatives.
» READ MORE: Philly DA Larry Krasner faces legal and political uncertainty after a judge said he may have committed crimes
On Tuesday, U.S. District Judge Paul Diamond said Stiegler and Krasner may have broken the law in their handling of the case, and said he had referred the matter to the U.S. Attorney’s Office to investigate whether the pair should be charged with crimes including conspiracy or obstruction of justice.
Stiegler came under public scrutiny this spring over his unit’s handling of the case of Dennis Johnson, who was convicted of second-degree murder in 2009. Prosecutors for years had opposed his bid for freedom.
Then, in 2022, Assistant District Attorney Jaclyn Mason, who worked under Stiegler, filed a brief saying she had discovered problems with Johnson’s case, and recommended the conviction be overturned.
Diamond scheduled an evidentiary hearing on the matter this spring.
Ahead of that hearing, Mason’s colleagues in the office’s law division reviewed the filings in the case and found what they called “material misstatements” in the brief. They sought to withdraw Mason’s filing, and apologized to Diamond.
Mason resigned. Diamond called a hearing on the matter.
Mason, during the first of a series of explosive hearings in front of Diamond, said she filed the brief only because Stiegler had pressured her to do so.
Stiegler, she said, had been “colluding” with Johnson’s defense attorneys from the Federal Community Defender Office and the Pennsylvania Innocence Project on the most effective paths to secure Johnson’s release. Neither of them had reviewed key evidence in Johnson’s case before seeking to overturn his murder conviction, she said.
“Matt told me: ‘If it’s good enough for the Innocence Project, it’s good enough for me,’” Mason said.
Stiegler denied this and said he has reviewed every case carefully.
In a subsequent hearing, supervisors in the law division testified that Stiegler, in an attempt to avoid blame, then suggested they review Mason’s cases to look for other errors in her work to paint her as a “rogue” prosecutor who was routinely making mistakes.
Those supervisors said Krasner later echoed that potential course of action, saying he had learned it from Stiegler and it was a “good idea.”
The supervisors refused.
Diamond said those actions were particularly troubling, and suggested Krasner and Stiegler were conspiring to “present a false narrative to the Court.”
Diamond also said he found Stiegler’s testimony “was often contradictory, evasive, or outright dishonest,” and that Stiegler may have committed perjury while on the stand.
In a statement Tuesday, Krasner said, “I respectfully and vigorously disagree” with Diamond’s findings.
“I look forward to appealing to the higher court as soon as the law allows,” he said, adding that he could not comment further because the case is pending.
Staff writer Chris Palmer contributed to this article.

Title: Eagles continue to keep Landon Dickerson's replacement close to the vest
Article_Text:
How will the Eagles replace Landon Dickerson? They’re trying their best to keep the answer close to the vest.
The Eagles insist that they are keeping Dickerson's replacement "in-house" and continued to play coy during the portion of Thursday's practice open to reporters.
The Eagles and their coaches are well aware of when and how long reporters and cameras are permitted to document practice, which means the early part of individual drills Thursday at the Jefferson Health Training Complex needed to be taken with a grain of salt.
There was Fred Johnson, not Drew Kendall, lining up at left guard with the first-team offensive line as they started their work for the day as a unit. But Kendall, the expected replacement for injured left guard Landon Dickerson, wasn’t with the backups. He lined up to the left of Jordan Mailata as the unit went through its first drill.
The Eagles are playing coy, and it’s possible — perhaps even likely — that the arrangement of the group was just a diversion tactic to try to hide from the Tennessee Titans as long as possible who will replace Dickerson for the first of at least four games the Eagles will be without him.
» READ MORE: Drew Kendall’s job replacing Landon Dickerson on Eagles O-line would be to ‘make sure we don’t skip a beat’
There are a few combinations the Eagles could go with, but we probably can write off one where Kendall lines up left of Mailata as a tight end.
Perhaps this is a mystery that can only be solved by Benoit Blanc or Ben Gates. Reporters have tried to crack the code this week, but the Eagles are holding their cards close.
“We’re going to keep that in-house in terms of what our plan is for this week, just for competitive reasons,” offensive coordinator Sean Mannion said Tuesday when asked about one possible combination that would involve moving center Cam Jurgens to left guard.
A day later, Nick Sirianni was asked if Kendall, who played center at Boston College but has been cross-training at guard, was a better fit at center or guard.
“That’s a tricky way you’re asking that question,” Sirianni said with a smile. “I think he’s able to do both.”
That is why the Eagles do indeed have a few options. They have multiple players who can play in more than one spot. Kendall is one of them, and Johnson — who may have been used as a pawn Thursday afternoon — and Willie Lampkin are others.
Johnson has exclusively been a backup tackle with the Eagles, but he did play some right guard when he was with Cincinnati. Of his 1,871 career snaps, 144 of them were at right guard. He has never played left guard in the NFL. Lampkin, meanwhile, can play center or guard but his only NFL snaps to date are on kickoff return, which he did in his NFL debut Sunday.
» READ MORE: Eagles wide receiver Hollywood Brown was ‘surprised’ by lack of playing time in Week 1 win
That’s why Kendall, who had a strong camp, seems like the most logical — and likely — choice. He replaced Dickerson during some practice reps with the starters in training camp. He was the backup left guard when the Eagles went through their pregame warmups in Week 1.
But Kendall didn’t bite when asked Wednesday after practice what his role was in practice earlier that day.
“A little bit of everything,” said Kendall, who already is well-trained in the art of public relations in his second NFL season. “We’re trying to keep everything in-house. Not trying to give out too much.
“I’m just excited for any opportunity ahead. We have a lot of good guys in our room. Everyone has been cross-training at different positions throughout the summer. So whatever the five is, I’m just excited to try to contribute to this team and we’ll get our best five out there.”
Kendall even kept his guard up when asked a hypothetical about the challenge, should his number be called Sunday, of starting a game with Titans interior lineman Jeffery Simmons lined up on the other side.
“He’s a great player,” Kendall said. “Whatever happens between the five that’s out there, we have a lot of respect for him, he’s been doing it at a high level for a very long time. We’re excited for it.”
» READ MORE: Eagles’ Jalen Carter will be ‘ready to play’ vs. Titans after suffering wrist injury in Week 1
Mailata didn’t reveal anything Wednesday, but he did exude confidence.
“We’re pretty lucky to have the depth that we do because I’d go to war with any one of these guys that are behind Landon, that are behind anybody,” he said.
Injury updates
Cooper DeJean (calf/abdomen) and Jalen Carter (wrist) returned to the practice field on Thursday after both were nonparticipants on Wednesday. Both players as limited participants on the team’s injury report, along with edge rusher Jonathan Greenard (pectoral).
Carter appeared to be sporting a sizable cast on his right arm. He finished the game Sunday but did not talk to reporters after the game as he left with a member of the team’s training staff.
While those key defensive starters returned Thursday, starting safety Andrew Mukuba was not on the field during the brief portion of practice open to reporters. The Eagles listed the safety as a nonparticipant with a knee injury after not appearing on Wednesday’s injury report.

Title: Upper Darby's new ICE ordinance aims to limit cooperation and data sharing
Article_Text:
Upper Darby passed an ordinance aiming to limit cooperation and data sharing with ICE
Timothy Bernhardt, Upper Darby's police superintendent, has "no objection" to the ordinance, which he said "isn’t going to change what the Upper Darby Police Department does.”
Upper Darby passed an ordinance on Wednesday aiming to restrict the township’s cooperation with federal immigration agents.
Township council unanimously approved legislation banning local police from assisting ICE and other federal agencies with immigration enforcement activities. The legislation bars federal agents from using township property to stage immigration raids, prohibits township staff from providing resident information to federal agents for civil immigration enforcement, and bans township personnel from recording or maintaining data about residents’ immigration statuses, unless it is required by law.
It also prohibits township police officers from wearing masks or obscuring their identities in most cases and “formally requests” that federal agents clearly identify themselves and do not wear masks.
The ordinance includes exemptions, including cases in which immigration agents possess a judicial warrant or there is a criminal law enforcement matter requiring Upper Darby officials’ cooperation.
The legislation codified many of the tenets of a resolution passed by Upper Darby’s council in February. It largely mirrors a sweeping legislative package passed by Philadelphia City Council earlier this year.
At the more than three-hour meeting on Wednesday, residents decried the actions of federal immigration agents and President Donald Trump and described a rich patchwork of races, religions, and backgrounds that defines Upper Darby, where nearly a quarter of the population is foreign-born.
Some described immigrant neighbors currently living in fear, unable to answer the door or go to religious services due to the anxiety of potentially being apprehended by ICE. Many said they moved to Upper Darby specifically for its diversity.
“Our history reminds us that legality and morality are not the same thing. Upper Darby Township cannot determine federal immigration policy, but it can determine how our own lawful authority and resources are used,” said State Rep. Heather Boyd, who spoke during public comment and represents parts of Upper Darby in the Pennsylvania House.
A smaller contingent of residents, however, pushed back against the proposal, warning that the ordinance makes few tangible changes to the police department’s policies while potentially putting a target on Upper Darby’s back for the federal government to strip away funding.
When asked if he believes the legislation is in the best interest of the police department, police superintendent Timothy Bernhardt said the ordinance “isn’t going to change what the Upper Darby Police Department does.”
The department has never been an immigration enforcement body, worn masks, worked with ICE under a 287(g) agreement, or stopped individuals simply to ask about their immigration status, Bernhardt said.
“I have no objection to it. It’s not going to change what we do every day, day in and day out,” the police superintendent added.
Township council members described the ordinance as a set of responsible guardrails for local officials in a municipality defined by its immigrant population.
“It’s an issue of establishing trust and making sure that people know that in Upper Darby, if you need help, you can call because this community serves you,” said council member Kyle McIntyre, who helped to draft the legislation.
“We will follow the law, but we will do everything in our power to protect our community and keep everyone safe,” Mayor Ed Brown said.

Title: A 43-unit apartment building that preserves historic features is proposed in Old City
Article_Text:
A 43-unit apartment building that preserves historic features is proposed in Old City
Old City is one of the few neighborhoods that still sees condo development. This project could become part of the trend.
A corner of Old City long considered for apartment development is now slated for a new 43-unit, seven-story building — an update from a smaller plan approved by the Philadelphia Historical Commission.
The property at 148 N. Second St. contains several buildings that are regulated by local historic regulations.
Two of the buildings have been approved for demolition — at 152 and 156 N. Second St. — while two are being preserved and incorporated into the project at 148 and 150 N. Second St.
The tallest points of the proposed structure are pushed back from the street to avoid overshadowing the older buildings and to keep in line with historic regulations.
“We … really made sure that those historic buildings at the corner were the star of the show, and our building wraps around those and gently steps down to them,” Derek Spencer, technical director with Gnome Architects, said at a Wednesday meeting of the Old City District.
The project, from Philadelphia-based developer Virgis Anusauskas, is seeking permission from the Zoning Board of Adjustment to build a taller and denser building than the underlying zoning allows.
It will include about 1,400 square feet of commercial space and parking for 15 vehicles. The project is replacing a number of buildings that were previously used as restaurant supply stores.
Anusauskas hopes to find a tenant that will not be open late at night — as his office will also be in the building.
The proposed project would contain a majority of two-bedroom apartments of about 900 square feet, with three three-bedroom units on the top levels between 1,100 and 1,500 square feet.
Anusauskas said a huge number of studio and one-bedroom apartments have been built in Philadelphia’s central neighborhoods in recent years, and he is seeing more market demand for larger apartments.
He is also keeping his options open when it comes to renting or selling the units.
The condo market in Philadelphia has been weak since the pandemic, but he thinks the sheer quantity of rental units available right now means there may be an opening to make this a condominium building.
“I’m not looking at studios at all, and one-bedrooms for the condos is not good,” Anusauskas said. “We want to have the people who live there to have some peace of mind, so we don’t want too many people.”
The plan approved by the Historical Commission had six stories, but Anusauskas says the new, taller version has received verbal affirmation. He is seeking the support of the Old City District ahead of an Oct. 28 Zoning Board of Adjustment hearing.
Attendees at Wednesday night’s community meeting asked why the project couldn’t remain within the rules that the existing zoning allows. For example, the height limit is 65 feet, where the proposed structure at its highest point is about 77 feet.
The development team argued that historic regulations made it more difficult to stick with their earlier plan, preventing them from maximizing the possible square footage on the site without going taller.
“Because we had to keep these two corner buildings, we can’t overbuild on top of them,” said Spencer of Gnome Architects. “We have to completely leave those pieces of those buildings untouched, so that really prevented us from maximizing the use of the site.”
Anusauskas says his team has a lot of experience with rehabilitating historic buildings, and he doesn’t foresee too many challenges, after he clears this last set of regulatory requirements.
He hopes to begin construction as soon as he gets zoning board approval.
If the zoning board doesn’t approve the project, he said, he will go back to the drawing board and find a way to make it work.
He says the cap over I-95 at Penn’s Landing and the new park that will be created there makes the neighborhood even more exciting.
“I love Old City. I love the history. The community is great,” Anusauskas said. The park ”will pick the whole neighborhood up, and we want to be part of it.”

Title: Pennsylvania lawmakers request 6-month extension as looming Skill Games deadline nears
Article_Text:
Pennsylvania lawmakers request 6-month extension as looming Skill Games deadline nears
CAMBRIA COUNTY, Pa (WJAC) — Dozens of business owners and nonprofit organizations rallied in Cambria County Wednesday evening to urge lawmakers to pass legislation related to the regulation and taxation of Skill Games.
The ongoing community rallies come as a looming October deadline approaches --- if lawmakers don't meet that deadline, the machines would be considered illegal throughout the commonwealth.
These Skill Game machines could be seized by state police in just weeks if state lawmakers do not come up with legislation by October 13th.
Restaurant owners and nonprofits are asking those lawmakers to take action as soon as possible.
At least one hundred people rallied Wednesday at the Cresson American Legion in Cambria County to urge lawmakers to pass legislation before the deadline.
Speakers at the event argued that Skill Games have become an important source of revenue for small businesses, veterans groups, volunteer fire companies and other nonprofits.
Supporters say that losing that source of revenue could have a major impact on services in the community.
“We contribute to the community in which we live, so it's the veterans, it's the girl scouts, it's the ball teams, it's the cancer society and if the Skill machines go away, there's gonna be a real shortfall and I’m not sure how we're gonna make that up; I think it's just gonna be less contributions going out,” said Scott Eberhart, commander of the Cresson American Legion.
“It just gives that supplemental income that helps small businesses and clubs. And for it to go away, that doesn't just hurt those businesses or clubs or military organizations, it hurts everybody in the community. It hurts local causes,” added Gary Sloan, owner of Our Station House Restaurant.
One manufacturer of Pennsylvania Skill Machines says that hundreds of jobs could be lost in the commonwealth.
“Our games are built by 170 employees. That's how many families I’m fighting for.”
Legislators also spoke out about the looming deadline.
“Best case scenario, we move it six months, which gives us really the time we need to put a proper bill out that's gonna address what needs to be regulated and how things are gonna be handled. Worst case scenario, I think, and I’m only speaking for myself, there's a chance that we end up passing a bad bill. I would rather pass a bad bill and then go back and make amendments and correct it than to not pass a bill,” said Rep. Jim Rigby.
Supporters are backing Senate Bill 1079 — sponsored by senators Gene Yaw and Anthony Williams — along with companion House Bill 2213.
The proposal would regulate Skill games and require a $500 monthly fee for each terminal.
Backers say the plan would bring in an estimated $300 million in state tax revenue in its first year.
They also say it would allow community organizations to keep using the money they rely on.
What I do worry about is that the legislators will not act quickly and we'll lose that and we'll have to pull all the machines come October 13th or 14th, and then everybody loses because the state loses out on potential income, we lose that supplemental income, and the local charities and organizations also lose out.
Those supporters are asking residents to call their legislators to share your story if your business or community would be impacted.
Again, that deadline is October 13th but lawmakers say that they have requested a 6 month stay to give them more time to work on a solution.

Title: USMNT camp highlighted by presence of 16-year-old F Cavan Sullivan
Article_Text:
Field Level Media
                
18 Sep 2026, 01:25 GMT+10
            
(Photo credit: Vincent Carchietta)
After taking MLS by storm over the past two months, 16-year-old Cavan Sullivan will get his first chance to play with the United States men's national team when it reconvenes this weekend at Atlanta.
The USMNT will take the field for the first time since the World Cup when it faces Peru on Sept. 26 at Orlando, Chile on Sept. 29 at St. Louis, Mexico on Oct. 3 at Glendale, Ariz., and Canada Oct. 6 in St. Paul, Minn.
Sullivan, who has put a charge into the Philadelphia Union of late, will headline a group of young players being introduced to national team duty. The other half of the team will be made up of USMNT veterans, although forwards Christian Pulisic and Folarin Balogun will not be on the squad.
Head coach Mauricio Pochettino stressed that the roster in no way represents the group that has priority heading toward the next World Cup in 2030.
'The 28 players that are going to be involved in these four games, for different circumstances, are the best players we want see and we want to work with. That's it,' Pochettino said at a press conference in New York on Thursday.
Pochettino will have 28 players in camp, with 13 of those seeking their first USMNT appearance.
Sullivan, a Philadelphia native, has shown his promise with six goals and 11 assists in 23 matches (16 starts) this season. He has goal contributions in seven consecutive games to lead Philadelphia's 10-game unbeaten run since the end of the World Cup break.
Among other players invited to USMNT camp for the first time are defender Neil Pierre, Sullivan's Union teammate, midfielder Zavier Gozo of English side Crystal Palace and forward Julian Hall of the New York Red Bulls, all of whom are 19 or younger.
Those players will get their first taste of USMNT culture alongside World Cup participants in Sebastian Berhalter, Alex Freeman, Gio Reyna, Auston Trusty and Malik Tillman.
'This is the beginning of a fresh start for everyone, and we are excited in these first matches to bring a group of experienced players along with some young talents who have great potential,' Pochettino said.
The United States got off to a promising start at the World Cup with a dominating victory over Paraguay before going through the red-card controversy created when Balogun was ejected from a knockout-round victory over Bosnia and Herzegovina only to be reinstated for the round-of-16 game against Belgium.
The USMNT was eliminated in a lackluster 4-1 loss to Belgium.
'It's a completely different approach than it was in the past,' Pochettino said of the start to another World Cup cycle. 'The World Cup is in four years. We need to work with different objectives and goals.'
--Field Level Media

Title: AAA: Gas Prices Continue to Climb as Crude Oil Remains High; Diesel Reaches New Record Highs
Article_Text:
AAA: Gas Prices Continue to Climb as Crude Oil Remains High; Diesel Reaches New Record Highs
Prices at the pump continue to climb. AAA reports that the national average for a gallon of regular gasoline is up 16 cents from last week at $4.43 and more than one dollar higher than it was a year ago. Crude oil remains high, averaging $100 per barrel amid continued volatility in the Strait of Hormuz. Gas prices are back to what they were earlier this year during the spring, and the national average is inching closer to this year’s record high of $4.56 set on May 21st. The all-time high for the national average is $5.01 set on June 14th, 2022. Diesel has reached a new record high at $6.39. today. Meanwhile, across the region, the Delaware gas price average is $4.36 today, up 4 cents in the last week and $1.31 higher than one year ago. The South Jersey gas price average is $4.41 today, up 5 cents in the last week and up $1.32 compared to one year ago. Diesel has reached new record highs across the region at $6.50 in Pennsylvania, $6.36 in New Jersey and $6.35 in Delaware.
Additional information from AAA:
In Pennsylvania, the gas average is $4.52 today, up 7 cents in the last week and up $1.21 from one year ago. The Philadelphia 5-county gas price average is $4.55 per gallon, up 7 cents from last week and up $1.28 from one year ago. The South Jersey gas price average is $4.41 today, up 5 cents in the last week and up $1.32 compared to one year ago. The Delaware gas price average is $4.36 today, up 4 cents in the last week and $1.31 higher than one year ago. Diesel has reached new record highs across the region at $6.50 in Pennsylvania, $6.36 in New Jersey and $6.35 in Delaware.
The national average per kilowatt hour of electricity at a public EV charging station stayed the same this past week at 42 cents.

According to new data from the Energy Information Administration (EIA), gasoline demand increased last week from 8.55 million barrels per day to 8.79 million. Total 
At the close of Wednesday’s formal trading session, WTI fell $3.40 to settle at $102.43 a barrel. The EIA reports that U.S. crude oil inventories decreased 0.6 million barrels to 423.4 million barrels, 1% above the five-year average.
The Weekend
“Drivers are facing another difficult week at the pump as prices keep climbing,” said Jana Tidwell, spokesperson for AAA Club Alliance. “Even more concerning, the average price of diesel has reached a record high of $6.50 in Pennsylvania and $6.35 in Delaware, putting additional pressure on commercial drivers, businesses and consumers who ultimately feel those higher transportation costs. With crude oil averaging around $100 per barrel and continued volatility in global energy markets, drivers should be prepared for fuel prices to remain elevated.”

Title: Business Ins & Outs: Bizzeria, UNIQLO and More Georgetown Openings
Article_Text:
Business Ins & Outs: Bombas, Alfie’s, Café Tulúm, Flavor Hive, Bizzeria, Uniqlo
By • September 17, 2026 0 45
By Robert Devaney
As previously forecast, we’re seeing an interesting mixture of retail and restaurants making their Georgetown debut: Uniqlo, Beso Besu, Garage, Joe & The Juice, Dayglow, Puree Juice Bar, Spicewalla, East Fork, Jones Road, Pop Mart, Dutch Darlings and Thursday Boot Company, as well as those listed here. Get ready for a busy fall season.
In: Uniqlo
Uniqlo Georgetown at 3262 M St. NW made its flashy debut on Aug. 28. The 22,618-square-foot store brings Uniqlo’s LifeWear philosophy “to one of Washington, D.C.’s most iconic neighborhoods, offering thoughtfully designed everyday apparel alongside unique local collaborations and community experiences,” the company tells us. Opening festivities included Japanese Taiko drum performances. People were seen walking around with Uniqlo bags all weekend.
In: Adriana Hoyos
Adriana Hoyos — high-end residential and commercial interior design, alongside luxury furniture collections — opened at 3328 M St. NW, part of the design-center vibe of the 3300 block of M Street and Cady’s Alley. Founded in 1994 by Ecuadorian interior designer Adriana Hoyos and her husband, Eduardo Pérez, the company is based in Miami with manufacturing facilities in Quito, Ecuador.
In: Bombas
“The comfort-focused apparel brand known for its One Purchased = One Donated mission,” Bombas opened its first Washington, D.C., store at 1400 Wisconsin Ave. NW. on Aug. 14. The socks-and-more retailer was co-founded by Georgetown University alum Randy Goldberg in 2013. To celebrate the opening, Bombas offered opening-day surprises, “including exclusive Crab Socks, available to the first 150 customers.”
In: Alfie’s
Chefs Alex McCoy and Justin Ahn opened Alfie’s — a northern Thai restaurant and natural wine bar — in the alley section of Hamilton Collective at 1228½ 31st St. NW on Sept. 2. Warning: It’s spicy.
“It’s got a bit of that feel of a hole-in-the-wall wine bar in Europe, but it also has the feel of a shophouse in Thailand,” McCoy told Washingtonian. “This wasn’t a restaurant before, but we worked really hard to make this place feel like it had been here for 40 or 50 years.”
In: Flora Pizzeria
Flora Pizzeria, which opened next to Alfie’s on Sept. 14, tells us: “We craft our artisanal pizza dough using a natural leaven, premium organic flour and authentic sea salt from Sicily.” Diliziusu!
In: Ellizabetta La Strega
Sommelier and restaurateur Elli Benchimol opened Ellizabetta La Strega in the West End on Sept. 9 at 2401 Pennsylvania Ave. NW, transforming the former Marcel’s space into a bar, restaurant and private dining destination. Benchimol also owns Georgetown’s Apéro and La Bohème on P Street.
In: Café Tulúm
Bringing beach vibes to Georgetown, Café Tulúm opened last month, offering “the vibrant flavors and lively atmosphere of southern México.” The restaurant joins the Grace Street Collective at 3210 Grace St. NW.
In: Flavor Hive
The popular Northern Virginia food truck Flavor Hive has opened a brick-and-mortar location at 3287½ M St. NW in the former Harmony Café space, offering samples to passersby to celebrate its debut.
In: O Street Collection
O Street Collection is a new art boutique at 3213 O St. NW that had a soft opening for Art All Night. It boasts a curated collection of 50-plus original artworks and artist-designed goods from more than 10 contemporary artists, with pieces ranging from $50 to over $10,000. The collection occupies a historic property that once housed the offices of Max N. Berry, Esq. — also a significant art collector — and, before that, a popular café.
In: Delhi Belly
Owned by Vikas Kakkar and Raj Manroy, Delhi Belly, which opened last month at 1560 Wisconsin Ave. NW, brings a casual dining experience inspired by the urban food culture of India. The spot at Wisconsin and Q — the original location of Dolcezza Gelato, now returning to Georgetown — has seen a lot of operators, also including La Jolie Bleue, Bharati and Oakberry.
Returning: Dolcezza Gelato
Once a Georgetowner, always a Georgetowner. Dolcezza Gelato, founded here in 2004 by Robb Duncan and Violeta Edelman, is slated to open in late fall or early winter in the former Pressed Juicery space at 1300 Wisconsin Ave. NW. Their return makes this corner spot their seventh location.
Dolcezza Gelato wrote on social media on Sept. 3: “the prodigal son & daughter are returning back to where it all began .. over 22 years ago when we set out on this beautiful titanic journey, it was in a 300 sq ft kitchen on wisconsin avenue & q street nw. we left our georgetown kitchen in 2013 to open our factory in the union market neighborhood .. & now we return .. down the street from where it started & it feels so sweet. we can’t wait to delight you georgetown. we’re coming home.”
Coming: Bizzeria
Michael Rafidi — who owns Albi and La’ Shukran, along with Yellow cafe and its “(not) pizza” on Wisconsin Avenue — is bringing Bizzeria to the back of 3246 Prospect St. NW, the same address as the upcoming Skillette, a cooking school by Kelly Singer. The pizza spot will have an entrance in the alleyway, entered from Potomac Street.
Coming: Kith
“Plans filed with the Old Georgetown Board show that Kith, the cult sneaker-and-streetwear label, is moving into 3040 M St. NW, adjacent to Barnes & Noble,” reports Urban Turf, which added: “Kith has built a devoted following since Ronnie Fieg opened his first store in New York in 2011, growing into one of the more prominent names in the streetwear-meets-luxury space through collaborations with brands like Nike, Adidas and New Balance.”
Coming: Edikted
Edikted, the women’s clothing retailer popular with Gen Zers, plans a 3,890-square-foot store in the space at 3135 M St. NW formerly occupied by Allbirds, according to the Washington Business Journal. Founded in Tel Aviv in 2020 by entrepreneurs Dedy Shwartzberg and Zvika Alon, the Los Angeles-based company lists 18 U.S. stores in 10 states.
Coming: Pop Mart
It’s another cult favorite. Pop Mart, a Beijing-based toy company, is heading to 3221 M St. NW. Think Hello Kitty and beyond — toys like Labubu, Harry Potter, the Powerpuff Girls and other pricey designer toys.
Coming: Brazilian Jiu Jitsu
Original Brazilian Jiu Jitsu & Mixed Martial Arts is coming to 3270 M St. NW, near Gold’s Gym, downstairs from the primary entrance. Think “discipline, community, self-defense, better humans” — offered at all levels, with private lessons as well.
Happy 1st Birthday to …
Amorino Gelato (3401 M St. NW), Andy’s Pizza (1065 Wisconsin Ave. NW), Flor Coffee + Books (1220 31st St. NW) and It’s a Secret Med Spa (1365 Wisconsin Ave. NW).
Thank you all for choosing Georgetown — you make us better.

Title: Column: The two-year waitlist to power modern life
Article_Text:
By Ken Silverstein
InsideSources.com
Every morning, millions of Americans run through the same unconscious routine: turn on the coffee maker, check the phone, adjust the air conditioner. Electricity is like air — invisible until it suddenly isn’t.
Behind your walls sits a network of copper, steel and high-voltage wire that keeps modern life humming. That network is now running short on the basic parts it needs. The risk: transformers, which are the metal boxes on utility poles that step down high-voltage power so it doesn’t blow out appliances.
Standard power transformers now take 2.5 years to deliver, according to data analysis firm Wood Mackenzie’s latest survey; the larger transformers used at substations — the fenced hubs that route power between plants and neighborhoods — are running three years in the firm’s newest survey and can take up to four. “Those lead time increases are not expected to improve in the near term,” Wood Mackenzie supply-chain analyst Ben Boucher told Utility Dive.
The Department of Energy estimates the U.S. imports 80 percent of its large power transformers. The steel inside those cores is even more concentrated: America has one domestic producer — Cleveland-Cliffs, whose Pennsylvania and Ohio plants can’t make enough to meet demand, so much of that steel is imported.
This isn’t theoretical. Builders nationwide report finished homes sitting dark — driveways poured, keys ready — because the utility is still waiting on a transformer. “We haven’t been able to catch up as a country,” said Alex Strong, senior federal legislative director at the National Association of Home Builders.
Entire subdivisions and factories are hostage to a missing box.
It’s tempting to demand heavy tariffs or rush every factory home. However, foundries take years to build, and trade barriers make scarce parts pricier for the utilities that need them.
The more realistic fix isn’t ideological — it’s economic self-interest. Utilities can’t afford to sit on their hands for three years while housing and factories wait to plug in. Market pressure is forcing their hand.
The fastest way out is modular standardization paired with strategic trade alliances.
Today, America’s 3,000 electric utilities order custom-engineered transformers, forcing manufacturers to build nearly every unit from scratch. Push utilities toward standard, interchangeable designs, and factories could mass-produce them far quicker.
Why hasn’t this happened? Habit. For a century, power companies operated as insulated monopolies, with engineers insisting on their own specifications. Factory owners won’t retool assembly lines until utilities guarantee big orders; utilities won’t abandon custom designs until standardized units sit cheap and ready on the shelf.
That standoff is breaking. The status quo now threatens utility revenue and growth.
Government’s role here is referee, not dictator. Federal agencies can offer matching grants to help factories retool. State utility commissions, which set rates, can give power companies incentives to buy standardized, modular gear.
Pairing that standardization with “friend-shoring” — building supply alliances with trusted partners like South Korea, Japan and Mexico, all established grid-equipment makers — could secure America’s electric network without stoking inflation or a trade fight.
Except “friend-shoring” is a harder sell than it sounds. Canada, long treated as America’s steadiest industrial partner, is now on the other side of a real trade fight. A 50 percent U.S. tariff on Canadian autos, alcohol and dairy took effect in August, and Washington let its trade pact with Canada lapse this summer. Ottawa retaliated September 8, doubling its tariffs on U.S. steel and aluminum to 50 percent. If our closest neighbor can end up in a tariff war, friend-shoring may be ill-fated too.
Standardization doesn’t carry that risk. It depends only on Washington and state regulators agreeing on a design, not on any foreign government’s goodwill. That is the most promising lever.
Utility commissions move slowly, and procurement departments resist change. Change is coming, because patience has run out. Build cutting-edge power plants or AI data centers, but without transformers to move that power, economies stagnate and die.
Next time you brew your coffee, look at the utility pole down the street. That silent metal box isn’t just hardware — it’s the linchpin of modern life. Fixing the bottleneck isn’t about political grandstanding. It’s about aligning market incentives and accepting that a three-year wait for basic parts is no longer an option.
Ken Silverstein has covered energy and international affairs for years. He wrote this for InsideSources.com.
