Title: Kennedy tells anti-vaccine activists they have a friend in Trump's White House
Article_Text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. gave the keynote address Thursday at a conference of an anti-vaccine activist group he once chaired, telling the hundreds in attendance that they had a friend in President Donald Trump's White House.
It was Kennedy's first time appearing at the Children's Health Defense conference since he became secretary. Kennedy took leave from the group when he launched his bid to become president in 2023, but his speech Thursday served as a sort of homecoming, offering him a platform from which to hail the administration's steps to scale back vaccine guidance and reassure the activists in attendance that he was working to turn their priorities into policy.
“Let me be clear: You have a strong and steadfast friend in the White House. We've accomplished in 19 months things that would have seemed unthinkable two years ago,” he said.
The speech, peppered with questions about long established vaccine safety, also highlighted how once fringe views on vaccines have been given a prominent pulpit under the Trump administration.
Kennedy boasted about the administration's moves to downsize the childhood vaccination schedule and reshape a key vaccine advisory board — steps that have since been halted by a judge.
Kennedy lauded Trump for pushing ahead with attempts to overhaul vaccine guidance, including an executive order last month calling for spacing out the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, against medical groups' recommendations.
That executive order and now Kennedy's keynote speech at the Children's Health Defense conference mark a pivot by the White House and the Department of Health and Human Services, who earlier this year had appeared to be moving beyond vaccine efforts and toward a less contentious agenda on healthy food ahead of November’s midterm elections. HHS promoted the speech on its social media channels.
Kennedy, a longtime anti-vaccine activist, chaired Children’s Health Defense for years. He served as the group’s chief legal counsel and expanded it. After becoming health secretary last year, Kennedy moved at a blistering pace to overhaul public health guidance and revamp long-held precedents in vaccine policymaking.
Critics, among them many of the country's top medical associations, have said the moves risk stoking vaccine hesitancy and sowing confusion among Americans who endured a crisis of trust in their public health agencies following the COVID-19 pandemic. That public confidence continues to erode.

Title: Exclusive: New CDC director talks measles outbreak, employee morale and distrust in agency
Article_Text:
Exclusive: New CDC director talks measles outbreak, employee morale and distrust in agency
ATLANTA, Ga. (Atlanta News First) — In her first media interview since becoming the director of the CDC, Dr. Erica Schwartz said restoring trust in the Atlanta-based agency is among her top priorities.
Speaking exclusively with Atlanta News First’s Abby Kousouris during the Health Connect South forum in downtown Atlanta, Schwartz said trust in the CDC is at an all-time low.
“How do we show the American people that the CDC is an incredibly exceptional public health institution?” Schwartz said. “Something that they should trust. Something that they should rely on. And so, I’m gonna be really laser-focused on how do we rebuild that trust.”
Schwartz also addressed a measles outbreak in Georgia, working with Health and Human Services Secretary Robert Kennedy Jr. and her plans to combat vaccine hesitancy.
Her remarks come as the nation faces its worst measles surge in 30 years, with more than 3,200 reported cases nationwide and kindergarten MMR vaccination rates dropping below the 95% community herd immunity threshold.
“Measles is the most contagious disease,” Schwartz said, noting that one infected individual can spread the virus to 12 to 18 susceptible people. “You could have pneumonia. You could get something called subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, which is nearly fatal, and you could die. The MMR vaccine is safe and effective.”
Schwartz’s defense of the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine stands in contrast to Kennedy, who has characterized measles as a mild illness and frequently questioned vaccine safety.
When asked whether she is prepared to push back against Kennedy when scientific evidence contradicts him, Schwartz pointed to her background in the uniformed services and as a former deputy surgeon general.
“In the uniformed services, we have something called ‘but sir, but ma’am,’ which basically means you can disagree with your superiors,” Schwartz said. “Secretary Kennedy and I have worked together for five weeks now, and I can tell you there have been a few ‘but sirs’ behind closed doors.”
Schwartz added that while she engages in debates with Kennedy, the final authority rests with him as cabinet secretary.
The CDC has also drawn scrutiny from congressional leaders after withholding certified measles-related deaths reported by Pennsylvania health officials, a move that followed public comments from Kennedy calling the reports “fabricated.”
Schwartz denied that death counts were altered for political reasons, stating that the agency historically lacked a standardized definition for a measles-related fatality.
“If someone got hit by a bus, and they happened to have COVID, often that was called a COVID-related death,” Schwartz said, drawing a comparison to early pandemic tracking disputes. “Definitions matter. In terms of my transparency as a CDC director, I want to be very accurate with the American people.”
Schwartz said the CDC has asked the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to develop a formal definition and is currently waiting for National Center for Health Statistics reviews to confirm measles as the underlying cause of death on death certificates.
Beyond measles, Schwartz responded to questions regarding the agency’s tracking of a massive summer Cyclospora parasite outbreak linked to imported iceberg lettuce that sickened nearly 20,000 people and hospitalized more than 1,000.
Critics raised concerns that the CDC quietly downgraded Cyclospora from mandatory tracking under FoodNet prior to the outbreak, but Schwartz defended the shift as an effort to remove “redundant reporting” while maintaining data through the National Notifiable Disease Surveillance System.
Schwartz also addressed concerns over unstaffed “zombie programs,” where Congress appropriated hundreds of millions of dollars for smoking cessation and Alzheimer’s disease prevention, but offices remain unstaffed following federal workforce reductions.
Schwartz said center leaders are overwhelmed by the staffing deficit and noted that agency leadership is actively studying whether the CDC’s long-term workforce should reflect pandemic-era levels or return to a lower pre-pandemic baseline.
Internationally, Schwartz addressed the ongoing, deadly Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, confirming that CDC experts are deployed with “boots on the ground” working alongside the DRC Ministry of Health, Uganda, and the U.S. Department of State to contain the spread amid active regional conflict.
Closer to home, Schwartz spoke to the persistent trauma inside the Atlanta headquarters following workforce cuts and the August 2025 shooting near the CDC campus that claimed the life of DeKalb County Police Officer David Rose.
Schwartz recounted an all-hands meeting shortly after her arrival where an employee appeared visibly frightened to speak publicly.
“There was a young man who was asking a question, and he was so nervous in asking the question — and actually, it wasn’t even nervousness. He was afraid to ask the question,” Schwartz said. “And so, you could tell that there was just a lack of psychological safety.”
Schwartz said her overarching priority during her first 100 days is rebuilding public and employee trust through scientific rigor, transparency, and humility.

Title: New wild cat species is identified for first time in 100 years – NBC10 Philadelphia
Article_Text:
For the first time in a century, researchers say they’ve identified a new species of wild cat previously unknown to science.
Leopardus tilcayo — or the Tilcayo tiger cat — is slender and spotted, with rounded ears. It is smaller than a typical house cat and lives in the Bolivian Yungas, the cloud forest where the Andes mountains meet the Amazon basin. The species was described for the first time in the journal Current Biology on Thursday.
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
It’s rare to find a new, relatively large mammal — unsurprisingly, most new animal species discovered are small in size, said Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, who co-authored the study and leads a wild cat conservation program called the Programa de Investigación de Félidos Bolivia (Bolivian Felid Research and Conservation Program).
“This time, it’s a cat. That’s really novel. And it hasn’t happened in 100 years,” she said. “No one else had named it. No one else had described it.”
The size of the Leopardus tilcayo population is not clear yet.
“We really don’t know how many cats are still in the wild,” said Nogales-Ascarrunz, whose work as a conservationist is funded by National Geographic. “We need science, we need more studies to answer this question, which is actually critical for its conservation.”
U.S. & World
Stories that affect your life across the U.S. and around the world.
Tiger cats — small, wild cats native to South and Central America in the Leopardus genus — face stiff conservation challenges as development and agriculture expand.
The new study says there are five tiger cat species in South America.
“All of them are in habitats that are vanishing fast,” said Tadeu de Oliveira, another coauthor of the study and an ecologist at the State University of Maranhão in Brazil.
Leopardus tilcayo might have continued to escape notice if not for Nogales-Ascarrunz’s sharp eyes. She volunteers at a wildlife rehabilitation center near La Paz called the Senda Verde Wildlife Sanctuary.
“I saw this cat, it was really, really small, and I couldn’t believe how small it was,” Nogales-Ascarrunz said. “I thought it was a kitten.”
The cat had been brought in by a man living in a community in the forest near La Paz, who had mistaken the cat for a domestic kitten, according to details recorded by the sanctuary. He had fed the animal noodles, rice and eggs, only to realize it was wild and that he could not take care of it. So he brought it to the sanctuary.
Initially, colleagues at the sanctuary thought the animal might be a known tiger cat species from Brazil, but Nogales-Ascarrunz wasn’t convinced.
“If you look at the spots or the tail, they really don’t match,” she said.
Nogales-Ascarrunz did genetic testing, using tissue from the tiger cat and a second animal that also turned up at Senda Verde. The results from those specimens revealed that the two cats were unique and from the same species, which had diverged from other tiger cat lineages about 1.4 million years ago. That’s enough genetic distance to consider it a new species.
Nogales-Ascarrunz said, however, that local communities in Bolivia have been aware of the species’ presence for generations.
“This cat, they call it Tilcayo. And when you ask, ‘Does it have some meaning in Quechua or Almyra and other indigenous languages?’ they say, ‘No, my grandpa told me that’s the Tilcayo,’” Nogales-Ascarrunz said. “This is a traditional knowledge that they have in the community. We want to preserve that knowledge and we didn’t want to give it another name.”
It’s not rare for scientists to add a mammal species to the taxonomy — they do so about 65 times a year, according to a study released last year. But many of those new species — including some recently named wild cats — are the results of a split. That’s when scientists realize what was once a single species has sufficient genetic distinctions to become two.
For example, the Sunda clouded leopard found on the island of Borneo — called Neofelis diardi — was first recognized in 2006 when its genome was distinguished from its mainland counterparts. But examples of the Sunda clouded leopard were already in museums at that point.
The Tilcayo, on the other hand, was completely novel to scientists.
“We didn’t have specimens in museums,” de Oliveira said. “It had never been collected before.”
Nogales-Ascarrunz said this new species is likely in danger. She views the discovery as yet another argument in favor of conservation.
“It’s a new reason to protect the world,” she said.

Title: Roosevelt Boulevard $134M safety upgrades move ahead – NBC10 Philadelphia
Article_Text:
Philadelphia and PennDOT are moving ahead with $134 million in changes to Roosevelt Boulevard by 2030, with projects aimed at improving traffic flow and pedestrian safety along one of Philadelphia’s most dangerous roads.
At the same time, supporters are renewing a decades-old push for a subway beneath the boulevard as the city and state consider longer-term transit options for the corridor.
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
The project on the boulevard is grouped into three stages: “Today,” “Tomorrow,” and “Reimagined.”
Projects that will be wrapped around the end of 2026 include the addition of automated speed cameras, improvements at the Summerdale/Adams intersection and Southampton Road intersection, improvements to crossover lanes (Cottman to Red Lion), addition of SEPTA Direct Bus B, and the installation of Business Access and Transit (BAT) Lanes (Bustleton to City Line).
The "tomorrow" projects are targeted by the end of 2030, including upgrades to traffic signals and lanes, shorter pedestrian crossing distances, sidewalks and other pedestrian safety improvements.
“In addition, they'll see landscaping improvements along key sections of the boulevard, as well as improved bus stops and some parking enhancements as well,” Kyle Brown, a city planner with the Philadelphia City Planning Commission, said.
Local
Breaking news and the stories that matter to your neighborhood.
Public meetings about the planned projects are set to begin next month, allowing residents to learn more and provide feedback. The first will be held virtually on Oct. 8 at 7 p.m.
An engagement session on the stretch from Pratt to Old Lincoln Highway will be held on Oct. 13 from 6 p.m. to 8 p.m. at Kleinlife, 10100 Jamison Avenue.
A separate engagement session will be held the following week, focused on the stretch from Broad Street to Pratt Street, on Oct. 14 from 6 p.m. to 8 p.m. at Esperanza Arts Center, 4261 N 5th Street.
Traffic safety is a major motivation for the changes. Between 2018 and 2022, Roosevelt Boulevard accounted for 10% of all traffic deaths in Philadelphia, according to the City Planning Commission.
The city says pedestrian crashes have been cut in half since speed cameras began operating on the boulevard in 2020.
State Rep. Jared Solomon, who represents Northeast Philadelphia, said the planned improvements are welcome but wants to see more progress on the longer-term vision for the boulevard.
“In the end, a couple signal changes, a couple crosswalks, rejiggering some particular intersections, that's not what is the real inspiring work that we need to do,” Solomon said.
Philadelphia and Pennsylvania are studying three longer-term transit possibilities for Roosevelt Boulevard: bus rapid transit, light rail and a subway.
The city's project website said the preferred recommendation is anticipated by 2026, but city planners said Thursday that more engagement will happen into 2027.
“There's really nothing more to study. We know the options. We know the benefits. We know that the biggest obstacle is always the cost,” Solomon said.
A 2025 study by New York University's Marron Institute of Urban Management projected a subway could attract 51,000 to 62,000 daily riders (depending on the model).
Years ago, SEPTA said the projected cost was at least $10 billion. It is now potentially much more.
While the topic was not discussed directly, subway supporters brought their case to the Philadelphia City Planning Commission, arguing that plans need to be advanced so the project could compete for federal infrastructure funding in the future.
“We can't get that infrastructure dollar if the plans are not ready,” Dr. Jay Arzu, an advocate for the Roosevelt Boulevard subway, told NBC10.
Arzu said supporters believe a subway could also spur economic development in Northeast Philadelphia.
“We would be turning the Boulevard of Death into the Boulevard of Life,” Arzu said.
This story was originally reported for broadcast by NBC Philadelphia. AI tools helped convert the story to a digital article, and an NBC Philadelphia journalist edited the article for publication.

Title: 'Godfather of AI' issues ominous warning to Congress – NBC10 Philadelphia
Article_Text:
Geoffrey Hinton, a Nobel laureate known as the “Godfather of AI,” issued an ominous warning to lawmakers: Congress may only have one year left to implement safeguards on artificial intelligence before it loses control of it.
“Maybe a year, but not much more than a year,” Hinton said Wednesday evening after he and other AI experts huddled with Senate and House lawmakers behind closed doors. “If you look at predictions for when we’ll get superintelligence,” he continued, “it used to be maybe 30 years, maybe 50 years. Then it came down to maybe 10 years, maybe 20 years. Now people are saying, a lot of the researchers are saying only a few years.”
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
Hinton and other experts came to Capitol Hill at the invitation of Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., one of the chamber’s chief critics of AI, who invited lawmakers of both parties to the private briefing. Louisiana Sen. John Kennedy was the only Republican to attend.
Hinton’s dire warning came as the House departed Washington for the last time before the November midterm elections. And there appeared to be lots of conversations but little sign of progress on any substantial AI regulation in the Senate.
“This is bats--- crazy, insane science fiction stuff that literally happened recently,” Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif., a member of House Democratic leadership, told NBC News after Wednesday’s briefing.
Lieu was referring to the Hugging Face incident, when a swarm of OpenAI agents accessed the internet, hacked the platform Hugging Face and tried to cover their tracks to deceive humans about their actions. Hinton, who resigned as a vice president and engineering fellow at Google in 2023 over concerns about AI safety and went on to win the Nobel Prize in physics the following year, called the hack a “little Chernobyl.”
“AI has now reached the point where AI is designing better AI,” Hinton told reporters after the briefing. “That’s called recursive self-improvement. ... It is going to get out of control unless we do something. We need to slow down.”
In response to the Hugging Face breach, Lieu teamed up with Rep. Nathaniel Moran, R-Texas, to introduce the AI Kill Switch Act to require AI developers of powerful models to preserve technical powers to suspend or shut down their systems. It would also create a framework to empower the government to trigger such a shutdown if needed.
“I hope it comes up this year,” Lieu said. “We still have a lame-duck session, and there’s also interest on the Senate side. It is a very simple, commonsense bill. At a very basic level, humans must be in control of AI, not the other way around.”
The Hinton briefing capped a flurry of activity on Capitol Hill this week after AI researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Claude-maker Anthropic and took to social media to warn that the people building AI systems believe it could “kill us all by the end of the decade.”
House and Senate lawmakers in both parties have rolled out legislation seeking to halt or slow down AI development in the last few years, though none has gone anywhere to date.
But the national interest in the issue has revived talks over past proposed AI regulations among Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D.; Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn.; Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas; and the panel’s ranking member, Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash.
“Look, my hope is that we can mark up legislation, in particular on catastrophic risk. I’ve been working closely with Amy Klobuchar and John Thune. It’s still not clear if we’re going to get bipartisan agreement,” Cruz told NBC News this week. “We’ve got to have bipartisan agreement before we have something that can move forward. And I would say those talks are ongoing.”
After hearing from Hinton, Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., said she believes “we are in the last minutes of being able to get some meaningful control over these agents that are beginning to replicate themselves.”
For years, Sanders has been sounding the alarm that AI will erase millions of jobs in America, harm children and young people who become overreliant on it and concentrate power in a “handful of oligarchs.”
“There is now growing alarm about the future of humanity and creating a technology that human beings cannot control,” Sanders said. “And I’m happy to tell you that I think there is a growing sense of urgency upon members of Congress that this has to be dealt with.”
Kennedy, the sole Republican attendee, said that the experts discussed the “larger risk” of “what happens when AI no longer is a tool controlled by humans, but AI through recursive self-improvement becomes an independent species.”
“If you have fire ants in your kitchen, you’re probably going to step on them,” he said. “What would happen if we created an independent species that became superior to a human species? Would they step on us? Would they create a virus or a bacteria that can spread as quickly as the common cold to kill all of us? Now, if there’s a 1% chance of that, we have to take it seriously. And I don’t think the United States Congress is ready yet to try to reach a global solution.”
Moments later, his suspicions appeared to be confirmed as Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., blocked Kennedy’s request for unanimous consent to pass his own “kill switch” bill, aimed at preventing AI agents from slipping out of human control.
“Right now, Congress can’t pass gas,” Kennedy quipped.
Frank Thorp V contributed.

Title: Rare footage captures humpback whale mom grieving her stillborn calf – NBC10 Philadelphia
Article_Text:
Rare footage has captured what scientists believe may be a humpback whale mother's response to losing her newborn calf.
According to a study published by Discover Animals, the encounter unfolded off the coast of Australia in July 2025, when observers spotted two adult humpback whales lingering near the surface.
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
One whale positioned itself vertically in the water with its tail pointed upward. About 30 minutes later, pieces of an amniotic membrane were spotted floating nearby, signaling a recent birth.
Curious about the missing calf, researchers lowered a GoPro camera beneath the surface and discovered a heartbreaking scene on the seafloor. A newborn humpback lay motionless at the bottom of the ocean while the presumed mother repeatedly returned to its side. The whale was filmed swimming alongside the calf, resting next to it, maintaining eye contact, touching the calf and moving a pectoral fin over its body.
Researchers interpreted the event as "postmortem attentive behavior" involving a stillborn calf.
"Reviews suggest that post-mortem attentive behaviour is largely absent or extremely rare among baleen whales, particularly in relation to dead calves," according to a 2018 study, Whale and dolphin behavioral responses to dead conspecifics.
U.S. & World
Stories that affect your life across the U.S. and around the world.
Part of what makes the observation so unusual is the biology of humpback whales. Unlike newborn toothed whales and porpoises, baby humpbacks lack enough blubber to float on their own. Without assistance from an adult, they sink shortly after death, making stillbirths nearly impossible for researchers to observe in the wild.
Researchers watched the mother for nearly two hours and believe the behavior may have continued for hours, or even days, after they left the area.
"Underwater footage documented the mother approaching the calf closely, making repeated contact using her head and pectoral fin, and positioning herself eye-to-eye alongside the corpse," according to the humpback whale post-mortem study.
Notably, the whale did not attempt to lift the calf toward the surface, a behavior documented in some dolphin and toothed whale species after a calf dies. Researchers say this may suggest the mother recognized the newborn was unresponsive, even as she continued returning to it.
Andrew Mulville, a rescue boat captain with the Sea World Foundation and co-author of the study, told Phys.org he initially thought he was simply looking at two whales resting on the surface.
"When I actually worked out what was happening, I was totally surprised," he said. "It was definitely not what I was expecting to see out at sea that day."

Title: PA ranks among the highest for student debt, as borrowers struggle to keep up
Article_Text:
PA ranks among the highest for student debt, as borrowers struggle to keep up
PENNSYLVANIA (WTAJ) -- As student loan debt continues to rise, Pennsylvania ranks third among states with the most student debt, according to the latest report.
The report, conducted by WalletHub, compared all states and the District of Columbia on a range of metrics, including student-loan indebtedness and economic opportunity, to find just how much of a financial burden student debt has become.
Pennsylvania ranked near the top in proportion of students with debt (5) and student debt as a percentage of income (5). It ranks near average for its unemployment rate for people aged 25 to 34 (21) and its percentage of student loans that are delinquent or in default (26).
The report also found that states like New Mexico, Washington, California, Hawaii, and Utah had the least student debt, WalletHub adds, with Mississippi ranked first in the most student debt.
Advertisement
Student debt relief has been a hot topic for many years. Many borrowers who saw some relief under the Saving on a Valuable Education (SAVE) program now have to move to repayment plans with higher monthly payments after a federal court ruling ended the program. Now many borrowers are struggling to keep up.
WalletHub reports that the average Pennsylvania resident with student loan debt owes "just under half, or 43% of the median income in the state," making it the fifth-highest rate in the country. Just over the border in Delaware, borrowers owe an average of almost $40,000 in student loans, with 60% of students having loans.

Title: Woman had 1 sudden ovarian cancer symptom before diagnosis – NBC10 Philadelphia
Article_Text:
Cathy Brockhoff thought she had very bad indigestion when she woke up early one morning with a stomachache.
She took a few antacid tablets, but the ache progressed from major discomfort to so much pain that it hurt to lie down. Brockhoff woke up her husband and told him she needed to go to the hospital. Something was very wrong.
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
She suspected a gallbladder problem or pancreatitis, but after multiple tests and imaging, a sonogram detected a mass on her ovary. At just 47, she was diagnosed with ovarian cancer — a disease that usually strikes women in their 60s.
“This literally came out of the blue. … It was very crazy,” Brockhoff, a teacher’s assistant who lives in Coram, New York, tells TODAY.com.
“I still process it when someone says to me, ‘ovarian cancer.’ Like it still makes your stomach drop, even though it’s three years later. Because I’m still like, wow, that’s me. That’s still surreal.”
Most ovarian cancers develop after menopause, the American Cancer Society notes.
But it can strike before then, says Dr. Antoinette Sakaris, a gynecologic oncologist at Northwell South Shore University Hospital in New York. She treated Brockhoff and calls her diagnosis “definitely on the younger side.”
Health
“That’s why her story is actually quite important to bring to the public,” Sakaris tells TODAY.com.
“So that women hopefully can be more in tune with looking for subtle symptoms of ovarian cancer.”
Brockhoff’s sudden and severe stomachache in 2023 wasn’t a typical warning sign, but it was actually “fortunate” because it triggered the ER visit that led to imaging that found the tumor, the doctor adds.
Ovarian cancer symptoms are often much more vague, allowing the cancer to grow and spread undetected — a big reason why it’s the most lethal gynecologic cancer, researchers note.
Most Cases Are Random
Ovarian cancer is rare — about 1% of women in the general population will be diagnosed during their lifetime, according to the National Cancer Institute.
Brockhoff says ovarian cancer was “completely off the radar” for her. No one in her family has had it, and genetic tests after her diagnosis found she didn’t have genetic mutations that can significantly raise the risk of the disease.
Like 75% of patients, Brockhoff’s case was “a random event,” Sakaris says.
Risk factors include older age, a family history of the disease and having a harmful genetic mutation. Up to 58% of women who inherit a BRCA1 mutation and up to 29% of women who have a BRCA2 mutation will develop ovarian cancer, according to the National Cancer Institute.
Never being pregnant can also raise the risk because “unrelenting ovulation” is a risk factor, Sakaris notes. Pregnancy and birth control pills are protective against ovarian cancer because they reduce the number of ovulations a woman has in her lifetime.
Still, most women who are diagnosed are not at high risk, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention notes.
There’s no screening — like a mammogram for breast cancer — or blood test available for the general population, so it’s key for women to know and report the symptoms to their doctor.
Ovarian Cancer Symptoms
When it comes to warning signs, think of the acronym BEAT, which stands for bloating, early satiety, abdominal pain and toilet changes, Sakaris advises:
Bloating
Feeling like your pants are too tight and noticing the abdomen getting larger is one of the main symptoms a doctor monitors in her own body.
It happens when excess fluid, called ascites, builds up in the belly, causing it to swell, the American Cancer Society notes.
Since bloating is very common, it’s the persistence of it that matters, Sakaris says. Watch for bloating that doesn’t go away with a bowel movement and continues for weeks.
“Imagine looking like you’re four or five months pregnant, but you’re not,” she notes.
“We tell women, ‘If for two weeks or more, you’re having a persistent daily bloating or fullness in the abdomen that’s not going away, bring it to your physician’s attention.’”
Early Satiety
This means feeling full quickly after eating and may happen because a tumor or fluid buildup in the belly limits how much food the stomach can hold.
“I often tell patients, ‘If you had your most favorite beverage and food in front of you from your favorite restaurant or cafe, you are getting ready to eat it, and you can’t eat beyond a few bites and you feel very full with or without nausea, that’s worrisome,’” she says.
“If there’s a mass … that can slow down the transit of our gut, and so everything feels like it’s backing up on you.”
Abdominal Pain
Brockhoff says this was the only symptom she experienced.
Her sudden stomachache is less common and was likely caused when the ovarian cancer tumor grew, then bled into itself and pushed on nearby organs, Sakaris says.
But most women describe a gradual, progressive onset of abdominal pain over a month or two, she adds.
Toilet Changes
This includes bowel and bladder changes such as frequent urination, narrow stools and feeling like the bowels don’t fully empty.
It happens because the bladder can’t hold as much urine as it normally would if there’s a tumor taking up space in the pelvis. Similarly, a mass could press on the rectum or the colon and cause constipation.
If you always drink a lot of water and are used to going to the bathroom frequently, notice any changes from baseline, Sakaris advises.
In a ‘Good Place’ After Treatment
After being diagnosed with Stage 3 ovarian cancer, Brockhoff underwent surgery to remove the tumor, her uterus and her ovaries, plus a portion of her colon that was near the mass as a precaution.
She then had six rounds of chemotherapy, followed by targeted therapy drugs. October marks three years since scans showed no evidence of disease. Brockhoff feels lucky she had a warning sign she couldn’t ignore and says she’s in a “good place” thanks to her family’s support.
She urges women to pay attention to their body, and not ignore symptoms.
“Working and raising kids, we don’t always take the time out to realize, ‘I’ve had this stomach ache for four days,’” she says.
“I feel like we constantly make excuses or push things (off) because we’re always going forward in another direction. We have to stop doing that.”

Title: Who holds the power for concert tours like Ed Sheeran's? – NBC10 Philadelphia
Article_Text:
Concert promoters wield great power. Venue owners can too but they rarely choose to. And artists capable of filling stadiums like Ed Sheeran usually have approval over everything that happens under their name.
That's the consensus view of music business players who talked to The Associated Press about how mammoth tours like Sheeran's generally work.
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
The singer's ongoing Loop Tour is mired in chaos after four supporting acts quit in solidarity with rapper Macklemore, who was dropped for making pro-Palestinian comments onstage at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium.
Sheeran said on Instagram that the decision was made by the promoter, and he had no power over it. The promoter said it had no choice because venues wouldn't allow Macklemore to perform.
Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium, which is among the remaining tour stops, said in a statement that the decision to drop Macklemore was a result of his recent comments “and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery.”
The promoter and the artist share power
The promoter is the primary business actor on a tour. At high levels, it's a company like Messina Touring Group, the promoter of Sheeran's tour.
“The promoter puts up the money, pays all of the acts, deals with the venue. They provide the stake, sell the tickets, and the artists come on and play,” said Ray Waddell, chief content director for media and conferences for the Oak View Group, an entertainment and venue management company whose properties include the concert trade publication Pollstar.
Sheeran said in his Instagram post that despite his attempts “to build a bridge” all week, “the venue’s and promoter’s decision was final.”
But do promoters generally have the ultimate say for who is on the bill?
“If you’re paying for everything, yes you can make that call,” Waddell said, “but almost without exception the promoter wants to do what the artists want.”
Dean Sheldon Serwin, an entertainment lawyer who works in the music industry, said that broadly speaking, “at the end of the day that superstar headliner is going to have approval over everything.”
And the artist's power derives from their ability to fill arenas and stadiums.
“The way to make money in the music industry for real is butts in seats, always has been, always will be,” Serwin said. “How many tickets can you sell and how consistently can you sell those tickets?”
But while it may be minimal with acts on the level of Sheeran or Ariana Grande, there is still a transactional relationship.
“When you want to play at the venues you want to play at, there’s a give and take,” Serwin said.
Lil Gary, a music artists manager who in the past worked in tour management for acts including the Rolling Stones and the Eagles, said touring musicians and their representatives would want say over “a great many things especially when it comes to creative control, but when it gets down to the minutiae, not very much.”
But she said on some nonmusical issues they’ll take a great interest.
“Artists of a certain stature, they would absolutely dictate how security works,” she said as an example.
She said it’s definitely very rare in her experience for supporting artists to have any effect on how the tour went or its fate.
“The opening acts that were on Rolling Stones tours, for the most part they were happy to be there,” Gary said. “They just suited up, showed up and did the job.”
Neither Gary nor Waddell nor Serwin are involved in the Sheeran tour.
The stadium owners' role is usually silent
Venues and their owners like Kraft are usually hands-off players, but they have say if they make the rare choice of wielding it.
“Certainly they can lock the doors,” Waddell said. “They usually hand the keys to the promoter. The promoter comes in and does the show whether it’s a club or a stadium, but that doesn’t mean they vacate all power and influence.”
Waddell said venue operators, like promoters, are usually savvy and can anticipate what an artist is likely to do or say based on past performances.
“I don’t see why it surprised anybody given the history of the artist involved,” he said. “That being said, I don’t know that Robert Kraft was up on his Macklemore.”
“But,” Waddell said, “he got wind of it and he didn’t like it and it’s his stadium.”
What if they have to cancel?
Concert tour cancellations are common but are usually based on things like artists’ health. And ideally, there’s immediate rescheduling with the very same tickets honored.
“That can’t always happen, but it is the best,” Gary said.
There is no strong evidence that Sheeran's entire tour is going to be scrapped over the opening act issue.
But if it did, multiple insurance companies would likely be involved in salvaging the aftermath.
The biggest artists generally have their own insurers, and the promoter has its own, to take care of refunding fans and paying people who are contractually owed.
“They would go to their respective carriers and sort out their respective losses,” Gary said.
The circumstances could easily lead to blame and broken business relationships, but Waddell said “they work it out because everybody wants to work together again in the future.”
“Ed Sheeran’s young. He’s got a lot of tours ahead of him and these tours make a lot of money,” he said. “It’s a business and it’s not going away. Everybody’s going to be doing this next year and 10 years after that, God willing.”

Title: 'Evil Genius' Review: Courteney Cox's Snarky Pizza Bomber Comedy
Article_Text:
If you were glued to “Evil Genius,” Netflix’s 2018 documentary series about the bizarre “pizza bomber” killing of 2003, but wished its true-crime study rang just a little less true, then Courteney Cox’s new film of the same title has you covered. Dramatizing that sad, sordid story of weaponized criminal incompetence into a heightened comedy of errors, the film has little to reveal that we don’t already know, so settles for raking over the stranger-than-fiction facts of the case with lurid, mocking glee. Viewers’ mileage will largely depend on their patience for Patricia Arquette’s unmodulated, to-the-rafters performance as the scheme’s criminal not-so-mastermind Marjorie Diehl-Armstrong, which is scarcely tempered by David Harbour’s more quietly shambling work as her co-conspirator and sometime lover Bill Rothstein.
Assembled with little formal style or finesse by Cox — in her first feature-length directorial effort since 2014’s Seann William Scott comedy “Just Before I Go” — this very broad affair likely has a built-in audience of rubberneckers, given the level of public fascination that this case has maintained in the U.S. for over 20 years. But it’s doubtful that many would venture out to a theater to see a rehash of a story they they previously binged on from the comfort of their couch. This iteration of “Evil Genius,” like its nonfiction predecessor, would make most sense as streaming fodder, with potential Emmy catnip in Arquette’s offputting but undeniably attention-grabbing characterization. As a gala Toronto premiere, however, the film felt a little small for the room.
Popular on Variety
The core details of the case are presented much as they were in the doc series and copious headlines before it. On August 28, 2003, middle-aged pizza deliverer Brian Wells (played by actor-filmmaker Tom McCarthy as a hopeless patsy) robbed a branch of PNC Bank outside Erie, Pennsylvania, claiming to be a hostage, with an explosive device collared to his neck that he said would be detonated if his demands were not met. Demanding $250,000 but making off with a four-figure sum, he was apprehended shortly afterwards by police, whereupon the bomb did indeed go off, killing him, and cuing a tortuous, years-long FBI investigation.
Structurally, at least, this calamity serves as the climax of the frenetically pinballing script by Courtenay Miles (a writer on Netflix’s hit crime drama “Mindhunter”), but it’s also nearly incidental to all the other narrative chaos at play, beginning with an entirely different murder at the outset of proceedings — as Rothstein calls the police to report the dead body of Diehl-Armstrong’s boyfriend in her freezer. Where the series worked backwards from the bomb to uncover the botched grand plan behind it, the film loopily joins the dots from an apparent crime of passion to a far more famous crime of greed.
There’s an awful lot of incident here to cram into 97 minutes — the series had more than twice as much time to unfold this saga, and the difference is felt — but Cox’s film distinguishes itself with a greater focus on the toxic, on-off amour fou between Diehl-Armstrong, presented here as an embittered harridan convinced the world owes her a break, and Rothstein, the hapless milquetoast in her thrall. Flashbacks to the characters’ youth (with Arquette’s own daughter Harlow Jane playing her younger self) identify Diehl-Rothstein as an intelligent, ingenuous young woman who just needs a little help to make something of herself. But neither the script nor Arquette’s showy but curdled, stridently one-note performance of terminal misanthropy persuasively draw a line between past and present, and it’s increasingly hard to feel for a character missing this much connective tissue.
Not that feeling is really the point of “Evil Genius,” which mostly dwells on the shouty, combative dysfunction of the relationship between the two principals, and punches down on their plain incapability as criminals: The title is strictly, snidely ironic, as “Evil Genius” flags and foreshadows their every miscalculation with a knowing, get-a-load-of-this smirk. Their accomplices — played by Garret Dillahunt and Danielle Macdonald, among others — are mostly figures of fun, granted limited personality and motivation, as the film increasingly stages their doomed venture as ragged farce.
Tonally, it all feels a bit over-egged: The absurdities of the case would, if anything, register even more startlingly in a more humane, character-oriented study of how it played out. But “Evil Genius” insists on casting a pretty ugly story in the ugliest possible light — quite literally so in the case of Eigil Bryld’s intentionally harsh, roughly framed lensing. The film’s pitiless gray images compete with the abrasive sound design (frequently submerging the dialogue in loud, blunt needle drops that run the rock gamut from Blue Oyster Cult to Radiohead) for maximum unloveliness in a story that, yes, offers precious little scope for grace or beauty. But a little empathy wouldn’t go amiss.

Title: 'Elf' movie immersive experience coming to Rockefeller Center – NBC10 Philadelphia
Article_Text:
Fans of the movie “Elf” should soon make plans to pass through the seven levels of the Candy Cane forest, past the sea of swirly, twirly gum drops, then walk through the Lincoln Tunnel and head to Rockefeller Center.
That’s where the world of Buddy the Elf will come to life this holiday season in an immersive experience for, as he says, humans who share an affinity for elf culture.
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
“The Elf Experience” opens Nov. 14 at HERO in Rockefeller Center, taking fans on a journey from New York City to the North Pole.
Guests can step into Papa Elf’s storybook to discover how elves live, work and play. They'll also be able to travel through sites from the movie like the Candy Cane Forest, Santa’s workshop and Gimbels department store. Perhaps they'll even find the world's best cup of coffee.
“We’ve assembled a group of artists that worked on the original film, as well as new ones who were inspired by it,” read a statement from actor Jon Favreau, the film’s director and the founder of Fairview Portals, which collaborated with Warner Bros. Global Experiences to create the experience. “Miniature work, forced perspective, zoetrope, and animatronics were all implemented to create a unique and handcrafted experience to capture the spirit of the film.”
The experience will be located at HERO, a venue at Rockefeller Center dedicated to immersive storytelling. It will also feature interactive activities, photo ops and holiday treats -- including those from the four main food groups: candy, candy canes, candy corns, and syrup.
“Watching 'Elf'" has become a holiday tradition for millions of fans, and Rockefeller Center is synonymous with the holidays in New York City,” said Simon Robinson, the president of global experiences and worldwide studio operations at Warner Bros. Discovery. “Bringing the two together gives fans from New York and around the world an entirely new way to immerse themselves in the 'Elf' story.”
In the 2003 film, Will Ferrell portrays a human who was raised by elves in the North Pole. He travels to Manhattan to find his birth father – who happens to be on the naughty list.
New York City has hosted recent events centered around the film. Last year, Warner Bros. held a “December the TwELFth” celebration in Times Square with pop-up photo stations and a performance from the cast of “Elf the Musical.”
In December 2023, the screen-used sleigh from the movie, complete with the Clausometer and Kringle 3000, traveled from its home at the Halesite Fire Department in Huntington, Long Island to 5th Ave., where fans were able to hop aboard and take photos -- or as some were saying: "Elfies."
The movie will now be celebrated at the site of New York’s top Christmas destination, and it's sure to make “Elf” and “Christmas” lovers smile….because smiling is their favorite.
Tickets are available at ElfTheExperience.com, with availability through Jan. 18. Prices range from $35 to $49, with children under 2 years old welcome to enter for free.
And for those who might be traveling to New York City for the first time, here’s a reminder of the advice Santa gave Buddy before his trip:“First off, if you see gum on the street, leave it there. It isn't free candy. Second, there are, like, thirty Ray's Pizzas. They all claim to be the original. But the real one's on 11th. And if you see a sign that says "Peep Show," that doesn't mean that they're letting you look at presents before Christmas.”

Title: Nara Smith reveals the 1 thing she can't make from scratch – NBC10 Philadelphia
Article_Text:
Bubble gum. Hot dogs. Candy canes. SpaghettiOs. Cornflakes. Flaming Hot Cheetos. Froot Loops. Jolly Ranchers. Takis.
TikTok star and mom of four Nara Smith has made all of the above from scratch. (And while dressed to the nines!)
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
There is one thing, however, that even Smith cannot make from scratch: baby formula.
“There’s so much that goes into it to where it’s just not safe to make it from scratch,” she tells TODAY.com. “It goes through a really long testing process with multiple trials, and you just have to make sure it’s safe because you’re feeding a tiny human being.”
Regardless of whether she welcomes the title or not, Smith has become associated with the tradwife movement that embraces a 1950s housewife aesthetic. Many of the women who adhere to this conservative lifestyle see breastfeeding as the most “natural” way to nourish your children.
Smith doesn’t agree.
Entertainment News
“I want women to feel empowered to make decisions that are best for their mental health and their physical health, but also for their family and their well-being overall,” Smith says.
Though she breastfed her four children, the experience was different for each.
For Rumble Honey, now 5, it took “a lot of learning” to figure out breastfeeding: “I remember when my milk came in, I was like, ‘What is happening? I feel like my boobs are on fire.’ It was really intense.”
She breastfed Rumble for 6 months, which was a shorter time than she planned, because she got pregnant and her milk “naturally dried up.”
She nursed her son, Slim Easy, now 4, for 9 months until she got pregnant with her third child.
With daughter Whimsy Lou, now 2, Smith really hoped to avoid formula altogether and breastfeed her for a full year.
“But then I was like, ‘You know what? I’m working so much. This doesn’t feel sustainable for my mental health, and also physically, I need to lug a pump and store my milk, and then ship it back to the states if I’m in Europe,’” she remembers thinking. “It just turned into this cycle that added a lot of stress to me, so I just decided to be done at 10 months.”
After baby Fawnie Golden, almost 1, was born last September, Smith was breastfeeding and pumping through a busy travel season.
And then Whimsy was diagnosed with cancer in late 2025.
Whimsy is now in remission, but in the months during her treatment, Smith and her husband Lucky Blue Smith took turns at the hospital, so she didn’t have much time to nurse Fawnie.
“That one was a tough one because I felt like it was a real mental struggle of figuring out: Am I ready to let go of this — because she’s also my last — or do I feel pressure?” Smith recalls. “So it was more complex than just saying, ‘I’m stopping.’”
Ultimately, Smith did switch completely to formula. “I was really glad because it just removed extra stress from my plate,” she adds.
Of course, choosing which formula to use was overwhelming.
“It was really tricky for me to find the perfect formula, and I went down rabbit hole after rabbit hole. It felt so daunting and overwhelming,” she says.
Seeking the “cleanest, most high-quality” product, Smith used European formulas for her first two children, but the shipping process was tedious. So she switched to Bobbie, a European-style infant formula manufactured right in the U.S.
In a satirical marketing campaign for the company, Smith departs from her usual perfect veneer: she’s panicked, wearing sweatpants ... and even (gasp!) cursing.
“I’m naturally just a very scheduled and meticulous person to where you probably will not find my house in a mess just because I don’t like that,” Smith laughs. “But with this campaign I just wanted to say that feeding isn’t perfect. No story is linear.”
Smith finds it “weird” that feeding your infant can be “connected to shame.” But then, “the more kids I had, and the more moms I talked to, the more I realized that there’s not a certain way to do it. It looks so different for every woman in her life.”
The postpartum period can be tricky for a lot of people, even for someone whose life looks “perfect” online, and Smith says that she faced some postpartum anxiety and depression along the way. She’d put on a brave face for the midwife, but then turn to her husband later and say, “I’m not OK.”
Smith admits, “I loved breastfeeding, and it was such a comforting and grounding experience for me, but then equally, I still got that same connection when I transitioned to formula.”

Title: The 7 missing women linked to Philadelphia's mystery house – NBC10 Philadelphia
Article_Text:
Editor's note: This article contains content that may be disturbing for some readers.
Seven missing women are connected to a mystery house in Philadelphia's Olney neighborhood, police and the FBI said Wednesday, and investigators now believe five of those women are deceased.
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
The conclusion comes after authorities recovered more than one million digital images and videos connected to Raymond "R.C." Horsch, who died in 2025 at age 82. Horsch was never charged in connection with any of the women's disappearances.
Despite months of searching the property, police said they have not recovered human remains or other physical evidence proving a homicide occurred inside the home.
Officials said they have reviewed about 30% of the digital evidence and still have hundreds of thousands of files left to examine.
On Wednesday, police said they had identified 58 people in photos and videos recovered from the Chew Avenue property. Investigators say the files depict women in a variety of situations and are continuing to be analyzed.
The Philadelphia Medical Examiner's Office said it reviewed images involving three additional women and advised investigators that, if the images are authentic and unaltered, the women depicted appear to be deceased.
Deputy Commissioner Frank Vanore said metadata connected to files involving three of the women indicates the videos were created in 2017.
Still, investigators have cautioned that digital evidence alone is not enough to prove a homicide and that additional corroborating evidence remains necessary.
What we know about the 7 women
Police say seven missing women have been connected to the house over a span of more than a decade.
Gabrielle Amarando was in her early 20s when she disappeared in 2012. In a Facebook post, her mother said Amarando suffered from "a drug addiction that she couldn't escape." Citing digital evidence, police believe Amarando is deceased.
Amy McHale was in her mid 40s when she disappeared in 2016. She was married to R.C. Horsch before divorcing him. Her daughter told NBC10 that McHale was actively using heroin and receiving methadone treatment at the time she vanished. According to her daughter, McHale was last seen at the West Chew Avenue home.
Maribel Fresses was in her early 20s when she was reported missing in 2018.
"My first reaction was pure shock," her brother, Dawson Fresses, told NBC10. "It's been eight years since I've seen her. Hearing that, I just couldn't believe it. I had gotten to the point where I thought I might never find out what happened to her."
Citing digital evidence, police believe Fresses is deceased.
Nicole Fusaro disappeared in 2018 at age 27. A family member told the NBC10 Investigators that police believe they have video showing R.C. Horsch strangling her. Fusaro was last seen near Kensington and Allegheny avenues, about four miles from the Chew Avenue home.
While police have not named her publicly, she is one of the women they suspect is deceased.
Blair Tonzelli was 35 when she disappeared in 2023. Police said a woman who was with Eugene Horsch at the time of his June arrest was carrying Tonzelli's identification card.
Police also say a sixth woman, who appeared to be about 25 years old in the recordings, is believed to be deceased. Authorities declined to release her identity at her family's request.
A seventh woman, identified only as Jane Doe, also appears deceased in the evidence, police said. Her identity remains unknown though investigators estimate she was in her 20s.
The investigation at the Chew Avenue home
The investigation has increasingly centered on Raymond "R.C." Horsch, a photographer and filmmaker who produced violent fetish films and wrote erotic books with sadomasochistic themes.
Police say they recovered a massive collection of digital files connected to R.C. Horsch and are examining whether the material could help explain what happened to the missing women.
Authorities have stressed that R.C. Horsch was never charged in connection with any of the disappearances before his death in 2025.
The investigation began in June when federal authorities arrested R.C. Horsch's son, Eugene Horsch.
Officials said investigators found Eugene Horsch carrying fake federal credentials and other items, leading authorities to search the Chew Avenue home he inherited after his father's death.
What began as a federal investigation quickly expanded after law enforcement uncovered an enormous archive of photos, videos and electronic devices inside the property.
Investigators are still awaiting the results of testing on chemicals recovered from the basement of the home.
Sources familiar with the investigation told the NBC10 Investigators that authorities are trying to determine whether any of the chemicals could have been used to destroy evidence or dissolve human remains.
Police have not publicly discussed the results of that testing.
Perhaps the biggest unanswered question remains whether physical evidence exists to corroborate what investigators believe they are seeing in the digital files. Investigators also found evidence suggesting an attempt to grow or produce narcotics.
Among the items seized during raids this summer was a piece of writing about serial killer Ted Bundy that referenced zip ties and a drum, a source familiar with the investigation told NBC10. The note also mentioned killings and "trash that needs to go."
It remains unclear who wrote it, though Eugene Horsch's attorney suggested in an earlier conversation that Ray Horsch was the author.
To date, authorities say no human remains have been recovered from the property.
On July 9, 2026, the NBC10 Investigators learned that a federal grand jury indicted Eugene Horsch on charges related to false FBI credentials.
At a preliminary hearing on Aug. 6, 2026, Pennsylvania prosecutors withdrew all five state charges against Eugene Horsch, 44, stemming from the investigation that led authorities to search the Olney home.
Eugene Horsch still faces federal charges of possession of a firearm by a felon and possession of an unlawfully produced document and authentication feature.
After those charges were filed, Eugene Horsch was transferred to federal custody. A jury trial is scheduled for January.
Anyone with information is asked to call Philadelphia police at 215-686-TIPS (8477). To speak directly with a homicide investigator, call 215-686-3334.
Nicole Fusaro's cousin releases statement
Following Wednesday's press conference, Jonathan Halloran-Koren, who said he is the cousin of one of the missing women, Nicole Fusaro, released the following statement criticizing the Philadelphia Police Department:
This morning, my family met with detectives from the Philadelphia Police Department regarding the death of my cousin, Nicole Fusaro. After that meeting, and after watching the department’s press conference later today, I am appalled by the way our family has been treated and by the complete lack of basic dignity and consideration shown to us as the family of a homicide victim.
During the meeting, I asked to speak privately with the detectives because I wanted to share information I had developed while investigating Nicole’s disappearance. I was told, “We are only here to give a next of kin notification.” I was also told, “We are aware you are trying to advocate for other victims.”
I have spent years advocating for victims and people who feel their voices are not being heard. I never imagined I would find myself having to do the same thing for someone in my own family. I find it deeply disturbing that, during a meeting about the killing of my cousin, my advocacy for other potential victims was brought up at all—particularly while the detectives were simultaneously unwilling to hear information I believed could be relevant to Nicole’s case. Whatever the reason for that comment, advocacy on behalf of victims should never be treated as a problem.
Then, just hours later, I watched a televised press conference and learned details about how Nicole was killed, including details of her strangulation, that had not been shared with our family that morning.
There is simply no excuse for a family having to learn details about the killing of someone they love from television after meeting face-to-face with the detectives investigating her death.
What happened today has made clear that our concerns can no longer be addressed by simply asking the Philadelphia Police Department for answers. I am assembling a team to conduct an independent and comprehensive investigation into the handling of Nicole’s case, beginning with her original missing-person investigation and continuing through the events of today. That review will examine the actions and failures of the department, whether Nicole and our family were afforded the protections required by law, and whether any of those failures constitute violations of federal civil-rights laws or other legal obligations.
This will not end with an internal complaint to the Philadelphia Police Department. The evidence and our findings will be formally submitted to the U.S. Department of Justice Civil Rights Division with a request for independent review and consideration of any appropriate civil or criminal investigation or enforcement action. Where supported by the evidence and the law, we will also pursue private civil litigation.
We intend to use every lawful avenue available to determine what happened, who was responsible for the decisions that were made, and whether those decisions violated the law.
Nicole deserved to have people fighting for her when she was missing. She deserves people fighting for her now. I intend to make sure that happens.
NBC10 later obtained the following statement from Philadelphia Police in response to Halloran-Koren:
Our deepest sympathy remains with every family whose loved one may be connected to this extraordinarily complex and deeply troubling investigation. Working alongside the FBI and our other partners, investigators continue to review and authenticate more than one million digital files, pursue every lead, work to locate the missing women, and provide verified information to their families as responsibly and compassionately as possible.
Prior to PPD's 9/16/26 Press Conference, PPD Homicide detectives traveled to northern New Jersey to speak with additional family members regarding information relevant to the investigation. Out of respect for those involved, we will not publicly discuss the details of that private conversation.
During the 9/16/26 briefing, the Department provided an update on the broader investigation but did not publicly identify either of the two additional women. This was consistent with requests made by their families during the official next-of-kin notification process.
Anyone with information relevant to this investigation is encouraged to contact the Homicide Unit at 215-686-3334.
The NBC10 Investigators can also be reached at david.charns@nbcuni.com and ali.ingersoll@nbcuni.com.

Title: Dad of slain PSU student faces parents of teen murder suspect – NBC10 Philadelphia
Article_Text:
The father of a Penn State student who was shot and killed in South Philadelphia in June faced the parents of one of the murder suspects accused of helping the teen escape.
“Everything is moving forward right now,” an emotional William Schmidt said as he left the courtroom on Thursday, Sept. 17. “It’s just the first start though.”
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
On June 6 around 1:30 a.m., Schmidt’s son, 22-year-old William “Billy” Schmidt, was steps from his front door near 20th and Durfor streets in South Philadelphia when two teenagers confronted him and stole his cellphone, according to investigators.
Video from a neighbor’s porch camera shows the teens – later identified as 16-year-old Azzubair Outen-Fleming and 16-year-old Kaiseem Smith – speaking with Schmidt, who is off camera, police said. Seconds later, Schmidt appears to follow them into the street.
The video captures Schmidt saying, “Give me back my phone,” before a gunshot is heard moments later.
Schmidt was rushed to Penn Presbyterian Medical Center where he was later pronounced dead.
A few days later on June 10, Philadelphia police released surveillance video of the shooting, prompting Outen-Fleming’s mother, 45-year-old Milika Abdulmalik, and his stepfather, 35-year-old Donte Abdulmalik, to make escape plans for the teen, according to prosecutors.
Local
Breaking news and the stories that matter to your neighborhood.
Milika Abdulmalik allegedly made two phone calls and sent a text to a number in Colorado Springs, Colorado. Within the next two hours, the mother, stepfather, and teen drove to family members in Colorado Springs, according to investigators.
Milika and Donte Abdulmalik were later arrested in Philadelphia on June 30 while Outen-Fleming was arrested by U.S. Marshals in Colorado a day later on July 1, investigators said.
Kaiseem Smith then surrendered to Philadelphia police on July 2, according to officials.
Outen-Fleming's 19-year-old brother was also arrested and charged with dropping the teens off in a stolen car prior to the deadly shooting.
On Sept. 17, Outen-Fleming, his brother and Smith all waived their right to preliminary hearings. Malika and Donte Abdulmalik appeared in court however and heard the evidence against them.
“They can’t put him in the car,” Donte Abdulmalik’s defense attorney said. “They don’t know who the car is registered to.”
Milika Abdulmalik's attorney made a similar statement.
“What we have is two phones went to Colorado and came back,” the attorney said. “People travel with other people’s phones."
William Schmidt, meanwhile, said it was tough to see Malika and Donte Abdulmalik in the courtroom, but he still felt good that his own family was there to support him.
All five suspects are due back in court on Oct. 8, 2026. Smith and Outen-Fleming are both charged with murder, robbery and other related offenses while Milika and Donte Abdulmalik are charged with hindering apprehension, obstruction of justice and tampering with evidence.

Title: Lawmaker fights to keep Academy of Natural Sciences Museum open – NBC10 Philadelphia
Article_Text:
We are just days away from the Academy of Natural Sciences Museum closing for good.
Sept. 27, 2026, is the last day for the museum with Drexel University pointing to declining attendance and rising operating costs which they said made operating the museum essentially unsustainable.
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
In response, there have been been rallies outside of the building on the Ben Franklin Parkway with families and supporters calling on the city and Drexel to find a way to keep it open.
City Councilmember At-Large Dr. Nina Ahmad was among those at a rally on Sept. 17 and introduced a resolution to hold hearings on the closure.
Dr. Ahmad partnered wtih also shared four possible routes that the city could take to stop the museum from closing.
In a statement on Thursday, her office wrote:
- "Orphans' Court Petition: Deputy Mayor Wellenbach and the Academy of Natural Sciences Board can petition the Philadelphia Orphans' Court under Pennsylvania Act 141 guidelines to release or modify a restriction under the following conditions: 1) a fund is older than 20 years, 2) total assets are small, 3) or the restriction has become "unlawful, impracticable, impossible to achieve, or wasteful."
- Emergency Capital Grants (The Municipal Route): Because the city cannot spend Drexel’s endowment, a more viable financial bridge is mobilizing capital through the Philadelphia Authority for Industrial Development (PAID) or requesting emergency state RACP (Redevelopment Assistance Capital Program) funds to cover the capital improvements directly. This strategy frees operational dollars, without triggering a lengthy and legally risky battle over donor intent.
- Explore using the approximately $3.5 million annual payout from the endowment to support a $41 million bond issue.
- Historic Tax Credits Program: with proper structures, Philadelphia could raise 20% of the capital costs from investor equity raised through the Historic Tax Credits program. To achieve this, the Academy would need to be placed on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places."
The Parker Administration told NBC10 that they have loans the deputy mayor to Drexel Universtiy and the Academy as a senior advisory to help them navigate these changes. The administration did not mention finding a potential path forward to stay open though.
Local
Breaking news and the stories that matter to your neighborhood.
History of the Academy of Natural Sciences Museum
The Academy was founded in 1812 by seven naturalists whose mission at the time was to advance scientific discovery. The museum then opened in 1828 as a way to share the Academy’s natural history collections with the public.
In 2011, the Academy became affiliated with Drexel University and changed its name from the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia to the Academy of Natural Sciences of Drexel University.
In October of last year, the museum reduced its operating hours from five days a week to Friday through Sunday. At that time, the Academy said the decision was due to visitation rates not rebounding to pre-pandemic levels, federal funding cuts and an “uncertain philanthropic landscape.”
In addition to the museum's closure, the Academy also announced that Scott Cooper, PhD, had stepped down as their president and CEO.

Title: Trump admin. again denies visas for Palestinian delegation – NBC10 Philadelphia
Article_Text:
The Trump administration has denied visas for a high-level Palestinian delegation to attend an annual meeting of world leaders at the United Nations for the second year in a row.
The State Department said Wednesday that Palestinian officials, including Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas, had failed to live up to their commitments under previous agreements to seek peace with Israel.
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
In a statement, the department said the Palestinian Authority had continued to pursue legal action against Israel at the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court and kept paying stipends to the families of prisoners convicted of attacks against Israelis. It also mentioned officials tied to the Palestine Liberation Organization, or PLO.
“As a consequence of their failure to reform, contrary to their commitments to the United States, and their ongoing activities that undermine the prospects for peace, the United States will extend sanctions that deny visas to PLO members and PA officials” in accordance with standing U.S. law, the department said.
The move is the latest by the Trump administration to restrict visas and it further signals the close U.S. alliance with Israel, which has faced international isolation over its war in Gaza following the deadly Oct. 7, 2023, attacks by Hamas. A fragile, U.S.-brokered ceasefire took hold in October, but Israel has continued to carry out strikes in the Palestinian territory.
It also comes as the Trump administration has launched a campaign to dismantle the ICC, accusing it of trying to unfairly prosecute U.S. and Israeli soldiers for alleged crimes in Afghanistan, Iraq and Gaza. Israel and the United States are not members of the global tribunal.
Despite the visa denials, the Palestinians will still be represented at next week's high-level meeting of the U.N. General Assembly by their diplomats who are already accredited to the United Nations. Last year, Abbas appeared by video.

Title: How Ed Sheeran's tour became a flashpoint over Gaza and free speech
Article_Text:
Updated September 18, 2026 at 3:37 PM EDT
When Ed Sheeran walks onto a Philadelphia stage Saturday, the people missing may be as noticeable as the person under the lights. There will be no opening act and no Beoga, the Irish band that once joined him midway through the show.
The tour began coming apart after Macklemore spoke about the war in Gaza.
During Sheeran's Sept. 5 concert at MetLife Stadium, Macklemore said "free Palestine" and performed "Hind's Hall," named for Hind Rajab, a 5-year-old Palestinian girl killed by Israeli troops in Gaza City in January 2024. Images of Gaza's destruction filled the screens behind him.
The performance drew quick criticism, including from the Anti-Defamation League. The Israeli-American Council circulated a petition urging Sheeran to drop Macklemore.
Macklemore said Sheeran later told him several stadiums would not host the tour if he remained. The rapper accused Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft of leading the effort. Kraft acknowledged barring Macklemore, citing what he called a history of antisemitic rhetoric and saying he would not "provide a platform for hate speech." Sheeran said the promoter and venues made the decision.
Music journalist and critic Zach Schonfeld told Morning Edition that the episode showed the power venue owners can have over who performs and what artists can say.
"I think it does show that a billionaire venue owner like Robert Kraft holds a lot of power to dictate who is allowed to perform in his venue and what these artists are allowed to say," Schonfeld said.
By Tuesday, other artists had begun leaving the tour in solidarity with Macklemore. Finneas, Aaron Rowe, Lukas Graham and Beoga all withdrew from upcoming dates. The next day, Macklemore said he would donate his $1 million in net earnings from the tour to six organizations supporting Palestinians and invited Kraft to do the same.
The fight over a stadium stage offers a window into changing American views of Israel. A July Economist/YouGov poll found 43% of U.S. adult citizens said Israel was committing genocide against Palestinian civilians, including 68% of Democrats and 17% of Republicans. Among adults under 30, the share rose to 55%.
Sheeran said he has personal views about the war but does not want his concerts to become political forums. That answer drew fresh criticism online, including comparisons with his 2022 performance at a benefit for Ukraine and a video in which he told Ukrainians, "I stand with you." He has also campaigned against racism in the U.K. and criticized the British government over cuts to arts funding.
Asked about precedents, Schonfeld pointed to Kneecap, the Irish rap trio that faced canceled shows after speaking about Gaza. The controversy also comes amid other cultural fights over speech about Israel and Gaza, including backlash against The Zone of Interest director Jonathan Glazer after his Oscar speech addressed Israel's occupation and the war, and protests surrounding No Other Land, the Oscar-winning documentary about displacement in the West Bank that initially lacked a mainstream U.S. distributor.
The pressure extends beyond public and online spaces in America. In Israel, the directors of the new documentary "NAZA," an investigation by two Israeli journalists into how Israeli intelligence selected targets in Gaza and calculated expected civilian deaths from strikes, faced calls from the culture minister to lose their citizenship.
Still, Schonfeld said Sheeran's enormous mainstream reach makes this the most high-profile example yet. He has tried to stay out of politics. In Philadelphia, the empty spaces onstage may make that position impossible to miss.
