Title: Long-term care facility at former Bradford hospital to close by December 1
Article_Text:
UPDATE, Sept. 17, 2026 @ 7:55 p.m.: This story was updated to include a comment from a LECOM spokesperson.
The Pavilion, a long-term care facility at the former hospital in Bradford will close on or before December 1, according to Kaleida Health officials.
The Pavilion was originally scheduled to close around May. Earlier this year, Kaleida officials submitted a closure notice for the nursing facility and the hospital to the Pennsylvania Department of Health, pointing to escalating financial pressures.
The Lake Erie College of Osteopathic Medicine, or LECOM, had been in talks to acquire parts of the hospital and the nursing facility. But, in a Sept. 8 meeting, LECOM's Board of Directors voted not to acquire any of the medical campus, according to a Kaleida Health press release. Kaleida officials did not say why LECOM is pulling out of discussions.
“We understand how deeply personal this is for our residents, their families and our employees,” said Don Boyd, the CEO of Kaleida Health. “For many residents, The Pavilion is their home. For our employees, it is a place where they have cared for people they know and love. We recognize that a transition like this brings uncertainty, concern and emotion, and we will do everything we can to support those who are affected.”
Kaleida officials say there are currently 45 residents living in The Pavilion, and that they'll work with families to find alternative care.
A Kaleida spokesperson also said they'll continue to provide ambulatory services.
A spokesperson for LECOM said in an emailed statement to WPSU that they invested "significant" time, resources and diligence when considering the transaction with Kaleida.
"Through that process, we identified substantive regulatory considerations and unresolved matters related to Kaleida Health's operational positions that could not be reconciled within the framework required for LECOM Health to move forward responsibly," said James Lin, the president of the LECOM Institute for Successful Living.
Rep. Martin Causer, whose district includes Bradford, said in a statement on social media that Kaleida Health did not negotiate in good faith.
"At a recent meeting with the Pennsylvania Office of Attorney General, Kaleida Health notified LECOM they now refuse to the sell the building to them," Causer said. "They alternatively stated that they might lease the building, but LECOM would have to accept a noncompete agreement in perpetuity. This would effectively ensure that BRMC would never again operate as a hospital."
Causer said community leaders are continuing to explore alternatives for care, such as an outpatient emergency department or the construction of a micro-hospital.

Title: Owner-Operators and Liability: When You Are the One Who Gets Hurt on the Road
Article_Text:
Owner-operators spend their careers being treated as the “deep pocket” in a crash. When a four-wheeler, a shipper’s dock, or a failed part puts them in the hospital, the rules for getting made whole are different, and the clock starts fast.
A car merges onto I-81 near Harrisburg without looking, clips the steer axle of a loaded tractor-trailer, and the rig goes into the median. The car’s driver walks away. The owner-operator has a torn rotator cuff and a truck that is out of service for six weeks–and no paycheck until both are fixed.
That scenario plays out more often than the public assumes. Federal crash studies have repeatedly found that in fatal truck-and-car collisions, the passenger vehicle driver is more often the one who initiated the crash. The trucker is frequently the injured party, not the defendant, and most owner-operators have never thought through what that means.
Who is actually on the hook?
When a passenger vehicle causes the crash, the claim is against that driver’s auto liability policy. The problem is the limits, according to many industry experts. Many states allow minimums of $15,000 to $25,000 per person–nowhere near enough to cover surgery, rehab, and months of lost revenue for a driver whose truck is the business. Underinsured motorist coverage on the owner-operator’s own policy fills that gap, and it is the coverage most drivers skip or carry at the lowest limit their lease allows.
Loading and unloading injuries are a separate category.
A driver hurt at a shipper’s dock by a forklift, an unsecured pallet, or a neglected floor may have a premises liability claim against the facility. Federal rules at 49 CFR 390.6 bar shippers from coercing drivers into unsafe operations, but the injury claim itself runs under state negligence law, and it turns on who controlled the dock and what they knew about the hazard.
Equipment failures are another issue.
A steer tire that delaminates well inside its service life, a brake component that fails after a recent replacement, or a coupling defect can support a product liability claim against the manufacturer or the shop that did the work.
“Drivers are conditioned to think every crash is their fault until proven otherwise, because that is how the industry treats them,” said Joseph Leeson, managing attorney at Leeson & Leeson, a personal injury firm based in Pennsylvania that handles truck accident cases.
“I have owner-operators come in after a crash where the police report clearly puts fault on the other car, and the first thing they ask is whether they are going to lose their authority. What they should be asking is who is going to pay for their shoulder and their downtime.”
What occupational accident coverage does and does not do
Most owner-operators leased to a carrier carry occupational accident insurance instead of workers’ compensation.
It is cheaper for a reason. Occ-acc policies pay defined benefits: a weekly disability amount with a cap, a medical benefit with a ceiling, and a lump sum for death or dismemberment. They are not designed to make an injured driver whole, and they say nothing about pain and suffering, the value of the truck sitting idle, or the contracts lost while the driver recovers.
Occ-acc also pays regardless of fault, which is useful, but the policy will often have a lien on any third-party recovery. A driver who settles with the at-fault motorist may owe part of that settlement back to the occ-acc carrier. That is manageable if planned for and a serious problem if discovered at the end.
Your own data is your best witness.
After a crash, the electronic logging device (ELD) and the dashcam that drivers often resent are the most credible evidence in the case. ELD data required under FMCSA’s hours-of-service rule establishes that the driver was legal and rested. Engine control module data shows speed and braking. A forward-facing camera settles the merge argument in about four seconds.
“The other side’s insurer is going to come after your logs anyway. When the logs are clean and the camera shows the car cutting you off, the case is over before it starts,” Leeson said. “Where I see drivers hurt themselves is by not preserving the footage, or by giving a recorded statement to the other insurer the day after the crash while they are still on pain medication.”
The final piece is timing.
Every state sets a deadline for filing an injury claim. In Pennsylvania, where I-78, I-80, I-81, and the Turnpike carry some of the heaviest through-truck volumes in the Northeast, it is two years from the date of injury; other states range from one to six. A driver who spends the first year dealing with the truck and the second arguing with insurers can lose the claim entirely.
Leeson says the drivers who come out of these situations in the best shape share one habit.
“They treat the injury like a breakdown. They document it, they get it looked at right away, and they do not let anybody talk them into driving on it.”

With a focus on drivers, the Trucker News Staff aims to provide relevant, objective content pertaining to the trucking segment of the transportation industry. The Trucker News Staff is based in Little Rock, Arkansas.

Title: Does your local government livestream and record its meetings?
Article_Text:
Does your local government livestream and record its meetings?
LIVE OR NOT. Governments are not required to post their meetings, although a good number do.
In the age of the internet and social media, many people look online for news and information.
Long gone are the days of public notices tacked to the town hall’s door. In this new age, some local governments have opted to livestream, record or post their meetings — the regular gatherings of public officials where most local policy decisions are made — online for the public to attend or view virtually.
Not all governments do, however.
A 2023 survey of municipalities by the New York Coalition for Open Government found that only 23 percent of local governments post instructions on their websites explaining how to access livestreams and video recordings of meetings.
Governments don’t have to. New York, Pennsylvania and New Jersey have no universal standard. Each county, city, town, village, borough, or school board can choose whether to livestream or record its meetings, and whether — and where — to post those recordings online.
Municipalities can also choose what equipment to use, which meetings to stream and whether to make staples of in-person government discourse, such as public comment, accessible online.
In New York state, the Open Meetings Law gives the public the right to attend any meeting held by a local governing body. It also gives the public the right to record and livestream meetings. It does not require local governments to livestream or record meetings themselves.
In Pennsylvania, the Sunshine Act guarantees the public’s right to attend and record government meetings. It does not require local governments to record their own meetings.
New Jersey residents fall under the Open Public Meetings Act, which guarantees the right to attend meetings of public bodies.
The law does not address recording, but the New Jersey Supreme Court in its Tarus v. Pine Hill decision has held that the public has a right to record meetings and that municipalities may reasonably restrict that recording.
Local governments are not required to post meetings online.
Does your local government livestream and record its meetings?
New York
The towns of Chester, Goshen, Warwick and Monroe all have official public YouTube channels that livestream meetings and upload them afterward.
The city of Port Jervis also has a public YouTube channel but does not livestream meetings; instead, the city uploads recordings to the channel after each meeting, typically within a day.
In Woodbury, the village and town share a YouTube channel and meetings from both governments are uploaded to the site, typically within a day of the meeting.
The villages of Chester and Goshen do not upload or livestream public meetings. Neither does the Village of Harriman, which also lacks an official Facebook page.
Florida livestreams meetings on the village’s official Facebook account.
The villages of Greenwood Lake and Warwick livestream and upload meetings to YouTube.
Some boards of education also record and livestream meetings. In Orange County, the Warwick Valley School District, Chester School District and Port Jervis City School District all livestream and record the video of their meetings. The Greenwood Lake School District records and posts meetings to Youtube, typically within one day of the meeting.
Pennsylvania
In Pennsylvania, the boroughs of Milford and Matamoras do not livestream or record their meetings on YouTube or Facebook.
The Delaware Valley School District, which includes Milford and Matamoras, uploads its board meetings to YouTube.
New Jersey
The Township of Sparta livestreams and records its meetings on YouTube. The town of Newton and the Township of Vernon livestream on Zoom and then upload the meetings to YouTube the following day.
Byram makes audio of its meetings available on the township’s website. Andover and Lafayette do not record general public meetings, though in Lafayette, residents can request footage from the town’s land use board.
In Wantage, the township records its meetings, but the recording is made available only upon a resident’s request.
The boroughs of Branchville, Hamburg, Franklin, Ogdensburg, Sussex and Stanhope do not record or livestream their meetings.
In West Milford, residents can watch local government meetings through a video player on the township’s website featuring footage of past meetings, which also air on WM-77.
The High Point Regional School District, Sparta Township Public School District, and Vernon Township School District all either livestream and upload, or record and upload, their meetings to YouTube.
The Montague Township School District uploads recordings of meetings to its official website.
Alternatively, the Wallkill Valley Regional High School District, Hamburg School, Lenape Valley Regional High School District and Newton Public School District do not.
The Andover Regional School District, Byram Township School District, Franklin Borough School District, Ogdensburg Borough School District and Lafayette Township School District do not record and upload their meetings.

Title: NFL TV coverage maps for Week 2: Announcer teams, broadcast schedule and more
Article_Text:
The NFL season is underway and Week 1 brought with it a ton of storylines and drama for the upcoming season. The return of football also saw the NFL spread out a lot of games over the course of the weekend, with action coming on Wednesday and Thursday in addition to a double doubleheader on Sunday before games to wrap it up on Sunday and Monday night.
Week 2 sees the more standard cadence of Thursday, Sunday and Monday games, which is a rarity given how much the league likes to spread out its inventory. There are a few intriguing games throughout the day on Sunday, including Bears-Vikings and Bengals-Texans, but what contests will be available in your area?
Read on for a look at that information, as well as who is calling each game, with a look at the NFL's Week 2 TV Coverage Maps. As always, the maps are provided by the fine folks over at 506 Sports.
Thursday, Sept. 16
Thursday Night Football (8:20 p.m. ET On Prime Video)
- Detroit Lions (1-0) At Buffalo Bills (1-0): Al Michaels, Kirk Herbstreit
The latest season of Thursday Night Football begins in Buffalo as the Bills open up the new Highmark Stadium in primetime against the Lions. The contest promises the potential for a lot of points to keep Al Michaels entertained throughout the evening.
Sunday, Sept. 20
CBS (Singleheader)
| Game | Announcers | Map Color | 
|---|---|---|
| Pittsburgh Steelers (1-0) At New England Patriots (0-1) | Jim Nantz, J.J. Watt | Red | 
| Cincinnati Bengals (1-0) At Houston Texans (0-1) | Kevin Harlan, Trent Green | Green | 
| New Orleans Saints (0-1) At Baltimore Ravens (1-0) | Spero Dedes, Adam Archuleta | Yellow | 
| Cleveland Browns (0-1) At Tampa Bay Buccaneers (0-1) | Tom McCarthy, Robert Turbin | Light Blue | 
| Jacksonville Jaguars (1-0) At Denver Broncos (0-1) (4:05 p.m. ET) | Ian Eagle, Ross Tucker | Dark Blue | 
| Las Vegas Raiders (1-0) At Los Angeles Chargers (0-1) (4:05 p.m. ET) | Andrew Catalon, Logan Ryan | Orange | 
CBS has a singleheader this week and will send the top team of Jim Nantz and J.J. Watt to Foxboro for the Patriots' home opener against Aaron Rodgers and the Pittsburgh Steelers. There are a pair of 4:05 games as well with Jaguars-Broncos in Denver being the most intriguing among them.
FOX (Early Window)
| Game | Announcers | Map Color | 
|---|---|---|
| Philadelphia Eagles (1-0) At Tennessee Titans (0-1) | Adam Amin, Drew Brees | Red | 
| Minnesota Vikings (1-0) At Chicago Bears (1-0) | Joe Davis, Greg Olsen | Blue | 
| Green Bay Packers (0-1) At New York Jets (1-0) | Kenny Albert, Jonathan Vilma | Green | 
| Carolina Panthers (0-1) At Atlanta Falcons (0-1) | Tim Brando, Matt Millen | Yellow | 
FOX has the Week 2 doubleheader and is giving most of the country the Vikings-Bears NFC North clash early that will assure the winner has at least a share of the division lead entering Week 2. Packers-Jets and Eagles-Titans are the top secondary options while Panthers-Falcons won't be seen outside of select NFC South markets.
FOX (Late Window)
| Game | Announcers | Map Color | 
|---|---|---|
| Washington Commanders (0-1) At Dallas Cowboys (0-1) | Kevin Burkhardt, Tom Brady | Red | 
| Miami Dolphins (0-1) At San Francisco 49ers (1-0) | Kevin Kugler, Daryl Johnston | Blue |

America's Game Of The Week will be in Dallas as the Commanders and Cowboys seek to avoid a disastrous 0-2 start in the NFC East. That contest will go to most of the country and with two additional undercard matchups (Dolphins-49ers and Seahawks-Cardinals) RedZone fans will have five games to enjoy in the late window.
Sunday Night Football (8:20 p.m. ET On NBC)
- Indianapolis Colts (0-1) At Kansas City Chiefs (1-0): Mike Tirico, Cris Collinsworth
The Sunday night game in Week 2 marks a second straight primetime appearance for Kansas City, which is aiming to improve to 2-0 at the expense of Daniel Jones and the Colts. Given the rough road ahead this spot could be as close to a must-win for Indianapolis as any team faces in the league in Week 2.
Monday, Sept. 21
Monday Night Football (8:15 p.m. ET On ESPN/ABC)
- New York Giants (1-0) At Los Angeles Rams (0-1): Joe Buck, Troy Aikman
Week 2 concludes in Los Angeles as the Rams look to put their disastrous Melbourne trip behind them against the Giants, who started the John Harbaugh era with a bang against the Cowboys. There will also be a Manningcast on ESPN2 as Peyton and Eli break down all the action.

Title: China, Not Iran, Is Trump's Real Foreign-Policy Debacle
Article_Text:
China, Not Iran, Is Trump’s Real Foreign-Policy Debacle
In 19 months, Washington has lost ground to Beijing on every conceivable front.
When future historians look back at U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term, the Iran debacle will probably feature as a decisive turning point in his presidency. The conflict exposed the limits of American power. It isolated the United States internationally, added inflationary pressures to the world economy, and drove the president’s domestic approval ratings to unprecedented lows just ahead of midterm elections.
But historians may ultimately deem a different development to be far more consequential: the failure of Trump’s China policy. Over the administration’s first year and a half, the United States let its most formidable geopolitical rival gain ground on nearly every front, from the economy and military balance to science, technology, and geopolitical influence.
When future historians look back at U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term, the Iran debacle will probably feature as a decisive turning point in his presidency. The conflict exposed the limits of American power. It isolated the United States internationally, added inflationary pressures to the world economy, and drove the president’s domestic approval ratings to unprecedented lows just ahead of midterm elections.
But historians may ultimately deem a different development to be far more consequential: the failure of Trump’s China policy. Over the administration’s first year and a half, the United States let its most formidable geopolitical rival gain ground on nearly every front, from the economy and military balance to science, technology, and geopolitical influence.
China, contrary to much commentary, has little interest in constructing a “Chinese world order” modeled on the postwar Pax Americana. But it is determined to constrain American power, push the United States out of its dominant position in Asia, blunt its financial leverage, weaken Western-oriented international institutions, and discredit its democratic system. Beijing seeks, in other words, to accelerate the historical trend President Xi Jinping has described as the rise of the East and the decline of the West. In less than two years, the Trump administration has done much to bring that outcome closer.
When Xi comes to Washington on Sept. 24, the summit’s pageantry should not obscure the larger picture: how far and how quickly the balance of power has shifted in Beijing’s favor. China has weathered the trade war, narrowed the technology gap, tightened its leverage over critical supply chains, increased pressure on Taiwan, and deepened ties with Russia and much of the global south. It is better positioned relative to the United States than it was when Trump returned to office.
If China has not yet been recognized as Trump’s gravest foreign-policy failure, it likely stems from two main factors: the administration’s lack of clearly articulated goals against which its record can be measured and the long-term nature of the damage incurred. Unlike with Iran, Trump and his administration never articulated a stable hierarchy of objectives toward China. Indeed, the administration’s 2025 National Security Strategy did not identify China as America’s paramount geopolitical competitor. Instead, it framed the China challenge primarily in economic terms, even as other parts of the administration continued to see Beijing as a major military, technological, and security threat. The damage is also harder to grasp because, rather than unfolding in a single, highly visible crisis like Iran, the costs of a failed China policy only emerge over time.
Some failures of the White House’s economic policies toward China are already apparent: The administration has not reduced the trade deficit, it has not significantly lowered U.S. economic vulnerabilities, and it has not prevented Beijing from narrowing the gap in AI competition.
Exhibit one is the trade deficit. Despite long being Trump’s bête noire, the balance of payment has hardly improved. The administration may well claim that “America First Trade Policy is working” and that “China is no longer the trading partner with which the United States has its largest trade deficit.” But, as a recent Peterson Institute study demonstrates, the trade war’s net effect was simply to reroute Chinese exports through third countries, chiefly Vietnam, Taiwan, and Mexico. Weighed against the substantial costs that tariff volatility has imposed on American manufacturers and consumers, Trump’s tariff policy has been a net negative for the U.S. economy.
Second, and more critically, the Trump administration failed to meaningfully reduce the U.S. economy’s supply-chain dependencies on China. This is for rare earths and magnets, the so-called chokepoints that the administration inexplicably failed to anticipate Beijing would use as leverage against Washington’s punitive tariffs. More broadly, though, it is also true for vast swaths of industrial inputs critical to U.S. manufacturing. After threatening to hike up tariffs, for example, the White House was quickly reminded that U.S. farmers’ revenues were to a large extent hostage to Chinese purchases of soy and animal products. As a result, when Beijing retaliated, Trump was forced to reach a truce.
The bigger implications for U.S. economic security are equally significant. Much as Iran discovered by blocking the Strait of Hormuz that its leverage over the United States was stronger than it could have imagined before the war, China has shown that it can withstand, find workarounds, and retaliate against even Washington’s most aggressive trade-war measures. The October 2025 Busan agreement when Trump and Xi met on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting made the point plain: Trump abandoned his threat of an additional 100 percent tariff on Chinese imports in exchange for a fragile truce on rare earths, soybeans, fentanyl, and export controls. The rest of the world duly took note of the limits of American economic leverage with China.
Most damaging in the long term is the administration’s failure to maintain America’s once-sizable advantage over China in artificial intelligence. The U.S. still leads, but China has gained ground in both innovation and adoption. Its large language models now rival, and in some functions exceed, U.S. models at a fraction of the cost. The popularity of China’s open-weight models, combined with its manufacturing strength and lead in industrial robot deployment, gives it significant strengths in spreading AI at home and abroad. It’s also making steady progress to overcome its key weakness: limited computing power.
Trump keeps claiming that the United States is “leading China by a lot” in AI. But that lead is narrowing, and not simply because of Chinese policy and ingenuity. The administration ignored the requirements of its own strategy and was incoherent in applying the tools it inherited. It failed to sustain the Biden-era controls on advanced semiconductors and moved too slowly against predictable workarounds. This allowed Chinese firms to train models on banned chips obtained directly or through third countries. Export controls can buy time, but their effectiveness depends on anticipating how a rival will adapt. The administration kept busy blacklisting companies, but its approach remained disorderly and reactive, while China worked methodically to close the gap through a combination of basic and applied research, process innovation, and the stealth exploitation of the advances and capabilities of U.S. AI companies.
Some observers will object that the overall balance sheet still favors Washington: The U.S. economy is powering ahead, markets are at record highs, and American firms are more richly capitalized than ever. Meanwhile, China struggles with a property-debt hangover, adverse demographic trends, and deadening political control. But this snapshot misses the long-term trend. Economic history shows that national power is less a function of pure scientific and technological innovation than the ability to dominate the full cycle of a new general-purpose technology: discovery, commercialization, and diffusion at scale. By that measure, the picture is far less favorable to the United States.
While Washington attacks universities, deters talent through punitive immigration rules, and subjects scientific funding to political review, China is on track to produce nearly twice as many STEM Ph.D.s each year, is filing more patents than the United States (while closing the gap on high-quality ones), and is actively recruiting the talent America turns away. While the White House dismantles support for wind power, electric vehicles, and other clean-energy industries, China is consolidating its worldwide dominance in batteries, solar, and EVs. And while Washington alienates trading partners with tariffs, threats, and the disruption of long-standing trade arrangements, China is expanding its own network of trade agreements and market-access deals, gaining markets across the world and running record surpluses increasingly powered by high-tech exports.
Washington has also lost ground on the military and security front. America’s long-standing strategic interest in the Asia-Pacific has been to prevent China from becoming the region’s hegemon. That strategy depends on working to counterbalance China by cooperating with other regional powers and deterring China from using force against Taiwan. This, in turn, requires substantial U.S. forces in the region, credible messaging over Taiwan, and strong, functioning alliances.
On each count, deterrence has weakened under Trump. The most visible aspect is force diversion. By launching a war against Iran, the Trump administration has shifted considerable resources away from the Asia-Pacific. Deploying the USS George Washington from Japan to the Middle East left the Western Pacific without a U.S. carrier. The conflict has also consumed large quantities of the very long-range precision missiles, Patriot interceptors, THAAD interceptors, and Tomahawks critical in any conflict with China.
Messaging has fared no better. Since late 2025, Beijing has conducted its largest and closest exercises around Taiwan, fired rockets into surrounding waters, rehearsed blockade operations, simulated strikes against U.S.-supplied systems, and conducted maritime surveys in Taiwan’ exclusive economic zone off the island’s eastern coast. Washington has protested some of these moves and pledged to continue to provide support to Taiwan. But Trump’s treatment of a $14 billion arms package as a “negotiating chip” has signaled to Beijing that he views Taiwan’s security as something that can be traded against concessions elsewhere in the relationship.
Across the region, the weakening of America’s security assurances is pushing countries to hedge in their relations with Beijing as a form of strategic balancing. South Korea is a case in point. Trump ordered the Pentagon to “substantially reduce” the annual U.S.-South Korea military exercise, citing Seoul’s refusal to support the Iran war and his “great relationship” with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, whom he called “unthreatening and respectful.” South Korean President Lee Jae-myung, for his part, has announced he was seeking “full restoration” of relations with China. Washington has also needlessly strained its relationship with India, patiently cultivated over several administrations as a key regional counterweight to China. Beijing and New Delhi remain distrustful of each other but are pragmatically converging through BRICS around alternative trade and financial systems insulated from U.S. interference.
The United States still fields the world’s most formidable military, and China remains far from matching its global reach. But America’s forces must meet commitments around the world, while China concentrates on narrower objectives near its shores. In the Western Pacific, Trump has left fewer U.S. assets immediately available, created greater uncertainty over Taiwan, and weakened confidence among key allies. These changes all serve Beijing’s broader aim of convincing regional states that American power is unreliable and that Chinese influence is too costly to resist.
The administration, for its part, argues that shedding financial and diplomatic burdens and demonstrating a readiness to use hard power outweigh the costs of eroding allies’ confidence. From Beijing’s perspective, though, the deterioration of America’s dense web of alliances is an unexpected gift.
China has long struggled to compete with the United States in soft power because the Chinese Communist Party’s authoritarianism, human rights abuses, and “wolf warrior” diplomacy limit its appeal. Under Trump, the gap has begun to narrow—not because China has overcome these liabilities, but because of the sharp deterioration of the United States’ image abroad. Trump’s policies have weakened three pillars of American soft power. They have undercut the appeal of the country’s political values, damaged its reputation as a reliable and generous partner, and eroded the long-standing perception that U.S. power by and large operates within rules and restraints, including honoring formal agreements.
At home, Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown, pressure on universities and left-leaning civil society organizations, and attacks on the press have damaged the global standing of the U.S. as a model of political freedom. In a Pew Research Center 2026 survey of 36 countries, only 39 percent of respondents said the U.S. government respects the personal freedoms of its people; 56 percent said it does not. In nearly every country where Pew had comparable data from 2021, perceptions of American respect for individual freedoms had fallen sharply.
Trump’s MAGA political culture has also weakened the image of the United States as a multicultural society in which people of different races, religions, and national origins can belong and succeed. Trump’s nativist rhetoric and its effort to draw tighter boundaries around American identity undermines Washington’s credibility when it condemns intolerance and repression abroad. This gives authoritarian governments, including China, ready-made material for portraying U.S. support for democracy and human rights as hypocritical. Brand Finance’s 2026 Global Soft Power Index registered the same trend: The U.S. recorded the largest decline among all 193 countries assessed.
Foreign aid was once another important source of American influence and goodwill. The Trump administration’s abrupt dismantling of the U.S. Agency for International Development disrupted development and humanitarian programs around the world. In 2025, U.S. aid fell by 57 percent. It now provides less international aid than Germany. The human toll aside, this chaotic withdrawal carries its own political cost: It tells countries that America no longer believes that economic development, public health, education, and poverty reduction around the world ultimately benefit the United States.
Trump has also increasingly relied on military coercion, with little regard for the international laws and norms the United States has traditionally claimed to uphold. In January, the U.S. government captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and flew him to New York. Trump made clear the operation was driven less by Maduro’s record as a ruthless autocrat than by its oil resources and political obedience from the country’s leaders. Washington subsequently struck an oil arrangement under which the U.S. government holds a 35 percent stake in a company controlling major Venezuelan fields. In February, the United States and Israel launched the war against Iran, without consultation with allies or even pro forma consideration for the prescriptions of the U.N. Charter. The Trump administration also continued military support for Israel without any effort to address mounting international concern over civilian casualties and the devastating humanitarian crisis in Gaza.
Xi’s China has not become more liberal domestically or benevolent internationally. But soft power is comparative. As America’s image deteriorates, China gains ground by default. Pew now finds China viewed more favorably than the United States in 25 places surveyed.
There is a more direct international dimension to this as well. The Trump administration has reduced the funding, diplomatic pressure, and coordinated pressure that previously provided a measure of constraint on authoritarian governments. Cuts to foreign aid and State Department democracy programs, as well as attempts to cut funding to the National Endowment for Democracy, have led to a freefall in support for civil society, independent media, election monitoring, and multilateral accountability mechanisms. With fewer of these in place, Beijing has gained more room to shape international norms in its favor, expand its political and media influence, and suppress critics with less coordinated resistance.
The defunding of China-related human rights and democracy work, in particular, has reduced the scrutiny on both Beijing’s domestic repression and its expanding authoritarian influence abroad. China-focused organizations monitoring dissent, labor rights, and religious persecution were forced to suspend projects and lay off staff, while cuts to Radio Free Asia disrupted a rare source of uncensored reporting in Mandarin, Tibetan, and Uyghur. These cuts, alongside the suspension of an initiative designed to combat foreign disinformation in the U.S., have weakened the capacity to monitor Chinese censorship and propaganda, as well as Beijing’s attempts to hollow out the U.N. human rights system.
Because the U.S.-led postwar international order carried a preference for liberal democracy, nondemocratic regimes have long carried a legitimacy deficit in international arenas such as the United Nations, limiting their ability to pursue their foreign-policy goals on equal normative terms. By weakening that constraint, the Trump administration has given China a freer hand to reshape the international system in ways more advantageous to authoritarian states, to the long-term detriment of democracy in the world and to the United States itself.
Taken together, it is striking the extent to which Washington’s setbacks were self-inflicted. Despite being the U.S.’s most formidable geopolitical rival and one of the very few subjects of bipartisan support, China was effectively neglected as a strategic priority. Most of the administration’s decisions were incoherent and reactive. Trump has also exposed how vulnerable the American economy was to China’s actions, narrowing policy options for future administrations.
That the United States has allowed China to gain so much ground in such a short span of time is all the more striking given how relatively unskillful Beijing has been at capitalizing on Washington’s disarray. As David Shambaugh and Steven F. Jackson have argued, China has been “squandering a golden opportunity” created by Trump’s missteps. Because of Beijing’s threats against Taiwan and maritime claims, many states are responding to U.S. unreliability by hedging against both superpowers rather than gravitating toward China. Meanwhile, Beijing’s economic reforms have ground to a halt, while its formidable export machine is generating a backlash even among countries alienated by Washington.
But China does not need to win the world’s embrace to benefit from America’s retreat. The Xi regime is primarily concerned with its own security and with cultivating an international environment conducive to China’s continued rise. By both these measures, it is doing better now than it was 19 months ago, with more markets, more leverage, more room to pressure Taiwan. Perhaps Trump’s greatest legacy will be confirming Xi’s belief that time is on China’s side.
This post is part of FP’s ongoing coverage of the Trump administration. Follow along here.
Nicholas Bequelin is a senior fellow at Yale Law School’s Paul Tsai China Center and at the Asia Society Center on U.S.-China Relations. X: @bequelin
Yaqiu Wang is a fellow at the Penn Project on the Future of U.S.-China Relations at the University of Pennsylvania.

Title: Pace Prints Acquires Printmaking Studio Brand X Editions
Article_Text:
Pace Prints has acquired Brand X Editions, the nearly 50-year-old New York printmaking studio and publisher known for its work with artists including Robert Rauschenberg, Roy Lichtenstein, Frank Stella, Helen Frankenthaler, Jeff Koons, Glenn Ligon, and Mickalene Thomas.
The acquisition brings Brand X under the leadership of Pace Prints president and CEO Jacob Lewis, who took ownership of Pace Prints from its founder, Richard Solomon, and his partners last year. Both companies will continue to operate their existing workshops, while Brand X will add to Pace Prints’ production capabilities in Manhattan and Brooklyn as well as a forthcoming gallery and printmaking facility in Los Angeles.
The deal formalizes a relationship that goes back decades. Brand X founder Robert Blanton, who established the studio in 1979 after beginning his career at Styria Studio, has for years worked with Solomon and Pace Prints. In a statement, Blanton said Pace Prints had been “foundational” to Brand X and called Lewis ideally positioned to lead the two companies.
Brand X built its reputation on ambitious screenprinting. David DeSanctis, who joined Blanton as a partner, established its publishing program in 2011, producing editions with artists including Alex Katz, Rashid Johnson, KAWS, Adam Pendleton, Loie Hollowell, Joel Mesler, and Tschabalala Self.
The studio’s history has recently gotten the museum treatment, too. In 2024, Blanton and DeSanctis established the Brand X Archive at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, comprising more than 400 prints made at the studio. The museum mounted a retrospective of Brand X the following year, while another exhibition devoted to its screenprinting is currently on view at the Dallas Museum of Art.
For Lewis, the acquisition is another step in an unusually busy period of expansion. A former Pace Prints intern who became president in 2019, Lewis took over ownership of the company in 2025. Pace Prints is also preparing to open its Los Angeles facility this fall.
“As we embark on our mission to preserve and challenge the technical possibilities of printmaking, Pace Prints is thrilled to now welcome our long-time partner Brand X under our creative umbrella,” Lewis told ARTnews in an email
He said the Brand X acquisition and Los Angeles expansion were both part of a larger attempt to push what can be done with the medium. “Given the collaborative nature of our studios, ideas are exchanged, an artist’s vision is realized, and the editioned work that is created becomes something that couldn’t have been crafted in isolation,” Lewis said.
The acquisition also puts Lewis in the somewhat unusual position of carrying on the businesses of two veteran New York printmakers who helped shape his career.
“I’ve been fortunate to have had not only one, but two mentors,” Lewis said in the announcement, referring to Solomon and Blanton. “It is an honor that each of them has entrusted me with their businesses, which carry such important artistic legacies.”
If all goes according to plan, Lewis sees the combined operation becoming something larger than a pair of print shops. Over the next decade, he said, Pace Prints’ bi-coastal studios could become places “to share and explore ideas in dialogue with artists and collectors for generations to come.”

Title: How pledges were recruited into drug trafficking operation at Penn State frat: grand jury
Article_Text:
How pledges were recruited into drug trafficking operation at Penn State frat: grand jury
CENTRE COUNTY, Pa. (WHP) — Former Penn State student Thomas Robinson used his leadership role at Delta Upsilon fraternity to recruit pledges to assist him with packaging and delivering drugs, according to new court documents.
READ MORE | PSU fraternity brother had handgun, drugs stored for sale in safe on campus: affidavit
According to a grand jury presentment released Thursday, Robinson was the frat's "pledge educator" during the 2024 spring and fall semesters. He allegedly used this role to recruit pledges to help him with the drug trafficking operation.
Robinson was part of Delta Upsilon's executive board and was known as a "well-respected brother," according to the presentment. The grand jury says this status gave him greater influence over the pledges and the ability to request them to do more tasks for him.
Robinson reportedly told the grand jury that brothers were already selling cocaine, marijuana and other controlled substances when he joined the frat. The presentment read:
Robinson indicated that the normal procedure was that when a DU Fraternity brother graduated or went overseas, they relinquished their roles in selling controlled substances and another brother would take their place.
Pledge testimony
Before pledges could join in the operation, they first had to pass a "shaky hand test." The grand jury said pledges would hold out their hands, and if they were steady, they were allowed to help Robinson bag and weigh cocaine.
Pledges testified that after they passed the test, they had to print and sign non-disclosure forms to give to Robinson. Robinson then tore up the forms and threw them away for unknown reasons, the presentment read.
Robinson would allegedly show pledges how to break down a cocaine brick and mix it with creatine. The pledges would then put this mixture into half-gram bags and weigh them.
One pledge told the grand jury that he prepared around 200-300 bags of cocaine. He said preparing a kilo of cocaine (1,000 grams) would take pledges about two days to complete.
Pledges also reportedly testified that they were asked to deliver these bags to people outside of the fraternity.
Prior to Robinson's arrest in December 2024, other Delta Upsilon brothers reportedly warned him that the operation was "getting too big" and could be putting him and others in the fraternity at risk of being arrested.
Damage control
After news broke of Robinson's arrest, Delta Upsilon leadership advised members who were involved with Robinson to get a lawyer and not talk to the police, according to the presentment.
The grand jury also detailed how Robinson's father, Paul Robinson, allegedly helped him conceal a safe that was full of drugs and money.
PREVIOUS COVERAGE | Safe with possible evidence at center of accused dad’s hearing in Penn State cocaine case
According to the presentment, Thomas Robinson kept one safe inside of his bedroom at the frat house, and he paid his good friend, Ryan Matson, to keep another safe at his apartment.
Robinson would visit Matson's apartment to take drugs and money out of the safe, or put more in, the grand jury said.
After Robinson was arrested, Matson buried the safe in a wooded area in State College, according to the presentment.
After Robinson posted bail, he returned to State College with his father to retrieve the buried safe, the grand jury said. Paul Robinson reportedly put the safe in his vehicle and left State College.
Thomas Robinson testified that when Paul Robinson returned the safe to him, the safe was emptied of any drugs and money.
Robinson and other frat brothers allegedly involved in the operation are due in court on Sept. 30.

Title: Mainetti & Mainetti Uptown Car show rolls into Uptown Sunday
Article_Text:
KINGSTON, N.Y. — Hundreds of classic, historic, custom and exotic cars are set to cruise into Uptown as the Mainetti & Mainetti Uptown Car Show returns Sunday, Sept. 20, from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m.
The car show is organized by brothers Michael and Alex Mainetti of the Kingston-based law firm Mainetti & Mainetti.
Alex Mainetti said this year’s show has already attracted a record number of pre-registrations, with hundreds of cars pre-registered, with some participants even coming from neighboring states including Massachusetts, Connecticut, Pennsylvania and New Jersey.
Alex Mainetti said this year will also see an expansion in the types of cars applying, with this year’s lineup set to feature a “funny car” a type of drag racing car, monster trucks and even custom tractors from semi-trucks.
He said the lineup will also feature at least 30 Corvettes from the First Capital Corvette Club, which assists in organizing the show, and customs from the Kingston-based Made 2 Envy car club, which brought back its Envy Frenzy Car show to the Rondout Area in August after a 14-year hiatus.
The cars will be lined up on North Front, Wall, John, Crown and Green streets.
“It definitely has much more interest than every prior year,” he said.
The brothers shared which cars are their personal favorites to seek out at each year’s show.
Alex Mainetti said he likes to see all the exotics, including Porsches and Ferraris, while Michael Mainetti said he likes the 90s Euro cars, including BMWs, along with the historic cars like Model Ts that he described as being almost like museum pieces.
The festival has updated its arrival procedure for participants to alleviate traffic concerns, Alex Mainetti said. The new procedure calls for all the participating cars to first be staged at Dietz Stadium, which he said will help avoid “jamming the streets.”
The car show will also feature several bands at the Pugsly’s Barbershop Stage on North Front Street, headlined by Reverend Horton Heat, who is traveling to the event from Texas. Michael Mainetti noted that Mike Conti, owner of Pugsly’s, recommended the act, with the law firm paying to bring the band to Kingston.
“It’s a collaborative effort, and we could never do it on our own,” Michael Mainetti said.
The lineup also features special performances by The Sci-Flies and Messer Chups.
“Some people may go to the show just to watch the bands,” Alex Mainetti said.
The show will also feature a kids zone sponsored by MyKingstonKids, featuring carnival games and activities for kids.
“Some of the young children are not overly interested in show cars, more interested in games, more family-oriented event,” Alex Mainetti said.
Each year the festival serves as a fundraiser for a local family in need.
All proceeds from this year’s Uptown Car Show will benefit Olivia Grace Maragoudakis, a local girl born prematurely at just 31 weeks and weighing just 2.7 pounds, a press release stated.
The release noted that Olivia spent 60 days in the neonatal intensive care unit at Albany Medical Center. She was born with “with several complex medical conditions, including sacral agenesis, a rare congenital condition affecting the development of the lower spine and legs,” the release stated.
The release said that Olivia uses a wheelchair and is working towards obtaining a power wheelchair and an accessible vehicle to provide her with greater independence.
Mainetti & Mainetti picks up the full tab for any expenses incurred in holding the event to ensure that every penny raised in the show will go to each year’s beneficiary, Michael Mainetti said.
“It’s impossible to make a profit,” Alex Mainetti said. “We do not want the final number to express deductions for expenses.”
“So when someone buys a T-shirt or raffle ticket, they can be sure that every penny goes to this little girl and her family,” Mainetti said.
Alex Mainetti said the car show has already collected tens of thousands of dollars for the Maragoudakis family, with a raffle for a side-by-side Honda UTV alone collecting almost $10,000.
The brothers said the show also seeks to boost businesses at Uptown.
“We want to bring as much foot traffic into Uptown as possible,” Alex Mainetti said. “We encourage people to stop into the local restaurants and shops Uptown,” Michael Mainetti added.
The brothers noted that even as the festival has expanded its roster of vendors, they specifically choose vendors who do not sell items that compete with stores and restaurants Uptown.
“We have tremendous support from local businesses who have expressed that they are pleased that the show is going to be returning,” Alex Mainetti said.
Mainetti said the only wild card this year is the weather.
The National Weather Service forecast for Kingston on Thursday called for a 100% chance of showers on Sunday with a high of 64 degrees.
“We are watching that closely,” Alex Manetti said. “We’re hoping the weather cooperates.”
He recommended checking the car show’s Facebook page and website for updates.
Admission is free for spectators. Registration fees for those entering vehicles are $15 for supporter registration, $25 for supporter registration, $50 for elite registration and $75 for premier registration.
Pre-registration for vehicle owners will remain open at https://mainetti.law/carshow/ through 5 p.m. on Friday, Sept. 18.
Day-of-event registration opens at 9 a.m. Sunday morning at Dietz Stadium.

Title: Phillies sign Jesús Luzardo replacement for stretch run, add trade deadline arm to 60-Day IL
Article_Text:
The Philadelphia Phillies were hit with a whopper of a gut punch earlier this week, learning that co-ace Jesús Luzardo will miss the remainder of the regular season with shoulder soreness. The team has publicly stated that they hope he'll be back in time for the playoffs, but it's anyone's guess if his overworked left shoulder will be ready to go by the time the Wild Card Round begins.
That put the Phillies' depth chart in a world of hurt, seeing as the organization isn't exactly teeming with capable starters waiting in the wings. Clearly, something needed to be done, but Dave Dombrowski's options were limited.
So, welcome to the bargain bin, folks. The Phillies have claimed José Urquidy off waivers from the Chicago White Sox, just days after the Pale Hose had designated the right-hander for assignment earlier this week. To make room on the 40-man roster for his arrival, Philly has stashed Caleb Kilian on the 60-day IL, all but confirming the premature end to his season.
Phillies make the best of a bad situation with José Urquidy claim
This isn't the first time the Phillies have sought out veteran pitching help recently; it was just last month that they signed Nestor Cortes to a one-year deal, in the hopes that the former All-Star could rebound from his offseason arm surgery and provide depth down the stretch. Since then, however, he's only tossed 2.2 (largely unsuccessful) innings at Triple-A. The chances that he'll able to help the big-league club are shrinking by the day.
Urquidy is better equipped to help right now, even if he isn't going to inspire a ton of confidence with his performances on the mound. He began the season with an ugly bullpen stint in Pittsburgh, eventually parlaying some successful work in the minors into another shot with the White Sox. He was far more respectable as a bulk reliever with them, though there are still major concerns surrounding his profile; he's allowed three or more runs in four of his 11 outings this year, despite the fact he's only eclipsed five innings twice.
Still, it's hard to argue with what the Phillies are trying to accomplish here. Urquidy was a well-regarded starter not too long ago -- the Astros nearly traded him for Willson Contreras back in 2022 -- and he's as reliable an innings-eater as any pitcher still available this late in the season. If he takes on the final two starts that Luzardo was scheduled for and saves the bullpen a few bullets prior to October, his tenure in Philadelphia will be an unmitigated success.
In a best-case scenario, Urquidy pitches well enough to effectively replace Kilian in the bullpen and makes the postseason roster. If he struggles, there won't be much harm done, considering the Phillies only owe him the meager amount that remains on his $1.5 million contract.

Title: Knicks' latest signings did what 76ers need to do but cannot
Article_Text:
The New York Knicks signed a bunch of different players to training camp contracts to compete for roster spots before the beginning of the season. Two of the guys they signed were James Wiseman and Drew Eubanks. The Knicks were able to take advantage of what the Philadelphia 76ers don't have: Roster flexibility.
Arguably, the Sixers need center depth more than the next two. New York only has one backup center, Andre Drummond, and the Sixers have two in Adem Bona and Ariel Hukporti. However, considering how much more of an injury risk Joel Embiid is compared to Karl-Anthony Towns, it feels like the Sixers could use extra centers more than the Knicks could. Plus, Drummond is more proven than Hukporti and Bona.
That said, Philadelphia doesn’t have standard roster spots to offer. It needs to be a lot more careful when considering which players to sign to training camp contracts, especially considering they already have some training camp players in place.
Knicks' James Wiseman and Drew Eubanks signings were what 76ers need to do but can't
The biggest difference between the Knicks and the Sixers right now is that the Knicks actually have standard roster spots to hand out. So, when players are considering where to sign training camp deals, they are more likely to sign with a team that can actually sign them at the end of camp.
Unfortunately for the 76ers, they don't have that. Their roster is completely full, so the only training camp guys they can sign are ones who know that they probably won't land a full roster spot at the end of the day.
Meanwhile, the Knicks can promise players a chance to compete for an actual roster spot in the NBA. For veteran players like Wiseman and Eubanks, that's a much more enticing situation.
That's good news for the Knicks, because that means they get a better crack at signing legitimate center depth compared to the Sixers, who are going to be left hanging out to dry.
Philadelphia did manage to sign Tacko Fall to a camp deal. He had a brief stint in the NBA. However, guys like Wiseman and Eubanks are a little bit more proven.
The Knicks will spend the next few weeks seeing which players they would like to sign. They didn't just sign centers, bringing in the likes of Bruce Brown, Ochai Agbaji, and John Konchar, too, but the center depth might be their biggest need.
Just like it's the biggest need for the 76ers. But luckily for the Knicks, they had the right situation to draw in the right players. Philadelphia just didn't.

Title: The US Considered Nuking the Moon. Jitish Kallat Studies Cold-War Scheme
Article_Text:
In a secret 1958 project, the Air Force considered detonating a nuclear bomb on the Moon.
Scientists believed then they would learn a lot from the exercise, code named Project A119, and the US might gain ground in the Cold War space race with the Soviets. What’s more, the blast would perhaps be visible on Earth, boosting morale at home and cowing our enemies abroad. The risks (including the blast affecting humankind’s home) were deemed to outweigh the benefits, though, and the US government turned its attention instead to putting a man on the Moon, which it predicted would be more popular, and which NASA would be first to accomplish, a decade later. The Air Force’s report on the potential bombing, titled “A Study of Lunar Research Flights,” remained secret until the project’s leader disclosed it in 2000.
The same heavenly body has lately been on the government’s mind again; US president Donald Trump, who announced the formation of the Space Force in 2019, declared in a recent Truth Social post that “The Moon is ours”; about a week later, with echoes of the Cold War, the Air Force Secretary revealed that the US has stationed weapons in Earth’s orbit.
Artist Jitish Kallat has been fascinated for years with the meanings of space exploration. Now, at the Menil Drawing Institute, in Houston, Texas, the artist has created a huge wall drawing, Wall Drawing / Redux: A119 (on view through August 8, 2027), that explores the abortive plan to nuke the moon.
He’s calling it site-specific, and in fact the Menil is only about 30 miles from the mission control facility at NASA’s Johnson Space Center (which Apollo 13 pilot Jack Swigert famously addressed with his oft-misquoted line, “Okay, Houston, we’ve had a problem here”). Kallat’s is the eighth in a series of projects hosted at the Drawing Institute; past participants have included Mel Bochner, Roni Horn, and Gladys Nilsson.
He has printed declassified pages from the (partly redacted) plan, also called “A Study of Lunar Research Flights,” on a wall. Inspired by the glass walls of the building, that wall has then been fronted with glass fitted with a film that changes levels of clarity and opacity with electrical signals, so that as an electrical pulse travels through the glass, images dissolve and reappear, serving nicely as a metaphor for secrecy and revelation, as well as the Moon’s limited and fugitive visibility from Earth.
“There was the question of what constituted a drawing,” the artist said in a video call, “but also what constitutes a wall. What could that wall be? Could a wall have a window, and could they go together?” He then was driven to explore the notion of “a window that can become opaque.”
Kallat also looked at Project A119 in thie piece Lunar Redux (2024–26), a photo-based installation that shows lenticular prints of the report’s pages; the artist described that treatment of the document as introducing “a field of visual instability verging on hallucination.”
Born in Mumbai and still living there, Kallat has shown at the Art Institute of Chicago (AIC), the Philadelphia Museum of Art, and the Gallery of New South Wales, and has been included in the Venice and Gwangju biennials, among others. He’s in the collections of museums including the Pompidou Center, M+ Museum, and the AIC.
Is Kallat obsessed with the Moon, and, by extension, with space? Maybe. A sculptural installation, Moon Treaty (2025), is named for a 1979 United Nations declaration that the Moon and other celestial bodies are the “common heritage of mankind,” outlawing national ownership or military use. In a large sculpture, aluminum facsimile pages are crumpled on the floor, reflecting the way spacefaring nations have more or less ignored it.
What’s more, a recent project shown recently at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco, “Covering Letter (Terranum Nuncius),” employs sounds and images launched into space in 1977 in the legendary Voyager 1 and 2 craft, which contained “golden records” encoded with representations of humanity and life on Earth, possibly to be retrieved by aliens.
“At some point A119 ceased to be purely a document of interest; it’s a political, militaristic, and scientific document, all entangled, the artist said, recalling his research. “It set out to do something completely outlandish, projecting anxiety, hubris, and diabolical intent. But in the course of the scientific exploration came reflection.”
Neatly drawing the line back to the themes of changing visibility in his own new project, he concluded, “It was essentially about optics.”

Title: How Ed Sheeran's tour became a flashpoint over Gaza and free speech
Article_Text:
Updated September 18, 2026 at 2:37 PM CDT
When Ed Sheeran walks onto a Philadelphia stage Saturday, the people missing may be as noticeable as the person under the lights. There will be no opening act and no Beoga, the Irish band that once joined him midway through the show.
The tour began coming apart after Macklemore spoke about the war in Gaza.
During Sheeran's Sept. 5 concert at MetLife Stadium, Macklemore said "free Palestine" and performed "Hind's Hall," named for Hind Rajab, a 5-year-old Palestinian girl killed by Israeli troops in Gaza City in January 2024. Images of Gaza's destruction filled the screens behind him.
The performance drew quick criticism, including from the Anti-Defamation League. The Israeli-American Council circulated a petition urging Sheeran to drop Macklemore.
Macklemore said Sheeran later told him several stadiums would not host the tour if he remained. The rapper accused Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft of leading the effort. Kraft acknowledged barring Macklemore, citing what he called a history of antisemitic rhetoric and saying he would not "provide a platform for hate speech." Sheeran said the promoter and venues made the decision.
Music journalist and critic Zach Schonfeld told Morning Edition that the episode showed the power venue owners can have over who performs and what artists can say.
"I think it does show that a billionaire venue owner like Robert Kraft holds a lot of power to dictate who is allowed to perform in his venue and what these artists are allowed to say," Schonfeld said.
By Tuesday, other artists had begun leaving the tour in solidarity with Macklemore. Finneas, Aaron Rowe, Lukas Graham and Beoga all withdrew from upcoming dates. The next day, Macklemore said he would donate his $1 million in net earnings from the tour to six organizations supporting Palestinians and invited Kraft to do the same.
The fight over a stadium stage offers a window into changing American views of Israel. A July Economist/YouGov poll found 43% of U.S. adult citizens said Israel was committing genocide against Palestinian civilians, including 68% of Democrats and 17% of Republicans. Among adults under 30, the share rose to 55%.
Sheeran said he has personal views about the war but does not want his concerts to become political forums. That answer drew fresh criticism online, including comparisons with his 2022 performance at a benefit for Ukraine and a video in which he told Ukrainians, "I stand with you." He has also campaigned against racism in the U.K. and criticized the British government over cuts to arts funding.
Asked about precedents, Schonfeld pointed to Kneecap, the Irish rap trio that faced canceled shows after speaking about Gaza. The controversy also comes amid other cultural fights over speech about Israel and Gaza, including backlash against The Zone of Interest director Jonathan Glazer after his Oscar speech addressed Israel's occupation and the war, and protests surrounding No Other Land, the Oscar-winning documentary about displacement in the West Bank that initially lacked a mainstream U.S. distributor.
The pressure extends beyond public and online spaces in America. In Israel, the directors of the new documentary "NAZA," an investigation by two Israeli journalists into how Israeli intelligence selected targets in Gaza and calculated expected civilian deaths from strikes, faced calls from the culture minister to lose their citizenship.
Still, Schonfeld said Sheeran's enormous mainstream reach makes this the most high-profile example yet. He has tried to stay out of politics. In Philadelphia, the empty spaces onstage may make that position impossible to miss.
Editor's note: This explainer grew out of a live Morning Edition interview conducted by Michel Martin, with contributions from Lindsay Totty and editing by Suzanne Nuyen.

Title: After ending winless ruts, NYCFC, Red Bulls meet for high-stakes derby
Article_Text:
Field Level Media
                
18 Sep 2026, 02:35 GMT+10
            
(Photo credit: Mark Smith)
Bragging rights in the Hudson River Derby might be secondary given the precarious nature of the playoff positioning for New York City FC and the New York Red Bulls when the teams convene Friday night at Yankee Stadium.
Both teams have nine games remaining and are separated by two points after stopping lengthy winless skids last week.
NYCFC (8-9-8, 32 points) begin the week in eighth and own the goal differential tiebreaker over ninth-place Cincinnati since they have outscored opponents 39-33, while Cincinnati has been outscored 59-52. NYCFC trail seventh-place Philadelphia by one point and sixth-place Orlando by two points, and those teams also have nine games remaining.
New York City heads into Friday 1-3-4 over the past eight matches. The Pigeons earned their first win since July 25 on Saturday with a 2-0 victory at Real Salt Lake, when Nicolas Fernandez and Luighi scored on either side of the halftime break.
'I think we found quite a decent balance when we play against the Red Bulls, but we're also very aware of what's at stake,' NYCFC coach Pascal Jansen said. 'It's a derby, it's emotional, means a lot to our fans from both sides. So it's going to be an intense game no matter what and for us, it's mainly about making sure we keep things under control, stick to the plan that we will make and make sure we get a good result.'
The Red Bulls (8-11-6, 30 points) sit in 10th and are two points behind NYCFC and Cincinnati while carrying a minus-15 goal differential. New York is attempting to win consecutive matches for just the third time this season and the first time since May 9-13.
Like their rivals, the Red Bulls ended a lengthy winless rut (0-4-2) Saturday with a 1-0 victory at Columbus. Ronald Donkor broke the stalemate in the 89th minute with his second goal of the year.
'We have not had enough to show for ourselves on certain days,' Red Bulls coach Michael Bradley said. 'We feel really good that now in this week-long road trip we take four points, two shutouts, and so, we are going to use this as a way to really build momentum.'
--Field Level Media

Title: Bluffton welcomes incoming class from nine states
Article_Text:
BLUFFTON, Ohio— Bluffton University welcomes a new class of students to campus this fall, with incoming students bringing a range of academic interests, athletic talents and connections to Bluffton.
Bluffton’s incoming class includes 62 first-generation college students, continued growth in first-time freshman enrollment and the University’s highest transfer enrollment in six years. Eleven students also have a family connection to Bluffton, with a parent, sibling or grandparent who is a Bluffton alumni.
Students in the incoming class represent nine states, with the majority coming from Ohio. The class includes 119 Ohio students, along with students from Indiana, Michigan, Kentucky, Tennessee, Iowa, Alabama, Illinois and Pennsylvania. The class also includes one international student.
The most popular areas of study among the incoming class include business, sport management, exercise science, education, nursing and accounting.
“We are excited to welcome this new group of students to Bluffton,” said Claire Kleman, vice president of enrollment and communication. “Each student brings unique experiences, interests and goals to our community, and our faculty and staff are committed to knowing, supporting and equipping them for what comes next.”
The incoming class continues Bluffton’s tradition of preparing students for life as well as vocation through relationships with faculty, hands-on learning and opportunities to connect classroom experiences with future goals.
Graduate programs at Bluffton University also reflect a continued interest in advanced education and professional development. The Master of Social Work (MSW) program welcomed 13 students to its incoming cohort this fall. In March 2026, the program achieved initial accreditation for eight years through the Council on Social Work Education, marking a significant milestone for students pursuing careers in social work. The program’s accreditation strengthens opportunities for students to prepare for meaningful careers serving individuals, families and communities.

Title: Robert Kennedy says anti-vaccine activists have White House
Article_Text:
WASHINGTON — Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. gave the keynote address Thursday at a conference of an anti-vaccine activist group he once chaired, telling the hundreds in attendance that they had a friend in U.S. President Donald Trump’s White House.
It was Kennedy’s first time appearing at the Children’s Health Defense conference since he became secretary. Kennedy took leave from the group when he launched his bid to become president in 2023, but his speech Thursday served as a sort of homecoming, offering him a platform from which to hail the administration’s steps to scale back vaccine guidance and reassure the activists in attendance that he was working to turn their priorities into policy.
“Let me be clear: You have a strong and steadfast friend in the White House. We’ve accomplished in 19 months things that would have seemed unthinkable two years ago,” he said.
The speech, peppered with questions about long established vaccine safety, also highlighted how once fringe views on vaccines have been given a prominent pulpit under the Trump administration.
Kennedy boasted about the administration’s moves to downsize the childhood vaccination schedule and reshape a key vaccine advisory board — steps that have since been halted by a judge.
Kennedy lauded Trump for pushing ahead with attempts to overhaul vaccine guidance, including an executive order last month calling for spacing out the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, against medical groups’ recommendations.
That executive order and now Kennedy’s keynote speech at the Children’s Health Defense conference mark a pivot by the White House and the Department of Health and Human Services, who earlier this year had appeared to be moving beyond vaccine efforts and toward a less contentious agenda on healthy food ahead of November’s midterm elections. HHS promoted the speech on its social media channels.
Kennedy, a longtime anti-vaccine activist, chaired Children’s Health Defense for years. He served as the group’s chief legal counsel and expanded it. After becoming health secretary last year, Kennedy moved at a blistering pace to overhaul public health guidance and revamp long-held precedents in vaccine policymaking.
Critics, among them many of the country’s top medical associations, have said the moves risk stoking vaccine hesitancy and sowing confusion among Americans who endured a crisis of trust in their public health agencies following the COVID-19 pandemic. That public confidence continues to erode.
“We have not taken vaccines away from anybody. We have preserved access. But we have started asking the questions that you and millions of American parents have been asking for years,” Kennedy told the group.
Mary Holland, the CEO of Children’s Health Defense, referred to Kennedy as “Bobby” and said the group has “gratitude beyond words” to the HHS secretary for “recognizing there are real consequential issues around childhood vaccinations.”
Kennedy’s appearance Thursday comes as the country faces its worst year for measles since 1991 and has seen seven reported measles-associated deaths in the last two years — more than the combined total of reported deaths over the previous three decades.
Pennsylvania officials have reported four measles-associated deaths this year. None of the four were vaccinated, according to the state health department. When state officials last month announced the first two of those deaths, it ignited a public feud between Gov. Josh Shapiro and Kennedy.
Shapiro blasted Kennedy’s appearance on the social media site X Thursday, saying Kennedy “chose to spend his time today addressing the premier vaccine-denial conference in America.”
Shapiro said the HHS secretary should have encouraged people to get vaccinated for measles, “yet he couldn’t bring himself to do it. Instead, he pushed a narrative that continues to stoke fear and mistrust.”
A representative from the White House did not respond to an Associated Press request for comment on Kennedy’s appearance at the event.
Following Kennedy onstage Thursday was Andrew Wakefield, an author of a since-discredited study that linked the MMR vaccine to autism, which has fuelled the anti-vaccine movement even though it was retracted.
Widespread scientific consensus and decades of studies have firmly concluded there is no link between vaccines and autism.
Shaughnessy Naughton, founder of 314 Action, a group that recruits scientists to run for public office, said Kennedy’s decision to give a speech at the conference shows “the lack of seriousness he brings to HHS.”
“With a deadly measles outbreak killing people in Pennsylvania, the best thing Kennedy can do for Americans is step aside.”
___
Stobbe contributed from New York.
Fatima Hussein And Mike Stobbe, The Associated Press

Title: Authorities: Scranton man arrested after April high-speed chase
Article_Text:
A Scranton man accused of leading police on a high-speed chase in April was arrested more than a month later in Big Run, Pennsylvania — nearly 200 miles away.
On April 28, officers initially pulled over Amir Hunter during a traffic stop on Main Street in Carbondale after receiving a tip from a confidential informant about a group “rolling through town” in a silver Dodge Challenger with West Virginia tags and guns in the trunk, according to a criminal complaint.
Officers spotted the vehicle driving erratically and conducted a stop on North Main Street with Hunter behind the wheel.
As police questioned Hunter and his two passengers, officers spotted a gun in a pants leg of the front-seat passenger, according to the complaint.
A struggle ensued, someone yelled “gun,” and a Carbondale Police Department officer discharged their service weapon, firing one round. No one was struck or injured.
Passengers Phillip DeBarry and Qu’Ran Na’Sir Baskerville then resisted police, according to officers. Baskerville attempted to pull away from officers before being handcuffed. DeBarry fled on foot and was taken into custody shortly after in the Lackawanna River under the Seventh Avenue bridge near Dunkin’.
Hunter reentered the vehicle and sped off toward Scranton, leading officers on a high-speed chase, according to the complaint.
Police pursued Hunter on Route 6 in Carbondale, through Mayfield and Archbald, and onto the Casey Highway. He continued onto the Biden Expressway and then onto Mulberry Street in Scranton.
Hunter ultimately crashed into another vehicle at Mulberry Street and Taylor Avenue before fleeing on foot.
A warrant was issued for Hunter, but local officers were unable to locate him despite an extensive search, according to the complaint.
On June 8, the U.S. Marshals Service Western Pennsylvania Fugitive Task Force arrested Hunter based on information provided by Detective Martin Connors of Lackawanna County.
Officers located Hunter at a residence in Big Run, Jefferson County, after spotting him walking a dog outside the building.
Hunter was jailed in Jefferson County before being transported to the Lackawanna County Prison. He was arraigned Wednesday before District Judge Alyce Farrell on a felony charge of flight to avoid apprehension.
Hunter remains at the Lackawanna County Prison in lieu of $20,000 bail. A preliminary hearing is scheduled for 10 a.m. on Sept. 29.

Title: USMNT camp highlighted by presence of 16-year-old F Cavan Sullivan
Article_Text:
By Field Level Media
Sep 17 (Field Level Media) – After taking MLS by storm over the past two months, 16-year-old Cavan Sullivan will get his first chance to play with the United States men’s national team when it reconvenes this weekend at Atlanta.
The USMNT will take the field for the first time since the World Cup when it faces Peru on Sept. 26 at Orlando, Chile on Sept. 29 at St. Louis, Mexico on Oct. 3 at Glendale, Ariz., and Canada Oct. 6 in St. Paul, Minn.
Sullivan, who has put a charge into the Philadelphia Union of late, will headline a group of young players being introduced to national team duty. The other half of the team will be made up of USMNT veterans, although forwards Christian Pulisic and Folarin Balogun will not be on the squad.
Head coach Mauricio Pochettino stressed that the roster in no way represents the group that has priority heading toward the next World Cup in 2030.
“The 28 players that are going to be involved in these four games, for different circumstances, are the best players we want see and we want to work with. That’s it,” Pochettino said at a press conference in New York on Thursday.
Pochettino will have 28 players in camp, with 13 of those seeking their first USMNT appearance.
Sullivan, a Philadelphia native, has shown his promise with six goals and 11 assists in 23 matches (16 starts) this season. He has goal contributions in seven consecutive games to lead Philadelphia’s 10-game unbeaten run since the end of the World Cup break.
Among other players invited to USMNT camp for the first time are defender Neil Pierre, Sullivan’s Union teammate, midfielder Zavier Gozo of English side Crystal Palace and forward Julian Hall of the New York Red Bulls, all of whom are 19 or younger.
Those players will get their first taste of USMNT culture alongside World Cup participants in Sebastian Berhalter, Alex Freeman, Gio Reyna, Auston Trusty and Malik Tillman.
“This is the beginning of a fresh start for everyone, and we are excited in these first matches to bring a group of experienced players along with some young talents who have great potential,” Pochettino said.
The United States got off to a promising start at the World Cup with a dominating victory over Paraguay before going through the red-card controversy created when Balogun was ejected from a knockout-round victory over Bosnia and Herzegovina only to be reinstated for the round-of-16 game against Belgium.
The USMNT was eliminated in a lackluster 4-1 loss to Belgium.
“It’s a completely different approach than it was in the past,” Pochettino said of the start to another World Cup cycle. “The World Cup is in four years. We need to work with different objectives and goals.”
(–Field Level Media)
